title: Day 1 — Abdomen, Pelvis & Perineum
description: 80 anatomy MCQs based on the Day 1 study materials.

questions.topic: Abdomen — Anterior Abdominal Wall, Sheath, & Inguinal Region (Q1–Q15)
questions.explanation: The level of the umbilical skin is segmentally supplied by the tenth thoracic nerve (T10), while the xiphoid is T7 and just above the inguinal ligament is L1.
questions.question: Which cutaneous nerve segment supplies the skin immediately around the umbilicus?
questions.imageAlt: Abdomen lecture slides, slide 5 — visual supporting question 1

questions.topic: Abdomen — Anterior Abdominal Wall, Sheath, & Inguinal Region (Q1–Q15)
questions.explanation: In the perineum, the deep membranous layer of superficial fascia (Scarpa's fascia) persists as Colles' fascia, attaching on each side to the pubic arch.
questions.question: In the lower perineum, what is the direct continuation and specialized persistence of Scarpa's fascia called?
questions.imageAlt: Abdomen lecture slides, slide 6 — visual supporting question 2

questions.topic: Abdomen — Anterior Abdominal Wall, Sheath, & Inguinal Region (Q1–Q15)
options: Genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve
questions.explanation: The cremasteric muscle is supplied by the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve, which causes it to elevate the testis.
questions.question: What is the primary nerve supply of the Cremasteric muscle?
questions.imageAlt: Abdomen lecture slides, slide 29 — visual supporting question 3

questions.topic: Abdomen — Anterior Abdominal Wall, Sheath, & Inguinal Region (Q1–Q15)
options: By the aponeurosis of the external oblique alone
By the posterior lamella of the internal oblique and the aponeurosis of the transversus abdominis
questions.explanation: Between the costal margin and the arcuate line, the posterior rectus sheath is formed by the posterior lamella of the internal oblique and the transversus abdominis aponeurosis.
questions.question: Above the arcuate line, how is the posterior wall of the rectus sheath formed?
questions.imageAlt: Abdomen lecture slides, slide 17 — visual supporting question 4

questions.topic: Abdomen — Anterior Abdominal Wall, Sheath, & Inguinal Region (Q1–Q15)
questions.explanation: The arcuate line marks the lowermost limit of the posterior rectus sheath wall, at which level the inferior epigastric vessels enter the rectus sheath.
questions.question: What significant anatomical structure enters the rectus sheath precisely at the level of the arcuate line?
questions.imageAlt: Abdomen lecture slides, slide 17 — visual supporting question 5

questions.topic: Abdomen — Anterior Abdominal Wall, Sheath, & Inguinal Region (Q1–Q15)
options: Medial half of the inguinal ligament
questions.explanation: Hesselbach's triangle is bounded medially by the rectus abdominis, superolaterally by the inferior epigastric artery, and inferiorly by the medial half of the inguinal ligament.
questions.question: Which structure forms the inferior boundary (floor) of Hesselbach's (inguinal) triangle?
questions.imageAlt: Abdomen lecture slides, slide 25 — visual supporting question 6

questions.topic: Abdomen — Anterior Abdominal Wall, Sheath, & Inguinal Region (Q1–Q15)
questions.explanation: Direct inguinal hernias push forward through the weakness of the inguinal (Hesselbach's) triangle, medial to the inferior epigastric vessels.
questions.question: A direct inguinal hernia typically protrudes through which anatomical landmark?
questions.imageAlt: Abdomen lecture slides, slide 25 — visual supporting question 7

questions.topic: Abdomen — Anterior Abdominal Wall, Sheath, & Inguinal Region (Q1–Q15)
questions.explanation: As structures traverse the deep ring in the fascia transversalis, they acquire the internal spermatic fascia.
questions.question: Which layer of the anterior abdominal wall gives rise directly to the internal spermatic fascia of the spermatic cord?
questions.imageAlt: Abdomen lecture slides, slide 31 — visual supporting question 8

questions.topic: Abdomen — Anterior Abdominal Wall, Sheath, & Inguinal Region (Q1–Q15)
options: Anteriorly: external oblique; posteriorly: latissimus dorsi; inferiorly: iliac crest
Anteriorly: rectus abdominis; posteriorly: quadratus lumborum; inferiorly: inguinal ligament
Anteriorly: internal oblique; posteriorly: erector spinae; inferiorly: 12th rib
Superiorly: costal margin; medially: spine; laterally: mid-axillary line
questions.explanation: The lumbar triangle is bounded anteriorly by the posterior border of the external oblique, posteriorly by the lateral border of the latissimus dorsi, and inferiorly by the middle part of the iliac crest.
questions.question: What are the exact boundaries of the lumbar (Petit's) triangle?
questions.imageAlt: Abdomen lecture slides, slide 22 — visual supporting question 9

questions.topic: Abdomen — Anterior Abdominal Wall, Sheath, & Inguinal Region (Q1–Q15)
options: Half an inch above the mid-inguinal point
Midway between the ASIS and pubic symphysis
Directly behind the superficial inguinal ring in adults
questions.explanation: The deep inguinal ring is an opening in the fascia transversalis located half an inch above the mid-inguinal point, just lateral to the inferior epigastric artery.
questions.question: Where is the deep inguinal ring located relative to surface landmarks?
questions.imageAlt: Abdomen lecture slides, slide 26 — visual supporting question 10

questions.topic: Abdomen — Anterior Abdominal Wall, Sheath, & Inguinal Region (Q1–Q15)
options: Fusion of external oblique and internal oblique aponeuroses
Fusion of the lowermost fibers of the internal oblique and transversus abdominis
Lower rolled border of the external oblique aponeurosis
Fusion of rectus abdominis and pyramidalis
questions.explanation: The conjoint tendon is formed by the lowermost arching fibers of the internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles inserting into the pubic crest and pectineal line.
questions.question: Which structure forms the conjoint tendon (falx inguinalis)?
questions.imageAlt: Abdomen lecture slides, slide 24 — visual supporting question 11

questions.topic: Abdomen — Anterior Abdominal Wall, Sheath, & Inguinal Region (Q1–Q15)
questions.explanation: The superficial inguinal ring transmits the spermatic cord (in males) or round ligament (in females), along with the ilioinguinal nerve.
questions.question: Which of the following contents passes through the superficial inguinal ring in the male?
questions.imageAlt: Abdomen lecture slides, slide 21 — visual supporting question 12

questions.topic: Abdomen — Anterior Abdominal Wall, Sheath, & Inguinal Region (Q1–Q15)
questions.explanation: External oblique fibers run downward, forward, and medially; internal oblique fibers run upward, forward, and medially; transversus abdominis fibers run horizontally forward.
questions.question: What is the direction of the fibers of the internal oblique muscle of the anterolateral abdominal wall?
questions.imageAlt: Abdomen lecture slides, slide 14 — visual supporting question 13

questions.topic: Abdomen — Anterior Abdominal Wall, Sheath, & Inguinal Region (Q1–Q15)
questions.explanation: Indirect inguinal hernias enter the inguinal canal via the deep inguinal ring (congenital remnant of the processus vaginalis) and travel down the canal.
questions.question: An indirect inguinal hernia enters the inguinal canal through which opening?
questions.imageAlt: Abdomen lecture slides, slide 26 — visual supporting question 14

questions.topic: Abdomen — Anterior Abdominal Wall, Sheath, & Inguinal Region (Q1–Q15)
questions.explanation: A Spigelian hernia is defined as a hernia occurring through the linea semilunaris.
questions.question: What type of hernia occurs when the sac protrudes through the linea semilunaris?
questions.imageAlt: Abdomen lecture slides, slide 18 — visual supporting question 15

options: Presence of rugae inside the mucosa
questions.explanation: The pylorus is identified by the thickening of the pyloric sphincter, an annular groove, and the prepyloric vein (vein of Mayo) running in front of it.
questions.question: Which anatomical feature helps clinically identify the pylorus of the stomach during surgery?
questions.imageAlt: Abdomen lecture slides, slide 47 — visual supporting question 16

options: Body of the pancreas and left kidney
questions.explanation: The stomach bed includes the transverse colon, transverse mesocolon, pancreas, spleen, splenic artery, left kidney, left suprarenal gland, and left crus of the diaphragm.
questions.question: Which structure forms part of the "stomach bed" (posterior relations separated by the lesser sac)?
questions.imageAlt: Abdomen lecture slides, slide 50 — visual supporting question 17

questions.explanation: The left gastric artery is a direct branch of the coeliac trunk, whereas the right gastric artery typically branches from the hepatic artery.
questions.question: Which arterial branch supplying the lesser curvature of the stomach arises directly from the coeliac trunk?
questions.imageAlt: Abdomen lecture slides, slide 52 — visual supporting question 18

questions.explanation: The transpyloric plane is situated at the level of the L1 body, corresponding to the pylorus of the stomach, fundus of the gallbladder, and neck of the pancreas.
questions.question: At what vertebral level is the transpyloric plane located, marking the position of the pylorus of the stomach?
questions.imageAlt: Abdomen lecture slides, slide 40 — visual supporting question 19

questions.explanation: The duodenum is retroperitoneal except for the first inch of the first part, which has peritoneal attachments from the greater and lesser omentum.
questions.question: Which part of the duodenum is completely invested by peritoneum (free and mobile) for its first inch?
questions.imageAlt: Abdomen lecture slides, slide 58 — visual supporting question 20

questions.explanation: The ampulla of Vater opens into the second part of the duodenum on the posteromedial wall at the summit of the major duodenal papilla.
questions.question: Where do the common bile duct and main pancreatic duct typically open?
questions.imageAlt: Abdomen lecture slides, slide 60 — visual supporting question 21

questions.explanation: The duodenojejunal flexure is anchored to the right crus of the diaphragm by the suspensory muscle.
questions.question: Which structure suspends the duodenojejunal flexure from the right crus of the diaphragm?
questions.imageAlt: Abdomen lecture slides, slide 61 — visual supporting question 22

options: Jejunal walls are thinner and narrower.
Jejunum features numerous prominent circular folds (plicae circulares) and fewer arterial arcades.
Jejunal mesentery contains abundant fat with no windows.
Ileum contains Peyer's patches on its mesenteric border.
questions.explanation: The jejunum has a thicker wall, larger/more numerous plicae circulares, simple arterial arcades (1-2), and less fat in its mesentery compared to the ileum.
questions.question: What anatomical characteristic distinguishes the jejunum from the ileum?
questions.imageAlt: Abdomen lecture slides, slide 66 — visual supporting question 23

options: The antimesenteric border of the lower ileum
The lesser curvature of the stomach
The anterior surface of the liver
questions.explanation: Peyer's patches are large aggregations of lymphoid follicles located in the mucosa along the antimesenteric border of the lower ileum.
questions.question: What are Peyer's patches (aggregate lymphoid nodules) typically found on?
questions.imageAlt: Abdomen lecture slides, slide 67 — visual supporting question 24

questions.explanation: Meckel's diverticulum represents the unobliterated proximal part of the fetal vitellointestinal duct, typically located about 2 feet from the ileocaecal junction.
questions.question: Meckel's diverticulum is an embryological remnant of which structure?
questions.imageAlt: Abdomen lecture slides, slide 67 — visual supporting question 25

questions.explanation: The midgut is supplied by the superior mesenteric artery, originating from the abdominal aorta at the lower border of L1.
questions.question: Which artery supplies the embryonic midgut derivatives (from the lower duodenum to proximal two-thirds of transverse colon)?
questions.imageAlt: Abdomen lecture slides, slide 71 — visual supporting question 26

options: 2% of people, 2 inches long, 2 feet from the ileocaecal junction
2 cm wide, 2 layers thick, 2 days of symptoms
questions.explanation: Meckel's diverticulum occurs in 2% of the population, is about 2 inches long, and lies 2 feet proximal to the ileocaecal junction on the antimesenteric border.
questions.question: What is the classic rule of 2s often associated with Meckel's diverticulum?
questions.imageAlt: Abdomen lecture slides, slide 67 — visual supporting question 27

questions.explanation: Parasympathetic supply to the foregut and midgut is delivered via the vagus nerve (anterior and posterior vagal trunks), whereas hindgut is supplied by pelvic splanchnic nerves.
questions.question: Which nerve provides parasympathetic innervation to the foregut and midgut?
questions.imageAlt: Abdomen lecture slides, slide 55 — visual supporting question 28

questions.topic: Abdomen — Liver, Biliary System, Spleen, & Pancreas (Q29–Q40)
options: Caudate process of the caudate lobe of the liver
Right free margin of the lesser omentum
questions.explanation: The caudate process of the caudate lobe forms the superior boundary of the epiploic (omental) foramen.
questions.question: Which structure forms the upper boundary (roof) of the omental foramen (foramen of Winslow)?
questions.imageAlt: Abdomen lecture slides, slide 86 — visual supporting question 29

questions.topic: Abdomen — Liver, Biliary System, Spleen, & Pancreas (Q29–Q40)
questions.explanation: The liver receives roughly 70% of its blood volume from the portal vein and 30% from the hepatic artery (though oxygen delivery is split evenly at 50/50).
questions.question: What percentage of blood flow to the liver is delivered via the portal vein versus the hepatic artery?
questions.imageAlt: Abdomen lecture slides, slide 93 — visual supporting question 30

questions.topic: Abdomen — Liver, Biliary System, Spleen, & Pancreas (Q29–Q40)
questions.explanation: The ligamentum teres is the obliterated left umbilical vein, running within the free margin of the falciform ligament to the left branch of the portal vein.
questions.question: What anatomical structure represents the obliterated fetal left umbilical vein?
questions.imageAlt: Abdomen lecture slides, slide 86 — visual supporting question 31

questions.topic: Abdomen — Liver, Biliary System, Spleen, & Pancreas (Q29–Q40)
options: Common bile duct, portal vein, and gastroduodenal artery
Cystic duct, common hepatic duct, and inferior surface of the liver (or cystic artery)
Main pancreatic duct and accessory duct
questions.explanation: Calot's cystohepatic triangle is bounded by the cystic duct, common hepatic duct, and the inferior surface of the liver (or right hepatic duct/cystic artery), containing the cystic artery.
questions.question: What structures are contained within Calot's triangle (cystohepatic triangle)?
questions.imageAlt: Abdomen lecture slides, slide 99 — visual supporting question 32

questions.topic: Abdomen — Liver, Biliary System, Spleen, & Pancreas (Q29–Q40)
questions.explanation: The pear-shaped gallbladder has a capacity ranging between 30 and 50 ml.
questions.question: What is the normal physiological capacity of the adult gallbladder?
questions.imageAlt: Abdomen lecture slides, slide 101 — visual supporting question 33

questions.topic: Abdomen — Liver, Biliary System, Spleen, & Pancreas (Q29–Q40)
questions.explanation: The spleen dimensions and features follow: 1 inch thick, 3 inches wide, 5 inches long, 7 ounces in weight, and related to ribs 9–11.
questions.question: The spleen is classically described by the mnemonic of numbers 1, 3, 5, 7, 9–11. What does "7" signify?
questions.imageAlt: Abdomen lecture slides, slide 78 — visual supporting question 34

questions.topic: Abdomen — Liver, Biliary System, Spleen, & Pancreas (Q29–Q40)
questions.explanation: The medial visceral surface of the spleen features impressions for the stomach, left kidney, left colic flexure, and tail of the pancreas.
questions.question: Which surface of the spleen bears the gastric, renal, colic, and pancreatic impressions?
questions.imageAlt: Abdomen lecture slides, slide 81 — visual supporting question 35

questions.topic: Abdomen — Liver, Biliary System, Spleen, & Pancreas (Q29–Q40)
questions.explanation: The disc-like head of the pancreas sits snugly within the C-shaped concavity of the duodenum.
questions.question: Which part of the pancreas lies directly within the concavity of the C-shaped loop of the duodenum?
questions.imageAlt: Abdomen lecture slides, slide 106 — visual supporting question 36

questions.topic: Abdomen — Liver, Biliary System, Spleen, & Pancreas (Q29–Q40)
options: At the minor duodenal papilla (one inch above the major papilla)
questions.explanation: The accessory pancreatic duct opens into the second part of the duodenum at the minor duodenal papilla, roughly one inch proximal/above the major papilla.
questions.question: Where does the accessory pancreatic duct (of Santorini) typically open into the duodenum?
questions.imageAlt: Abdomen lecture slides, slide 104 — visual supporting question 37

questions.topic: Abdomen — Liver, Biliary System, Spleen, & Pancreas (Q29–Q40)
questions.explanation: The portal vein is formed immediately behind the neck of the pancreas by the junction of the superior mesenteric and splenic veins.
questions.question: Behind which specific part of the pancreas is the portal vein formed by the union of the splenic and superior mesenteric veins?
questions.imageAlt: Abdomen lecture slides, slide 74 — visual supporting question 38

questions.topic: Abdomen — Liver, Biliary System, Spleen, & Pancreas (Q29–Q40)
questions.explanation: The splenorenal ligament connects the spleen to the left kidney, carrying the tail of the pancreas and splenic vessels.
questions.question: Which ligament connects the hilum of the spleen to the left kidney and contains the splenic vessels and pancreatic tail?
questions.imageAlt: Abdomen lecture slides, slide 80 — visual supporting question 39

questions.topic: Abdomen — Liver, Biliary System, Spleen, & Pancreas (Q29–Q40)
questions.explanation: The triangular bare area of the liver is bounded by the coronary ligaments and directly apposed to the diaphragm without peritoneal intervention.
questions.question: Which area of the liver is completely devoid of peritoneal covering and directly contacts the diaphragm?
questions.imageAlt: Abdomen lecture slides, slide 88 — visual supporting question 40

questions.topic: Pelvis & Perineum — The Sigmoid Colon & Rectum (Q1–Q11)
questions.explanation: The sigmoid colon begins as a continuation of the descending colon at the pelvic brim and ends at the middle piece of the sacrum (S3), where it becomes the rectum.
questions.question: At which vertebral level does the sigmoid colon typically end and become the rectum?
questions.imageAlt: Pelvis & Perineum lecture slides, slide 2 — visual supporting question 41

questions.topic: Pelvis & Perineum — The Sigmoid Colon & Rectum (Q1–Q11)
options: Shaped as a straight vertical column
questions.explanation: The root of the sigmoid mesocolon is shaped as an inverted V, attached to the left external iliac artery (left limb) and to the sacrum until the 3rd piece by the right limb.
questions.question: What is the shape of the root of the sigmoid mesocolon attached to the posterior pelvic wall?
questions.imageAlt: Pelvis & Perineum lecture slides, slide 3 — visual supporting question 42

questions.topic: Pelvis & Perineum — The Sigmoid Colon & Rectum (Q1–Q11)
questions.explanation: The rectum is about 5 inches (13 cm) long, following the curve of the sacrum and coccyx.
questions.question: What is the normal length of the adult human rectum?
questions.imageAlt: Pelvis & Perineum lecture slides, slide 5 — visual supporting question 43

questions.topic: Pelvis & Perineum — The Sigmoid Colon & Rectum (Q1–Q11)
questions.explanation: The puborectalis part of the levator ani forms a U-shaped sling that pulls the anorectal junction forward, creating an acute anorectal angle.
questions.question: Which part of the levator ani muscle forms a sling around the anorectal junction to create the anorectal angle?
questions.imageAlt: Pelvis & Perineum lecture slides, slide 20 — visual supporting question 44

questions.topic: Pelvis & Perineum — The Sigmoid Colon & Rectum (Q1–Q11)
options: Two folds on the right and one on the left
Two folds on the left and one on the right
Two folds anteriorly and two posteriorly
Three folds exclusively on the left side
questions.explanation: The mucosa and circular muscle form 3 transverse folds: two at the left wall (upper and lower) and one at the right wall (middle).
questions.question: How many transverse folds (valves of Houston) are typically present in the rectum, and how are they distributed?
questions.imageAlt: Pelvis & Perineum lecture slides, slide 5 — visual supporting question 45

questions.topic: Pelvis & Perineum — The Sigmoid Colon & Rectum (Q1–Q11)
options: Covered completely on front and sides
Covered entirely by the pelvic mesocolon
questions.explanation: The upper 1/3 of the rectum is covered on front and sides, the middle 1/3 on the front only, and the lower 1/3 is not covered by peritoneum.
questions.question: What is the peritoneal covering of the lower one-third of the rectum?
questions.imageAlt: Pelvis & Perineum lecture slides, slide 6 — visual supporting question 46

questions.topic: Pelvis & Perineum — The Sigmoid Colon & Rectum (Q1–Q11)
options: Superior rectal artery (single branch from the inferior mesenteric artery)
questions.explanation: The superior rectal artery is a single branch from the inferior mesenteric artery supplying the upper part.
questions.question: Which artery supplies the upper third of the rectum?
questions.imageAlt: Pelvis & Perineum lecture slides, slide 7 — visual supporting question 47

questions.topic: Pelvis & Perineum — The Sigmoid Colon & Rectum (Q1–Q11)
options: Inferior mesenteric vein -> Splenic vein -> Portal vein
Internal pudendal vein -> Common iliac vein
questions.explanation: The superior rectal vein drains into the inferior mesenteric vein, which joins the splenic and portal systems.
questions.question: Where does venous blood from the superior rectal vein ultimately drain?
questions.imageAlt: Pelvis & Perineum lecture slides, slide 7 — visual supporting question 48

questions.topic: Pelvis & Perineum — The Sigmoid Colon & Rectum (Q1–Q11)
questions.explanation: The rectum and upper anal canal are supplied by autonomic nerves from the inferior hypogastric plexuses and are only sensitive to stretch.
questions.question: What is the primary sensory modality to which the rectum and upper anal canal respond?
questions.imageAlt: Pelvis & Perineum lecture slides, slide 8 — visual supporting question 49

questions.topic: Pelvis & Perineum — The Sigmoid Colon & Rectum (Q1–Q11)
options: Urinary bladder base, seminal vesicles, and ampulla of the vas
Posterior surface of the vagina and uterus
questions.explanation: In males, the lower 2/3 of the anterior rectum relates to the base of the urinary bladder, seminal vesicles, and the ampulla of the vas deferens.
questions.question: In the male, what structures are directly related to the anterior surface of the lower 2/3 of the rectum?
questions.imageAlt: Pelvis & Perineum lecture slides, slide 8 — visual supporting question 50

questions.topic: Pelvis & Perineum — The Sigmoid Colon & Rectum (Q1–Q11)
options: Pararectal lymph nodes -> Inferior mesenteric lymph nodes
questions.explanation: Pararectal lymph nodes receive lymph from the rectum and channel it to the inferior mesenteric lymph nodes.
questions.question: Lymph from the upper and middle parts of the rectum drains primarily into which lymph nodes?
questions.imageAlt: Pelvis & Perineum lecture slides, slide 7 — visual supporting question 51

questions.explanation: When full, the urinary bladder is oval with a maximum capacity in the adult of 500 ml or more.
questions.question: What is the maximum physiological capacity of the adult urinary bladder when full?
questions.imageAlt: Pelvis & Perineum lecture slides, slide 10 — visual supporting question 52

options: Because it is lined by pseudostratified columnar epithelium
Because it lacks a muscular coat entirely
Because it is composed of elastic tissue and firmly attached to the muscular coat
Because it is covered by a thick layer of peritoneum
questions.explanation: The trigone remains smooth because it is composed of elastic tissue firmly anchored to the underlying muscle, preventing the formation of rugae.
questions.question: Why is the mucosal surface of the trigone of the bladder characteristically smooth?
questions.imageAlt: Pelvis & Perineum lecture slides, slide 10 — visual supporting question 53

options: Superior vesical artery (from the umbilical artery)
questions.explanation: The superior vesical artery branches from the obliterated umbilical artery to supply the bladder.
questions.question: Which vessels provide arterial blood to the upper parts of the urinary bladder?
questions.imageAlt: Pelvis & Perineum lecture slides, slide 11 — visual supporting question 54

questions.explanation: Parasympathetic innervation to the bladder originates from spinal segments S2, 3, and 4 via pelvic splanchnic nerves.
questions.question: What nerve fibers provide parasympathetic innervation responsible for emptying the bladder (detrusor contraction)?
questions.imageAlt: Pelvis & Perineum lecture slides, slide 12 — visual supporting question 55

questions.explanation: In females, the peritoneum reflects from the bladder to the uterus, forming the uterovesical pouch.
questions.question: Which peritoneal pouch is formed behind the urinary bladder in the female?
questions.imageAlt: Pelvis & Perineum lecture slides, slide 11 — visual supporting question 56

questions.explanation: Veins from the bladder form the vesical venous plexus, communicating with the prostatic plexus and draining into the internal iliac vein.
questions.question: The vesical venous plexus of the bladder drains directly into which major veins?
questions.imageAlt: Pelvis & Perineum lecture slides, slide 12 — visual supporting question 57

questions.explanation: The interureteric crest forms the upper boundary of the trigone, stretching between the two ureteric orifices.
questions.question: What is the transverse mucosal ridge connecting the two ureteric orifices on the interior of the bladder base called?
questions.imageAlt: Pelvis & Perineum lecture slides, slide 10 — visual supporting question 58

questions.topic: Pelvis & Perineum — The Anal Canal, Ischiorectal Fossa, & Pudendal Canal (Q19–Q30)
questions.explanation: The anal canal is about 4 cm (1.5 inches) long, extending from the anorectal junction to the anus.
questions.question: What is the typical length of the adult human anal canal?
questions.imageAlt: Pelvis & Perineum lecture slides, slide 15 — visual supporting question 59

questions.topic: Pelvis & Perineum — The Anal Canal, Ischiorectal Fossa, & Pudendal Canal (Q19–Q30)
options: Ectoderm of proctodeum; stratified squamous epithelium
Endoderm of hindgut; columnar epithelium forming anal columns
questions.explanation: The upper half originates from hindgut endoderm, is lined by columnar epithelium with anal columns (of Morgagni), and is sensitive to stretch.
questions.question: What is the embryological origin and epithelial lining of the upper half of the anal canal?
questions.imageAlt: Pelvis & Perineum lecture slides, slide 22 — visual supporting question 60

questions.topic: Pelvis & Perineum — The Anal Canal, Ischiorectal Fossa, & Pudendal Canal (Q19–Q30)
questions.explanation: The pectinate (dentate) line corresponds to the site of anal valves and the embryonic cloacal membrane.
questions.question: What anatomical structure marks the junction between the upper and lower halves of the anal canal (site of anal valves/embryologic cloacal membrane)?
questions.imageAlt: Pelvis & Perineum lecture slides, slide 21 — visual supporting question 61

questions.topic: Pelvis & Perineum — The Anal Canal, Ischiorectal Fossa, & Pudendal Canal (Q19–Q30)
options: Thickening of the outer longitudinal smooth muscle layer
Thickening of the inner circular layer of smooth muscle (upper 2/3)
Striated skeletal muscle from levator ani
questions.explanation: The internal sphincter is an involuntary thickening of the inner circular smooth muscle layer covering the upper 2/3 of the anal canal.
questions.question: Which muscle forms the internal sphincter of the anal canal?
questions.imageAlt: Pelvis & Perineum lecture slides, slide 17 — visual supporting question 62

questions.topic: Pelvis & Perineum — The Anal Canal, Ischiorectal Fossa, & Pudendal Canal (Q19–Q30)
questions.explanation: The external sphincter is skeletal muscle divided into subcutaneous, superficial, and deep parts.
questions.question: How many distinct parts make up the voluntary external anal sphincter?
questions.imageAlt: Pelvis & Perineum lecture slides, slide 18 — visual supporting question 63

questions.topic: Pelvis & Perineum — The Anal Canal, Ischiorectal Fossa, & Pudendal Canal (Q19–Q30)
options: Internal sphincter, deep part of external sphincter, and puborectalis muscle
Subcutaneous sphincter and superficial sphincter only
Transversus perinei muscles and perineal body
questions.explanation: The anorectal ring is a palpable muscular ring formed by the union of the internal sphincter, deep external sphincter, and puborectalis.
questions.question: What structures combine to form the clinically important "anorectal ring"?
questions.imageAlt: Pelvis & Perineum lecture slides, slide 20 — visual supporting question 64

questions.topic: Pelvis & Perineum — The Anal Canal, Ischiorectal Fossa, & Pudendal Canal (Q19–Q30)
options: Inferior rectal nerve (branch of pudendal nerve, somatic)
questions.explanation: The lower half of the anal canal is somatic and supplied by the inferior rectal nerve, making it sensitive to pain, touch, and temperature.
questions.question: What is the sensory nerve supply of the lower half of the anal canal and perianal skin?
questions.imageAlt: Pelvis & Perineum lecture slides, slide 18 — visual supporting question 65

questions.topic: Pelvis & Perineum — The Anal Canal, Ischiorectal Fossa, & Pudendal Canal (Q19–Q30)
options: Obturator internus muscle and pudendal canal
Levator ani muscle and anal canal
questions.explanation: The medial wall of the ischiorectal fossa is formed by the levator ani and anal canal, while the lateral wall is formed by the obturator internus and pudendal canal.
questions.question: What structures form the anatomical boundaries of the ischiorectal (ischioanal) fossa medially?
questions.imageAlt: Pelvis & Perineum lecture slides, slide 25 — visual supporting question 66

questions.topic: Pelvis & Perineum — The Anal Canal, Ischiorectal Fossa, & Pudendal Canal (Q19–Q30)
options: A splitting of the obturator fascia
A gap between the levator ani and coccygeus
The attachment of the perineal membrane
A tunnel within the sacrotuberous ligament
questions.explanation: The pudendal canal is a tunnel formed within the obturator fascia on the lateral wall of the ischiorectal fossa.
questions.question: What is the pudendal canal (Alcock's canal) formed by?
questions.imageAlt: Pelvis & Perineum lecture slides, slide 27 — visual supporting question 67

questions.topic: Pelvis & Perineum — The Anal Canal, Ischiorectal Fossa, & Pudendal Canal (Q19–Q30)
options: Internal pudendal vessels and pudendal nerve
questions.explanation: The pudendal canal contains the internal pudendal vessels and the pudendal nerve.
questions.question: Which major vascular and neural structures are enclosed within the pudendal canal?
questions.imageAlt: Pelvis & Perineum lecture slides, slide 28 — visual supporting question 68

questions.topic: Pelvis & Perineum — The Anal Canal, Ischiorectal Fossa, & Pudendal Canal (Q19–Q30)
options: Superficial part of the external anal sphincter
questions.explanation: The perineal body is formed by the superficial part of the external anal sphincter, anterior fibers of levator ani, deep and superficial transversus perinei, and bulbospongiosus.
questions.question: Which of the following muscles contributes directly to the formation of the central "perineal body"?
questions.imageAlt: Pelvis & Perineum lecture slides, slide 23 — visual supporting question 69

questions.topic: Pelvis & Perineum — The Anal Canal, Ischiorectal Fossa, & Pudendal Canal (Q19–Q30)
options: Medial group of superficial inguinal lymph nodes
questions.explanation: Lymph from the lower half of the anal canal drains into the medial group of superficial inguinal lymph nodes.
questions.question: Where does lymphatic drainage from the lower half of the anal canal primarily go?
questions.imageAlt: Pelvis & Perineum lecture slides, slide 22 — visual supporting question 70

questions.explanation: A direct inguinal hernia protrudes through Hesselbach’s triangle, medial to the inferior epigastric vessels. An indirect hernia enters the deep inguinal ring lateral to these vessels.
questions.question: A patient has an inguinal hernia that passes medial to the inferior epigastric vessels. Which type is most likely?
questions.imageAlt: Abdomen lecture slides, slide 25 — visual supporting question 71

questions.explanation: The external oblique aponeurosis forms the anterior wall of the inguinal canal along its length; the internal oblique reinforces it laterally.
questions.question: Which structure forms the anterior wall of the inguinal canal throughout its length?
questions.imageAlt: Abdomen lecture slides, slide 26 — visual supporting question 72

questions.explanation: The coeliac trunk supplies the foregut. The superior mesenteric artery supplies the midgut, and the inferior mesenteric artery supplies the hindgut.
questions.question: Which artery is the principal arterial supply to the foregut?
questions.imageAlt: Abdomen lecture slides, slide 70 — visual supporting question 73

options: Thinner wall, more mesenteric fat, and many arterial arcades
Thicker wall, prominent circular folds, and fewer arterial arcades
Peyer’s patches concentrated on the mesenteric border
Short vasa recta and a narrow lumen
questions.explanation: The jejunum generally has a thicker wall, more prominent plicae circulares, fewer arterial arcades, longer vasa recta, and less mesenteric fat than the ileum.
questions.question: Compared with the ileum, which combination is typical of the jejunum?
questions.imageAlt: Abdomen lecture slides, slide 66 — visual supporting question 74

questions.explanation: The cystic artery usually traverses the cystohepatic triangle, a key anatomical region used to identify structures during gallbladder surgery.
questions.question: During cholecystectomy, which artery is usually sought within the cystohepatic (Calot’s) triangle?
questions.imageAlt: Abdomen lecture slides, slide 99 — visual supporting question 75

questions.explanation: The upper third of the rectum is covered anteriorly and laterally; the middle third is covered anteriorly only, and the lower third has no peritoneal covering.
questions.question: Which part of the rectum is covered by peritoneum on its anterior and lateral surfaces?
questions.imageAlt: Pelvis & Perineum lecture slides, slide 6 — visual supporting question 76

questions.explanation: The lower anal canal is supplied somatically by the inferior rectal nerve, a branch of the pudendal nerve, and is sensitive to pain, touch, and temperature.
questions.question: A painful lesion below the pectinate line is most likely to have somatic sensory innervation from which nerve?
questions.imageAlt: Pelvis & Perineum lecture slides, slide 18 — visual supporting question 77

options: Parasympathetic pelvic splanchnic fibers from S2–S4
Somatic fibers in the pudendal nerve
questions.explanation: Parasympathetic fibers from S2–S4 travel via pelvic splanchnic nerves and promote detrusor contraction during micturition.
questions.question: Which autonomic pathway contracts the detrusor muscle during bladder emptying?
questions.imageAlt: Pelvis & Perineum lecture slides, slide 11 — visual supporting question 78

questions.explanation: Puborectalis forms a sling around the anorectal junction and pulls it forward, helping maintain the anorectal angle and continence.
questions.question: Weakness of which muscle would most directly reduce the forward pull that maintains the anorectal angle?
questions.imageAlt: Pelvis & Perineum lecture slides, slide 20 — visual supporting question 79

options: Internal is skeletal and voluntary; external is smooth and involuntary
Internal is smooth muscle and involuntary; external is skeletal muscle and voluntary
Both are smooth muscle and involuntary
Both are skeletal muscle and voluntary
questions.explanation: The internal anal sphincter is a thickening of the circular smooth muscle layer and is involuntary. The external anal sphincter is skeletal muscle under voluntary control.
questions.question: Which statement best distinguishes the internal anal sphincter from the external anal sphincter?
questions.imageAlt: Pelvis & Perineum lecture slides, slide 17 — visual supporting question 80

title: Day 2 — Upper Limb, Lower Limb & Thorax (Breast)
description: 80 anatomy MCQs: 30 Upper Limb, 30 Lower Limb, and 20 Thorax questions. Thorax coverage is limited to the available Breast lecture slides.

references.label: Upper Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics lecture slides PDF
Lower Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics lecture slides PDF
The Breast lecture slides PDF (Thorax scope)

questions.question: Which structures pass through the quadrangular space?
options: Axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral vessels
Radial nerve and profunda brachii vessels
Ulnar nerve and superior ulnar collateral artery
questions.explanation: The quadrangular space transmits the axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral vessels.
questions.imageAlt: Upper Limb lecture slides, slide 18, supporting question 1
questions.sourceRef: The Upper Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf, PDF page 18
questions.sourceEvidence: Contents: axillary nerve & posterior circumflex humeral vessels.

questions.question: Which vessels traverse the upper triangular space?
questions.explanation: The upper triangular space contains the circumflex scapular vessels.
questions.imageAlt: Upper Limb lecture slides, slide 19, supporting question 2
questions.sourceRef: The Upper Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf, PDF page 19
questions.sourceEvidence: Contents: circumflex scapular vessels.

questions.question: A nerve and artery pass through the lower triangular space to the posterior arm. Which pair is it?
options: Axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery
Radial nerve and profunda brachii vessels
Musculocutaneous nerve and lateral thoracic artery
questions.explanation: The lower triangular space transmits the radial nerve and profunda brachii vessels.
questions.imageAlt: Upper Limb lecture slides, slide 20, supporting question 3
questions.sourceRef: The Upper Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf, PDF page 20
questions.sourceEvidence: Contents: radial nerve & profunda brachii vessels.

questions.question: Which superficial veins arise from the dorsal venous arch of the hand?
options: Median cubital medially and brachial laterally
questions.explanation: The dorsal venous arch gives rise to the basilic vein medially and cephalic vein laterally.
questions.imageAlt: Upper Limb lecture slides, slide 23, supporting question 4
questions.sourceRef: The Upper Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf, PDF page 23
questions.sourceEvidence: It gives 1. basilic vein medially and 2. cephalic vein laterally.

questions.question: Where does the basilic vein pierce the deep fascia?
options: At the middle of the arm
At the lower border of teres major
questions.explanation: The basilic vein ascends medially and pierces deep fascia at the middle of the arm.
questions.imageAlt: Upper Limb lecture slides, slide 24, supporting question 5
questions.sourceRef: The Upper Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf, PDF page 24
questions.sourceEvidence: Pierces deep fascia at the middle of arm.

questions.question: Which course and termination characterize the cephalic vein?
options: Medial forearm and arm, then joins axillary vein at teres major
Lateral forearm and arm, through deltopectoral groove and clavipectoral fascia, into axillary vein
Runs with ulnar artery and ends in brachial vein
Passes through the cubital fossa to become subclavian vein
questions.explanation: The cephalic vein ascends laterally, enters the deltopectoral groove, pierces clavipectoral fascia, and drains into the axillary vein.
questions.imageAlt: Upper Limb lecture slides, slide 25, supporting question 6
questions.sourceRef: The Upper Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf, PDF page 25
questions.sourceEvidence: Entering into deltopectoral groove, piercing the clavipectoral fascia. Ends by draining into axillary vein.

questions.question: At what point does the axillary vein become the subclavian vein?
options: At the lower border of teres major
At the upper border of pectoralis minor
At the lateral border of the first rib
At the medial border of the first rib
questions.explanation: The axillary vein continues as the subclavian vein at the lateral border of the first rib.
questions.imageAlt: Upper Limb lecture slides, slide 26, supporting question 7
questions.sourceRef: The Upper Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf, PDF page 26
questions.sourceEvidence: Ends by becoming subclavian vein at lateral (outer) border of first rib.

questions.question: Which nodes receive lymph from the medial side of the hand and forearm before sending efferents toward the axillary nodes?
questions.explanation: Supratrochlear nodes receive afferents from the medial hand and forearm and send efferents to lateral axillary nodes.
questions.imageAlt: Upper Limb lecture slides, slide 31, supporting question 8
questions.sourceRef: The Upper Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf, PDF page 31
questions.sourceEvidence: Receives afferent from medial side of hand & forearm. Sends efferent to lateral axillary LN.

questions.question: Which axillary lymph-node group receives afferents from the anterior, posterior, and lateral groups?
questions.explanation: The central group receives afferents from the anterior, posterior, and lateral axillary groups.
questions.imageAlt: Upper Limb lecture slides, slide 34, supporting question 9
questions.sourceRef: The Upper Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf, PDF page 34
questions.sourceEvidence: Receives afferent from anterior, posterior & lateral groups.

questions.question: Which landmark divides the axillary artery into three parts?
questions.explanation: Pectoralis minor divides the axillary artery into three parts, with the second part deep to the muscle.
questions.imageAlt: Upper Limb lecture slides, slide 38, supporting question 10
questions.sourceRef: The Upper Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf, PDF page 38
questions.sourceEvidence: Axillary artery is divided into 3 parts by pectoralis minor.

questions.question: Which branch arises from the second part of the axillary artery?
questions.explanation: The second part gives the lateral thoracic and thoracoacromial arteries.
questions.imageAlt: Upper Limb lecture slides, slide 39, supporting question 11
questions.sourceRef: The Upper Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf, PDF page 39
questions.sourceEvidence: 2nd part gives: lateral thoracic artery; thoracoacromial artery.

questions.question: Which artery is a branch of the subscapular artery and reaches the infraspinous fossa?
questions.explanation: The subscapular artery gives the circumflex scapular artery, which supplies the infraspinous fossa.
questions.imageAlt: Upper Limb lecture slides, slide 43, supporting question 12
questions.sourceRef: The Upper Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf, PDF page 43
questions.sourceEvidence: Subscapular artery gives circumflex scapular to infraspinous fossa.

questions.question: Which arterial connection contributes to the scapular anastomosis between the subclavian and axillary systems?
options: Suprascapular artery with circumflex scapular branch of subscapular artery
Anterior circumflex humeral artery with inferior ulnar collateral artery
Superior thoracic artery with radial recurrent artery
Thoracoacromial artery with profunda brachii artery
questions.explanation: The lecture describes a scapular anastomosis linking the subclavian suprascapular artery with axillary subscapular/circumflex scapular branches.
questions.imageAlt: Upper Limb lecture slides, slide 44, supporting question 13
questions.sourceRef: The Upper Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf, PDF page 44
questions.sourceEvidence: Branches from subclavian: suprascapular artery; branches from axillary: subscapular artery and its circumflex scapular branch.

questions.question: Where do the anterior and posterior circumflex humeral arteries anastomose?
options: Around the surgical neck of the humerus
Around the anatomical neck of the radius
questions.explanation: Both circumflex humeral arteries are third-part axillary branches and anastomose around the surgical neck.
questions.imageAlt: Upper Limb lecture slides, slide 45, supporting question 14
questions.sourceRef: The Upper Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf, PDF page 45
questions.sourceEvidence: Both are branches of 3rd part axillary artery, anastomose around surgical neck of humerus.

questions.question: Which spinal nerve roots form the brachial plexus?
questions.explanation: The brachial plexus is formed by the ventral primary rami of C5, C6, C7, C8, and T1.
questions.imageAlt: Upper Limb lecture slides, slide 47, supporting question 15
questions.sourceRef: The Upper Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf, PDF page 47
questions.sourceEvidence: Roots of brachial plexus: ventral primary rami of C5.6.7.8 and T1 nerves.

questions.question: The posterior cord of the brachial plexus is formed by which divisions?
options: Anterior divisions of upper and middle trunks
Anterior division of the lower trunk only
Posterior divisions of upper and middle trunks only
Posterior divisions of all three trunks
questions.explanation: The posterior cord is formed by the union of the posterior divisions of all three trunks.
questions.imageAlt: Upper Limb lecture slides, slide 48, supporting question 16
questions.sourceRef: The Upper Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf, PDF page 48
questions.sourceEvidence: Posterior cord: union of posterior divisions of the 3 trunks.

questions.question: Which nerve arises directly from the C5 root and supplies the rhomboids?
questions.explanation: The dorsal scapular nerve arises from the C5 root and supplies levator scapulae and both rhomboids.
questions.imageAlt: Upper Limb lecture slides, slide 55, supporting question 17
questions.sourceRef: The Upper Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf, PDF page 55
questions.sourceEvidence: Arise from C5 root ... Supplies levator scapulae, rhomboid minor & major.

questions.topic: Upper Limb — Major nerves and injuries
questions.question: A fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus may injure which nerve, causing deltoid weakness and sensory loss over the lower deltoid region?
questions.explanation: The axillary nerve is vulnerable at the surgical neck; injury weakens deltoid and causes sensory loss over the lower deltoid area.
questions.imageAlt: Upper Limb lecture slides, slide 65, supporting question 18
questions.sourceRef: The Upper Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf, PDF page 65
questions.sourceEvidence: Fracture of surgical neck ... paralysis of deltoid & teres minor ... loss of sensation over lower part of deltoid.

questions.topic: Upper Limb — Major nerves and injuries
questions.question: An upper-trunk (C5–C6) brachial plexus injury classically produces which posture?
options: Adducted arm, extended elbow, and pronated forearm
Ape-like hand with loss of thumb opposition
questions.explanation: Erb palsy from upper-trunk injury produces the described 'waiter's tip' posture.
questions.imageAlt: Upper Limb lecture slides, slide 66, supporting question 19
questions.sourceRef: The Upper Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf, PDF page 66
questions.sourceEvidence: Arm hangs by side, adducted; extended elbow, pronated forearm.

questions.topic: Upper Limb — Major nerves and injuries
questions.question: Which nerve injury is associated with winging of the scapula due to serratus anterior paralysis?
questions.explanation: Long thoracic nerve injury paralyzes serratus anterior, producing a winged scapula.
questions.imageAlt: Upper Limb lecture slides, slide 64, supporting question 20
questions.sourceRef: The Upper Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf, PDF page 64
questions.sourceEvidence: Paralysis of serr. ant. ... → winged scapula.

questions.question: Which nerve pierces coracobrachialis and then descends between biceps and brachialis?
questions.explanation: The musculocutaneous nerve pierces coracobrachialis and runs between biceps and brachialis.
questions.imageAlt: Upper Limb lecture slides, slide 56, supporting question 21
questions.sourceRef: The Upper Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf, PDF page 56
questions.sourceEvidence: Enters the arm by piercing coracobrachialis ... descends between biceps & brachialis.

questions.topic: Upper Limb — Radial nerve terminal branches
questions.question: Which cutaneous area is supplied by the superficial radial branch of the radial nerve?
options: The lateral two-thirds of the dorsum of the hand and proximal phalanges of the lateral 3½ fingers
The medial one-third of the palmar and dorsal hand
The posterior forearm skin from the elbow to the wrist
The palmar surfaces of the lateral 3½ fingers
questions.explanation: The lecture describes the superficial radial branch as cutaneous, supplying the lateral two-thirds of the dorsum of the hand and the proximal phalanges of the lateral 3½ fingers.
questions.imageAlt: Upper Limb lecture slides, slide 113, supporting question 22
questions.sourceRef: The Upper Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf, PDF page 113
questions.sourceEvidence: Supply skin of lateral 2/3 of dorsum of hand & dorsum of proximal phalanges of lateral 3 1/2 fingers.

questions.question: Which nerve supplies the skin over the back of the forearm from elbow to wrist?
questions.explanation: The posterior cutaneous nerve of the forearm, a radial nerve branch, supplies the posterior forearm skin.
questions.imageAlt: Upper Limb lecture slides, slide 95, supporting question 23
questions.sourceRef: The Upper Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf, PDF page 95
questions.sourceEvidence: Branch of radial nerve. Supplies skin of back of forearm (from elbow to wrist).

questions.question: On the palmar surface of the hand, which nerve supplies the medial one and a half fingers?
questions.explanation: The ulnar nerve supplies palmar and dorsal sensation to the medial one and a half fingers.
questions.imageAlt: Upper Limb lecture slides, slide 96, supporting question 24
questions.sourceRef: The Upper Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf, PDF page 96
questions.sourceEvidence: Ulnar N. (medial 1 1/2 fingers) palmar & dorsal.

questions.question: Through which passage does the median nerve enter the hand?
options: Guyon canal superficial to flexor retinaculum
Ulnar canal deep to flexor retinaculum
Carpal tunnel deep to flexor retinaculum
questions.explanation: The median nerve enters the hand through the carpal tunnel, deep to the flexor retinaculum.
questions.imageAlt: Upper Limb lecture slides, slide 101, supporting question 25
questions.sourceRef: The Upper Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf, PDF page 101
questions.sourceEvidence: Enters the hand through carpal tunnel, deep to flexor retinaculum.

questions.question: Which muscles receive motor supply from the anterior interosseous nerve according to the lecture?
options: Thenar muscles and first two lumbricals
Flexor pollicis longus, pronator quadratus, and lateral half of flexor digitorum profundus
All interossei and medial two lumbricals
Flexor carpi ulnaris and medial half of flexor digitorum profundus
questions.explanation: The anterior interosseous branch supplies flexor pollicis longus, pronator quadratus, and the lateral half of flexor digitorum profundus.
questions.imageAlt: Upper Limb lecture slides, slide 102, supporting question 26
questions.sourceRef: The Upper Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf, PDF page 102
questions.sourceEvidence: Muscular to FPL, PQ and lateral 1/2 of FDP.

questions.question: In the upper two-thirds of the forearm, between which muscles does the ulnar nerve descend?
options: Flexor carpi radialis and flexor digitorum superficialis
Flexor carpi ulnaris and flexor digitorum profundus
Pronator teres and flexor pollicis longus
questions.explanation: The ulnar nerve lies between flexor carpi ulnaris above and flexor digitorum profundus below in the upper two-thirds of the forearm.
questions.imageAlt: Upper Limb lecture slides, slide 109, supporting question 27
questions.sourceRef: The Upper Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf, PDF page 109
questions.sourceEvidence: Lies between FCU (above) and FDP (below) in upper 2/3 forearm.

questions.question: Which structure is described as entering the clavipectoral fascia?
questions.explanation: The cephalic vein enters the clavipectoral fascia; the lateral pectoral nerve and thoraco-acromial artery are described as passing out through it.
questions.imageAlt: Upper Limb lecture slides, slide 6, supporting question 28
questions.sourceRef: The Upper Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf, PDF page 6
questions.sourceEvidence: Cephalic vein (drains into axillary vein) — entering fascia.

questions.question: Which set of structures does the lecture list in the deltopectoral groove?
options: Cephalic vein, deltoid branch of thoracoacromial artery, and deltopectoral lymph nodes
Basilic vein, lateral thoracic artery, and central axillary nodes
Axillary artery, cords of the brachial plexus, and axillary vein
Suprascapular nerve, suprascapular artery, and circumflex scapular vessels
questions.explanation: The groove between deltoid and pectoralis major contains the cephalic vein, deltoid branch of the thoracoacromial artery, and deltopectoral (infraclavicular) lymph nodes.
questions.imageAlt: Upper Limb lecture slides, slide 7, supporting question 29
questions.sourceRef: The Upper Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf, PDF page 7
questions.sourceEvidence: Deltopectoral groove: a groove between deltoid & pectoralis major, it contains: 1. deltoid branch of thoracoacromial artery. 2. cephalic vein (uppermost part). 3. delto-pectoral (infraclavicular) lymph nodes.

questions.question: At the suprascapular notch, how does the suprascapular nerve pass relative to the ligament?
options: Above the suprascapular ligament, with the artery below it
Below the suprascapular ligament, while the artery passes above it
Through the ligament together with the artery
Around the inferior border of the ligament, separate from the artery
questions.explanation: The suprascapular nerve passes below the suprascapular ligament, whereas the suprascapular artery passes above it.
questions.imageAlt: Upper Limb lecture slides, slide 58, supporting question 30
questions.sourceRef: The Upper Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf, PDF page 58
questions.sourceEvidence: Runs through suprascapular notch [below the suprascapular ligament] ... It passes together with suprascapular artery but the artery runs above suprascapular ligament.

questions.question: Which structure passes through the greater sciatic foramen superior to piriformis?
questions.explanation: The superior gluteal neurovascular bundle passes above piriformis; the other listed structures pass below it.
questions.imageAlt: Lower Limb lecture slides, slide 7, supporting question 31
questions.sourceRef: The Lower Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf, PDF page 7
questions.sourceEvidence: Superior gluteal nerve & vessels pass above piriformis; others below it in GSF.

questions.topic: Lower Limb — Cutaneous nerves of buttock
questions.question: Which nerve supplies the lower medial quadrant of the buttock?
options: Inferior cluneal branches of posterior cutaneous nerve of thigh
questions.explanation: The posterior cutaneous nerve of the thigh gives inferior cluneal branches to the lower medial quadrant.
questions.imageAlt: Lower Limb lecture slides, slide 4, supporting question 32
questions.sourceRef: The Lower Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf, PDF page 4
questions.sourceEvidence: Lower medial quadrant: branches of posterior cut. nerve of thigh — inferior cluneal.

questions.topic: Lower Limb — Cutaneous nerves of thigh
questions.question: Which nerve supplies the small cutaneous area over the medial aspect of the thigh?
questions.explanation: The lecture assigns a small area of medial-thigh skin to the obturator nerve.
questions.imageAlt: Lower Limb lecture slides, slide 13, supporting question 33
questions.sourceRef: The Lower Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf, PDF page 13
questions.sourceEvidence: Obturator nerve: supplies small area over medial aspect of the thigh.

questions.question: From which part of the dorsal venous arch does the great saphenous vein begin?
questions.explanation: The great saphenous vein begins at the medial end of the dorsal venous arch.
questions.imageAlt: Lower Limb lecture slides, slide 20, supporting question 34
questions.sourceRef: The Lower Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf, PDF page 20
questions.sourceEvidence: Great saphenous vein beginning: from medial end of dorsal venous arch.

questions.question: Where does the small saphenous vein typically terminate?
questions.explanation: The small saphenous vein ascends posteriorly and drains into the popliteal vein.
questions.imageAlt: Lower Limb lecture slides, slide 22, supporting question 35
questions.sourceRef: The Lower Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf, PDF page 22
questions.sourceEvidence: Small saphenous vein end: by draining into popliteal vein.

questions.question: The vertical group of superficial inguinal lymph nodes lies along which structure?
options: Terminal part of the great saphenous vein
questions.explanation: The vertical superficial inguinal group follows the terminal part of the great saphenous vein.
questions.imageAlt: Lower Limb lecture slides, slide 26, supporting question 36
questions.sourceRef: The Lower Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf, PDF page 26
questions.sourceEvidence: Vertical group: lies along terminal part of great saphenous vein.

questions.topic: Lower Limb — Femoral sheath and canal
questions.question: Which structure is outside the femoral sheath?
questions.explanation: The sheath encloses the femoral vessels and canal, while the femoral nerve lies outside it.
questions.imageAlt: Lower Limb lecture slides, slide 31, supporting question 37
questions.sourceRef: The Lower Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf, PDF page 31
questions.sourceEvidence: Fascia surrounds femoral vessels (femoral N. outside F. sheath).

questions.question: What forms the medial boundary of the femoral triangle?
questions.explanation: The femoral triangle is bounded medially by the medial border of adductor longus.
questions.imageAlt: Lower Limb lecture slides, slide 34, supporting question 38
questions.sourceRef: The Lower Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf, PDF page 34
questions.sourceEvidence: Boundaries: superior inguinal ligament; laterally medial border sartorius; medially medial border adductor longus.

questions.question: Which nerve is a content of the adductor canal?
questions.explanation: The canal contains the saphenous nerve along with vessels and additional nerve branches.
questions.imageAlt: Lower Limb lecture slides, slide 37, supporting question 39
questions.sourceRef: The Lower Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf, PDF page 37
questions.sourceEvidence: Contents: saphenous nerve, obturator N. terminal part and N. to vastus medialis.

questions.question: Which muscle forms the superolateral boundary of the popliteal fossa?
questions.explanation: Biceps femoris forms the superolateral boundary; the hamstrings on the medial side form the superomedial boundary.
questions.imageAlt: Lower Limb lecture slides, slide 39, supporting question 40
questions.sourceRef: The Lower Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf, PDF page 39
questions.sourceEvidence: Boundaries: supero-lateral — biceps femoris.

questions.question: The femoral artery becomes the popliteal artery after passing through which opening?
questions.explanation: The femoral artery traverses the adductor hiatus and continues as the popliteal artery.
questions.imageAlt: Lower Limb lecture slides, slide 44, supporting question 41
questions.sourceRef: The Lower Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf, PDF page 44
questions.sourceEvidence: Femoral artery end: at adductor hiatus by becoming popliteal artery.

questions.question: Which artery is the largest branch of the femoral artery?
questions.explanation: The profunda femoris is identified as the largest branch of the femoral artery.
questions.imageAlt: Lower Limb lecture slides, slide 47, supporting question 42
questions.sourceRef: The Lower Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf, PDF page 47
questions.sourceEvidence: Profunda femoris artery: it is the largest br. of femoral artery.

questions.question: At what level does the popliteal artery divide into the anterior and posterior tibial arteries?
questions.explanation: The popliteal artery terminates at the lower border of popliteus by dividing into the two tibial arteries.
questions.imageAlt: Lower Limb lecture slides, slide 51, supporting question 43
questions.sourceRef: The Lower Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf, PDF page 51
questions.sourceEvidence: End: at lower border of popliteus muscle by dividing into anterior & posterior tibial arteries.

questions.question: At the apex of the femoral triangle, how is the femoral vein positioned relative to the femoral artery?
options: Deep and posterior to the femoral artery
questions.explanation: The lecture traces the femoral vein as lateral near the adductor hiatus, deep/posterior to the artery at the apex of the femoral triangle, and medial near the femoral sheath.
questions.imageAlt: Lower Limb lecture slides, slide 56, supporting question 44
questions.sourceRef: The Lower Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf, PDF page 56
questions.sourceEvidence: At the apex of the femoral triangle, the femoral vein lies deep, posterior to the artery.

questions.question: At which landmark is the cruciate anastomosis formed?
questions.explanation: The cruciate anastomosis is formed at the level of the lesser trochanter.
questions.imageAlt: Lower Limb lecture slides, slide 59, supporting question 45
questions.sourceRef: The Lower Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf, PDF page 59
questions.sourceEvidence: Cruciate anastomosis: formed at level of lesser trochanter.

questions.question: Which nerve supplies the quadriceps femoris muscle?
questions.explanation: The posterior division of the femoral nerve gives the muscular supply to quadriceps.
questions.imageAlt: Lower Limb lecture slides, slide 65, supporting question 46
questions.sourceRef: The Lower Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf, PDF page 65
questions.sourceEvidence: Branches from posterior division: muscular to quadriceps muscle.

questions.question: The sciatic nerve usually divides into its terminal branches in which region?
questions.explanation: Although variation occurs, the lecture notes that division most commonly occurs in the lower third of the thigh.
questions.imageAlt: Lower Limb lecture slides, slide 69, supporting question 47
questions.sourceRef: The Lower Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf, PDF page 69
questions.sourceEvidence: It ends most commonly at lower 1/3 of thigh.

questions.question: Which are the terminal branches of the tibial nerve?
options: Medial and intermediate cutaneous nerves of thigh
questions.explanation: The tibial nerve terminates in the plantar surface by dividing into medial and lateral plantar nerves.
questions.imageAlt: Lower Limb lecture slides, slide 74, supporting question 48
questions.sourceRef: The Lower Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf, PDF page 74
questions.sourceEvidence: End in plantar surface by dividing into medial & lateral plantar nerves.

questions.question: The common peroneal nerve winds around which part of the fibula?
questions.explanation: The nerve passes behind the head and around the neck of the fibula, making it vulnerable to injury there.
questions.imageAlt: Lower Limb lecture slides, slide 77, supporting question 49
questions.sourceRef: The Lower Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf, PDF page 77
questions.sourceEvidence: Passes behind head of fibula & rounds around the neck of fibula.

questions.topic: Lower Limb — Cutaneous innervation of foot
questions.question: Which nerve supplies the skin in the interval between the first and second toes?
questions.explanation: The deep peroneal nerve supplies the adjacent sides of the first and second toes, including their interdigital cleft.
questions.imageAlt: Lower Limb lecture slides, slide 81, supporting question 50
questions.sourceRef: The Lower Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf, PDF page 81
questions.sourceEvidence: Deep peroneal N. supplies adjacent sides of 1st & 2nd toes.

questions.topic: Lower Limb — Arteries of leg and foot
questions.question: Which artery continues as the dorsalis pedis artery in front of the ankle?
questions.explanation: The anterior tibial artery continues across the ankle as the dorsalis pedis artery.
questions.imageAlt: Lower Limb lecture slides, slide 84, supporting question 51
questions.sourceRef: The Lower Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf, PDF page 84
questions.sourceEvidence: Anterior tibial artery end: continues as dorsalis pedis artery in front of ankle.

questions.topic: Lower Limb — Arteries of leg and foot
questions.question: Which two arteries arise as terminal branches of the posterior tibial artery behind the medial malleolus?
questions.explanation: The posterior tibial artery divides beneath the flexor retinaculum into the medial and lateral plantar arteries.
questions.imageAlt: Lower Limb lecture slides, slide 86, supporting question 52
questions.sourceRef: The Lower Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf, PDF page 86
questions.sourceEvidence: End by dividing into medial & lateral plantar arteries behind medial malleolus.

questions.question: According to the lecture, which anastomosis provides the main blood supply to the neck of the femur?
questions.explanation: The lecture identifies the trochanteric anastomosis as the main blood supply to the femoral neck.
questions.imageAlt: Lower Limb lecture slides, slide 62, supporting question 53
questions.sourceRef: The Lower Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf, PDF page 62
questions.sourceEvidence: Trochantric anastomosis provides main blood supply to the neck of femur.

questions.topic: Lower Limb — Clinical notes: tendon reflexes
questions.question: Which spinal nerve roots are associated with the Achilles tendon reflex in the lecture?
questions.explanation: The Achilles (ankle jerk) reflex is associated with S1 and S2.
questions.imageAlt: Lower Limb lecture slides, slide 106, supporting question 54
questions.sourceRef: The Lower Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf, PDF page 106
questions.sourceEvidence: Achilles tendon reflex (ankle jerk) → S1 & S2.

questions.topic: Lower Limb — Clinical notes: nerve lesions
questions.question: A common peroneal nerve injury paralyzes which leg compartments according to the lecture?
questions.explanation: The common peroneal nerve injury note describes paralysis of the anterior and lateral compartments of the leg.
questions.imageAlt: Lower Limb lecture slides, slide 110, supporting question 55
questions.sourceRef: The Lower Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf, PDF page 110
questions.sourceEvidence: Effects — Motor: paralysis of ant. & lateral compartment of leg.

questions.topic: Lower Limb — Clinical notes: nerve lesions
questions.question: What is the characteristic motor deficit of femoral nerve injury described in the lecture?
options: Loss of knee extension from quadriceps paralysis
questions.explanation: Femoral nerve injury can paralyze quadriceps, causing loss of knee extension.
questions.imageAlt: Lower Limb lecture slides, slide 107, supporting question 56
questions.sourceRef: The Lower Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf, PDF page 107
questions.sourceEvidence: Motor: quadriceps paralysis → loss of knee extension by it.

questions.topic: Lower Limb — Clinical notes: gluteal injection
questions.question: Which site is identified as the safest for an intramuscular injection in the gluteal region?
questions.explanation: The upper lateral quadrant is specified as the safest site, helping avoid the sciatic nerve.
questions.imageAlt: Lower Limb lecture slides, slide 72, supporting question 57
questions.sourceRef: The Lower Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf, PDF page 72
questions.sourceEvidence: The safest site for intramuscular injection is the upper lateral quadrant of gluteal region.

questions.topic: Lower Limb — Superficial inguinal lymph nodes
questions.question: According to the lecture, which sources drain to the medial members of the horizontal group of superficial inguinal lymph nodes?
options: Anterior abdominal wall below the umbilicus and the perineum
Most deep structures of the lower limb
Lateral side of the foot and leg
questions.explanation: The medial members of the horizontal group receive lymph from the anterior abdominal wall below the umbilicus and from the perineum.
questions.imageAlt: Lower Limb lecture slides, slide 25, supporting question 58
questions.sourceRef: The Lower Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf, PDF page 25
questions.sourceEvidence: Horizontal group, medial members: receive lymph vessels from anterior abdominal wall below umbilicus and perineum.

questions.question: Which named lymph node is noted in the lecture as receiving lymph from the glans penis and clitoris?
options: A vertical superficial inguinal lymph node
A lateral member of the horizontal superficial inguinal group
questions.explanation: The lecture specifically notes that the Cloquet lymph node receives lymph from the glans penis and clitoris.
questions.imageAlt: Lower Limb lecture slides, slide 28, supporting question 59
questions.sourceRef: The Lower Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf, PDF page 28
questions.sourceEvidence: Clocquet LN recieves lymph from glans penis and clitoris.

questions.question: Which structure is listed as a content of the femoral canal?
options: One deep inguinal lymph node (Cloquet node)
questions.explanation: The lecture lists fatty connective tissue, one deep inguinal (Cloquet) lymph node, and efferent lymph vessels among the femoral canal contents.
questions.imageAlt: Lower Limb lecture slides, slide 32, supporting question 60
questions.sourceRef: The Lower Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf, PDF page 32
questions.sourceEvidence: Contents are: 1. Fatty C.T. 2. one deep inguinal LN (Cloquet LN). 3. efferent lymph vessels from deep ing. L.N.

questions.question: Which description best characterizes the mammary gland?
options: A specialized accessory gland that secretes milk
A modified sebaceous gland that secretes sebum
A lymphoid organ that produces antibodies
A skeletal muscle that produces milk
questions.explanation: The female breast is formed by the mammary gland, a specialized accessory gland that secretes milk.
questions.imageAlt: The Breast lecture slides, slide 4, supporting question 61
questions.sourceRef: The Breast — Slides.pdf, PDF page 4
questions.sourceEvidence: The mammary gland is a specialized accessory gland secreting milk.

questions.question: In the midclavicular line, the base of the breast typically extends between which ribs?
questions.explanation: The stated vertical extent of the breast base is from the second to the sixth ribs in the midclavicular line.
questions.imageAlt: The Breast lecture slides, slide 6, supporting question 62
questions.sourceRef: The Breast — Slides.pdf, PDF page 6
questions.sourceEvidence: Base extends from the second to the sixth ribs in the midclavicular line.

questions.question: Which pair of landmarks describes the usual medial-to-lateral extent of the breast base?
options: Lateral border of sternum to midaxillary line
questions.explanation: The slide gives the breast base as extending from the lateral sternal border to the midaxillary line.
questions.imageAlt: The Breast lecture slides, slide 6, supporting question 63
questions.sourceRef: The Breast — Slides.pdf, PDF page 6
questions.sourceEvidence: Base extends from lateral border of sternum to the midaxillary line.

questions.question: Which muscle forms the principal muscle bed beneath the breast?
questions.explanation: Pectoralis major is identified as the main muscle bed of the breast.
questions.imageAlt: The Breast lecture slides, slide 6, supporting question 64
questions.sourceRef: The Breast — Slides.pdf, PDF page 6
questions.sourceEvidence: Muscle bed lists pectoralis major as the main muscle bed.

questions.question: What distinguishes the axillary tail from most of the breast in relation to fascia?
options: It pierces deep fascia at the lower border of pectoralis major and enters the axilla
It passes through the pectoral fascia into the mediastinum
It remains entirely superficial to the deep fascia
It traverses the rectus sheath into the abdomen
questions.explanation: Most of the breast lies in superficial fascia, while the axillary tail pierces deep fascia and enters the axilla.
questions.imageAlt: The Breast lecture slides, slide 6, supporting question 65
questions.sourceRef: The Breast — Slides.pdf, PDF page 6
questions.sourceEvidence: Axillary tail pierces deep fascia at lower border of pectoralis major and enters axilla.

questions.question: Approximately how many lobes are described in the breast?
questions.explanation: The slides describe 15–20 lobes, each with a duct, in the breast.
questions.imageAlt: The Breast lecture slides, slide 8, supporting question 66
questions.sourceRef: The Breast — Slides.pdf, PDF page 8
questions.sourceEvidence: Breast consists of 15–20 lobes separated by fibrous septa.

questions.question: What forms the suspensory (Cooper’s) ligaments?
options: Smooth muscle fibers around each duct
Fibrous septa, especially developed in the upper part near the skin
Fat lobules attached to the nipple
questions.explanation: Fibrous septa are more developed in the upper part near the skin, where they form the suspensory ligaments.
questions.imageAlt: The Breast lecture slides, slide 8, supporting question 67
questions.sourceRef: The Breast — Slides.pdf, PDF page 8
questions.sourceEvidence: Fibrous septa more developed near skin form suspensory (Cooper's) ligament.

questions.question: What is the retromammary space?
options: A glandular cavity within each lobe
A lymphatic channel beneath the areola
A space between pectoralis major and serratus anterior
Loose areolar tissue separating the breast from the deep fascia
questions.explanation: The retromammary (submammary) space is a layer of loose areolar tissue between the breast and underlying deep fascia.
questions.imageAlt: The Breast lecture slides, slide 8, supporting question 68
questions.sourceRef: The Breast — Slides.pdf, PDF page 8
questions.sourceEvidence: Breast is separated from deep fascia by loose areolar tissue called retromammary space.

questions.question: Which sequence correctly describes milk flow from the secretory units to the exterior?
options: Areolar glands → lactiferous sinus → deep fascia
questions.explanation: Acini secrete milk, which passes through a lactiferous duct that opens at the nipple.
questions.imageAlt: The Breast lecture slides, slide 8, supporting question 69
questions.sourceRef: The Breast — Slides.pdf, PDF page 8
questions.sourceEvidence: Acini secrete milk and each lobe transmits it by a lactiferous duct opening into the nipple.

questions.question: At what landmark is the nipple typically located according to the slide?
questions.explanation: The typical nipple position is opposite the fourth intercostal space, though it may be lower with a large breast.
questions.imageAlt: The Breast lecture slides, slide 10, supporting question 70
questions.sourceRef: The Breast — Slides.pdf, PDF page 10
questions.sourceEvidence: Nipple lies opposite the 4th intercostal space.

questions.question: Which glands in the areola form visible cutaneous tubercles?
questions.explanation: The areola contains prominent sebaceous glands called Montgomery glands, which form cutaneous tubercles.
questions.imageAlt: The Breast lecture slides, slide 10, supporting question 71
questions.sourceRef: The Breast — Slides.pdf, PDF page 10
questions.sourceEvidence: Areola contains large visible sebaceous glands forming cutaneous tubercles (Montgomery gland).

questions.topic: Thorax — Breast: clinical anatomy of ducts
questions.question: Why does the slide recommend making an incision radially in breast tissue?
options: To follow the course of Cooper’s ligaments
To avoid the internal thoracic artery
To keep the incision parallel to the areola
To avoid cutting across ducts that radiate outward from the nipple
questions.explanation: Because lactiferous ducts radiate outward from the nipple, a radial incision avoids cutting across them.
questions.imageAlt: The Breast lecture slides, slide 10, supporting question 72
questions.sourceRef: The Breast — Slides.pdf, PDF page 10
questions.sourceEvidence: Ducts radiate outwards from nipple; incision should be radial to avoid cutting across ducts.

questions.question: Where does lymph from the skin of the lateral breast quadrants (excluding nipple and areola) primarily drain?
options: Anterior (pectoral) group and lateral axillary nodes
questions.explanation: The skin of the lateral quadrants drains to the anterior (pectoral) group and lateral axillary nodes.
questions.imageAlt: The Breast lecture slides, slide 13, supporting question 73
questions.sourceRef: The Breast — Slides.pdf, PDF page 13
questions.sourceEvidence: Lateral quadrants drain into anterior (pectoral) group and lateral axillary LN.

questions.question: The skin of the medial breast quadrants (excluding nipple and areola) drains primarily to which nodes?
questions.explanation: The medial quadrant skin drains to internal thoracic (parasternal) nodes.
