questions.imageAlt: The Breast lecture slides, slide 13, supporting question 74
questions.sourceRef: The Breast — Slides.pdf, PDF page 13
questions.sourceEvidence: Medial quadrants drain into internal thoracic (parasternal) nodes.

questions.topic: Thorax — Breast: lymph drainage of breast tissue
questions.question: Approximately what proportion of lymph from breast tissue, including nipple and areola, drains to axillary lymph nodes?
questions.explanation: The slide estimates that 75% of lymph from breast tissue drains to axillary lymph nodes.
questions.imageAlt: The Breast lecture slides, slide 15, supporting question 75
questions.sourceRef: The Breast — Slides.pdf, PDF page 15
questions.sourceEvidence: 75% of breast tissue lymph drains to axillary lymph nodes.

questions.question: The lateral thoracic artery is described as supplying approximately which part of the breast?
questions.explanation: The source-and-share table assigns the lateral thoracic artery to the lateral part, about 60%.
questions.imageAlt: The Breast lecture slides, slide 21, supporting question 76
questions.sourceRef: The Breast — Slides.pdf, PDF page 21
questions.sourceEvidence: Lateral thoracic artery supplies lateral part (60%).

questions.question: Invasion and shrinkage of Cooper’s suspensory ligaments by breast cancer may produce which finding?
options: Diffuse breast enlargement from fat deposition
questions.explanation: The slides associate cancer invasion and shrinkage of suspensory ligaments with skin dimpling (peau d’orange is also noted).
questions.imageAlt: The Breast lecture slides, slide 23, supporting question 77
questions.sourceRef: The Breast — Slides.pdf, PDF page 23
questions.sourceEvidence: Cooper's ligament invasion and shrinkage can cause skin dimpling.

questions.question: Breast cancer invading the retromammary space and underlying muscle may cause which clinical effect?
questions.explanation: The slide states that invasion of the retromammary space into muscle causes fixation of the breast.
questions.imageAlt: The Breast lecture slides, slide 23, supporting question 78
questions.sourceRef: The Breast — Slides.pdf, PDF page 23
questions.sourceEvidence: Cancer may invade retromammary space into muscle causing fixation of breast.

questions.question: What is the term used for enlargement of the male breast in some diseases?
questions.explanation: The slide calls disease-associated enlargement of the male breast gynaecomastia.
questions.imageAlt: The Breast lecture slides, slide 23, supporting question 79
questions.sourceRef: The Breast — Slides.pdf, PDF page 23
questions.sourceEvidence: Male breast may enlarge in some disease: gynaecomastia.

questions.question: Which imaging method is identified in the slides as being used to screen for breast tumours?
questions.explanation: The slides state that a breast mammogram is used for screening of tumours.
questions.imageAlt: The Breast lecture slides, slide 25, supporting question 80
questions.sourceRef: The Breast — Slides.pdf, PDF page 25
questions.sourceEvidence: Breast mammogram is used for screening of tumours.

title: Day 3 — Diagnostic Pathology, Cell Injury & Inflammation
description: 80 pathology MCQs from Lectures 1–3: Principles of Diagnostic Pathology, Cell Injury and Death, and Inflammation. Supplementary items are derived only from the matching lecture slides.

questions.question: Which diagnostic tool is considered the fundamental cornerstone of microscopic pathology analysis?
questions.explanation: Cellular and nuclear morphology is identified as the cornerstone of microscopic diagnosis alongside tissue architecture and disease patterns.
questions.imageAlt: Slide text describing gross examination and microscopic analysis.
questions.imageSourceLabel: Lecture 1 — Principles of Diagnostic Pathology, PDF page 5
questions.sourceRef: Principles of Diagnostic Pathology — Question bank Q1

questions.question: What is the standard ratio of fixative to tissue volume required for optimal fixation using 10% Neutral Buffered Formalin (NBF)?
questions.explanation: The source specifies 10 parts of 10% NBF for 1 part of tissue; it also notes a penetration rate of about 1 mm/hour.
questions.imageAlt: Slide summary of specimen handling and fixation facts.
questions.imageSourceLabel: Lecture 1 — Principles of Diagnostic Pathology, PDF page 13
questions.sourceRef: Principles of Diagnostic Pathology — Question bank Q2

questions.question: What is the recommended minimum and optimal tissue fixation duration in 10% Neutral Buffered Formalin for routine surgical specimens?
questions.explanation: The source gives a minimum fixation period of 6–8 hours and an optimal period of 24 hours.
questions.imageAlt: Slide listing minimum and optimal fixation periods.
questions.imageSourceLabel: Lecture 1 — Principles of Diagnostic Pathology, PDF page 13
questions.sourceRef: Principles of Diagnostic Pathology — Question bank Q3

questions.question: Which type of biopsy provides a partial removal of a lesion for diagnosis rather than cure and requires inclusion of the interface between normal and abnormal tissue?
questions.explanation: An incisional biopsy removes only part of a lesion, with the normal–abnormal interface included; the source also advises avoiding central necrotic areas.
questions.imageAlt: Slide contrasting partial and complete lesion removal.
questions.imageSourceLabel: Lecture 1 — Principles of Diagnostic Pathology, PDF page 11
questions.sourceRef: Principles of Diagnostic Pathology — Question bank Q4

questions.question: Which percutaneous biopsy technique preserves tissue architecture and allows receptor and molecular studies, but carries risks of hematoma and sampling error?
questions.explanation: CNB obtains small cylinders of tissue using a hollow needle; the source lists preserved architecture and ancillary studies as advantages and hematoma and sampling error as limitations.
questions.imageAlt: Slide comparing FNA and core needle biopsy features.
questions.imageSourceLabel: Lecture 1 — Principles of Diagnostic Pathology, PDF page 10
questions.sourceRef: Principles of Diagnostic Pathology — Question bank Q5

questions.question: What is a critical handling rule when an excisional biopsy of a skin lesion or lymph node is performed?
options: Always section the specimen in half before placing it in formalin.
Do not section the specimen before sending it to the laboratory; document orientation with sutures.
Wash the specimen vigorously in normal saline before immersion in formalin.
Freeze the specimen immediately on dry ice inside the operating theatre.
questions.explanation: The source instructs that an excisional specimen should not be sectioned before laboratory submission and that its orientation should be documented with sutures.
questions.imageAlt: Slide with handling directions for an excisional biopsy.
questions.imageSourceLabel: Lecture 1 — Principles of Diagnostic Pathology, PDF page 11
questions.sourceRef: Principles of Diagnostic Pathology — Question bank Q6

questions.question: What suture convention is stated for surgical specimen orientation unless otherwise agreed with the pathology laboratory?
options: Short suture = inferior; long suture = superior
Short suture = superior; long suture = lateral
Short suture = anterior; long suture = posterior
Short suture = lateral; long suture = medial
questions.explanation: The source gives the convention short suture = superior and long suture = lateral, or as agreed with the laboratory.
questions.imageAlt: Slide presenting suture and ink orientation conventions.
questions.imageSourceLabel: Lecture 1 — Principles of Diagnostic Pathology, PDF page 17
questions.sourceRef: Principles of Diagnostic Pathology — Question bank Q7

questions.question: Where should specimen labels be physically placed according to the stated laboratory best practice?
options: Directly on the removable lid of the container
On the side of the container itself, not on the lid
Wrapped tightly around the biohazard transport bag
Written directly onto the surgical specimen
questions.explanation: The source says to write on the container rather than its lid, which could become separated or mismatched.
questions.imageAlt: Slide listing specimen labeling best practices.
questions.imageSourceLabel: Lecture 1 — Principles of Diagnostic Pathology, PDF page 16
questions.sourceRef: Principles of Diagnostic Pathology — Question bank Q8

questions.question: What approximate diagnostic sensitivity of frozen section biopsy is stated in the source?
questions.explanation: The source states an approximate frozen-section biopsy sensitivity of 95%.
questions.imageAlt: Slide with a sensitivity figure and frozen-section role.
questions.imageSourceLabel: Lecture 1 — Principles of Diagnostic Pathology, PDF page 8
questions.sourceRef: Principles of Diagnostic Pathology — Question bank Q9

questions.question: How should a surgical specimen intended for routine frozen section be transported to the pathology laboratory?
options: Submerged in 10% NBF at room temperature
Placed in sterile normal saline inside a sealed glass bottle
Sent fresh, immediately on ice or dry, and never fixed in formalin
questions.explanation: The source requires frozen-section specimens to be sent fresh, immediately on ice or dry, and not fixed in formalin.
questions.imageAlt: Slide comparing biopsy procedures and frozen-section handling.
questions.imageSourceLabel: Lecture 1 — Principles of Diagnostic Pathology, PDF page 12
questions.sourceRef: Principles of Diagnostic Pathology — Question bank Q10

questions.question: Which fixative is specifically required if electron microscopy analysis of a specialized tissue specimen is anticipated?
questions.explanation: The source specifies glutaraldehyde for electron microscopy and states that NBF is not suitable for this purpose.
questions.imageAlt: Slide table relating specimen types to handling conditions.
questions.imageSourceLabel: Lecture 1 — Principles of Diagnostic Pathology, PDF page 14
questions.sourceRef: Principles of Diagnostic Pathology — Question bank Q11

questions.question: Which artificial distortion artifact is typically induced by squeezing tissue too tightly with surgical forceps?
questions.explanation: The source attributes crush artifact to tissue being squeezed by forceps during handling.
questions.imageAlt: Slide describing tissue artefacts and their causes.
questions.imageSourceLabel: Lecture 1 — Principles of Diagnostic Pathology, PDF page 15
questions.sourceRef: Principles of Diagnostic Pathology — Question bank Q12

questions.question: What cellular changes are associated with delayed or inadequate tissue fixation in the source?
options: Cell swelling, shrinkage, and poor staining
Complete nuclear dissolution without cytoplasmic changes
questions.explanation: The source links delayed or inadequate fixation with cell swelling, shrinkage, and poor staining.
questions.imageAlt: Slide listing effects associated with fixation artefact.
questions.imageSourceLabel: Lecture 1 — Principles of Diagnostic Pathology, PDF page 15
questions.sourceRef: Principles of Diagnostic Pathology — Question bank Q13

questions.question: Which skin biopsy technique provides a cylindrical full-thickness sample, typically 2–8 mm, and is indicated for inflammatory dermatoses and melanocytic lesions?
questions.explanation: The source describes punch biopsy as a cylindrical full-thickness skin sample of 2–8 mm and lists those indications.
questions.imageAlt: Slide outlining punch and shave biopsy features.
questions.imageSourceLabel: Lecture 1 — Principles of Diagnostic Pathology, PDF page 12
questions.sourceRef: Principles of Diagnostic Pathology — Question bank Q14

questions.question: Why is a shave biopsy unsuitable for evaluating suspected malignant melanoma according to the source?
options: It causes massive local bleeding that obscures the surgical field.
It makes a horizontal cut through the superficial dermis and does not assess deep margins.
It dissolves melanocytic cells upon contact with air.
It requires general anesthesia in an operating suite.
questions.explanation: The source says shave biopsy cuts horizontally through superficial dermis and does not assess deep margins, and should not be used for suspected melanoma.
questions.imageAlt: Slide stating the depth and limitation of shave biopsy.
questions.imageSourceLabel: Lecture 1 — Principles of Diagnostic Pathology, PDF page 12
questions.sourceRef: Principles of Diagnostic Pathology — Question bank Q15

questions.question: Which color-coded ink convention is given for resected specimen margins?
options: Black = posterior; Blue = anterior; Yellow = superior; Green = inferior
Red = posterior; White = anterior; Black = superior; Orange = inferior
Yellow = posterior; Green = anterior; Blue = superior; Black = inferior
Purple = posterior; Orange = anterior; Red = superior; White = inferior
questions.explanation: The source lists black for posterior, blue for anterior, yellow for superior, and green for inferior margins.
questions.imageAlt: Slide listing distinct ink colors for specimen margins.
questions.imageSourceLabel: Lecture 1 — Principles of Diagnostic Pathology, PDF page 17
questions.sourceRef: Principles of Diagnostic Pathology — Question bank Q16

questions.question: Which set is listed as essential patient demographic and identification information on the pathology request form?
options: Surgeon's home address and telephone number
Full patient name, date of birth or age, hospital number, gender, ward, and consultant
Operating room temperature and humidity logs
Insurance billing codes and financial status
questions.explanation: The source lists full name, date of birth or age, hospital number, gender, ward, and consultant as patient demographics.
questions.imageAlt: Slide listing demographics and other request-form sections.
questions.imageSourceLabel: Lecture 1 — Principles of Diagnostic Pathology, PDF page 18
questions.sourceRef: Principles of Diagnostic Pathology — Question bank Q17

questions.question: What is a stated consequence of submitting a pathology request form without relevant clinical history?
options: Immediate destruction of the tissue sample
Non-specific reporting and failure to consider important differential diagnoses
Automatic doubling of routine turnaround time
Mandatory re-excision of the surgical site
questions.explanation: The source says missing clinical history can lead to non-specific reporting and important differential diagnoses not being considered.
questions.imageAlt: Slide table connecting request-form errors with consequences.
questions.imageSourceLabel: Lecture 1 — Principles of Diagnostic Pathology, PDF page 19
questions.sourceRef: Principles of Diagnostic Pathology — Question bank Q18

questions.question: What routine turnaround time is stated for small diagnostic biopsies processed in surgical pathology?
questions.explanation: The source states that small biopsies typically take 1–3 working days; frozen sections are reported intraoperatively.
questions.imageAlt: Slide listing routine turnaround-time ranges.
questions.imageSourceLabel: Lecture 1 — Principles of Diagnostic Pathology, PDF page 7
questions.sourceRef: Principles of Diagnostic Pathology — Question bank Q19

questions.question: What is the legal and clinical significance of the final surgical pathology report according to the source?
options: It is an optional summary that can be altered verbally without documentation.
It is a legal document where accuracy is paramount and it influences surgical and oncological management.
It serves purely as an administrative billing record.
It is secondary in importance to radiological imaging findings.
questions.explanation: The source identifies the report as a legal document, emphasizes accuracy, and notes its role in management decisions.
questions.imageAlt: Slide on the pathologist's role and report responsibility.
questions.imageSourceLabel: Lecture 1 — Principles of Diagnostic Pathology, PDF page 8
questions.sourceRef: Principles of Diagnostic Pathology — Question bank Q20

questions.question: According to the lecture, what must be integrated with pathological findings to interpret them appropriately?
options: Clinical context, including age, site, history, and imaging
Only the gross appearance of the specimen
questions.explanation: The lecture says pathological findings must always be interpreted in clinical context, including age, site, history, and imaging.
questions.imageAlt: Slide outlining diagnostic principles and clinical context.

questions.question: Which set of activities is shown as contributing to morphological diagnosis in the diagnostic workflow?
options: Request form completion and specimen transport
Receptor testing and clinical history alone

questions.question: Which use of immunohistochemistry is identified in the lecture as predictive?
questions.explanation: The lecture describes immunohistochemistry as helping identify tumor origin and as predictive through hormone receptor status.

questions.question: Which specimen type is indicated as requiring fresh handling for flow cytometry or lymphoma workup?

questions.imageAlt: Table comparing handling requirements for fresh and fixed specimens.

questions.question: What is the stated purpose of an additional radial suture or clip on a surgical specimen?
options: To mark an area of concern or closest margin for re-excision guidance
To indicate the time fixation began
To identify the container as containing multiple specimens
To substitute for documenting patient identifiers
questions.explanation: The orientation slide says a radial suture or clip can mark an area of concern or the closest margin to guide re-excision.
questions.imageAlt: Slide describing specimen orientation markers and their use.
questions.imageSourceLabel: Lecture 1 — Principles of Diagnostic Pathology, PDF page 17

questions.question: Which clinical information is specifically requested on the pathology form in addition to relevant history?
options: Duration, growth rate, previous treatment, and relevant imaging findings
Fixative penetration rate and tissue-to-fixative ratio
questions.explanation: The request-form slide lists duration, growth rate, previous treatment, and relevant ultrasound, CT, or MRI findings under clinical information.

questions.question: Which item is listed as something to avoid during specimen transportation?
questions.explanation: The transportation slide says to avoid unlabeled containers, delayed submission, and plastic bags without containers.
questions.imageAlt: Slide listing specimen transportation requirements and cautions.
questions.imageSourceLabel: Lecture 1 — Principles of Diagnostic Pathology, PDF page 20
questions.sourceRef: Supplementary question derived from Lecture 1 slides, PDF page 20

questions.question: Which intracellular event represents the critical point of no return from reversible injury to cell death?
options: Detachment of ribosomal subunits from rough endoplasmic reticulum
Severe mitochondrial damage with failure of ATP production and marked Ca²⁺ influx
Reversible hydropic swelling due to temporary Na⁺/K⁺ pump sluggishness
Mild plasma membrane blebbing and blunting of microvilli
questions.explanation: Severe mitochondrial damage, profound ATP depletion, marked calcium influx, and lysosomal rupture signal irreversible injury and lead to cell death.
questions.imageAlt: Comparison of reversible and irreversible cell injury features
questions.imageSourceLabel: Lecture 2 — Cell Injury and Death, PDF page 5
questions.sourceRef: Cell injury and death — Q1

questions.question: What is the earliest morphological manifestation of almost all forms of acute reversible cell injury?
options: Complete dissolution of the plasma membrane
questions.explanation: Cellular swelling is the earliest manifestation of reversible injury and follows failure of the energy-dependent Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase pump.
questions.imageAlt: Morphologic findings associated with reversible cell injury
questions.imageSourceLabel: Lecture 2 — Cell Injury and Death, PDF page 12
questions.sourceRef: Cell injury and death — Q2

questions.question: Which pattern of necrosis preserves basic tissue architecture as ghost outlines for days after ischemic death in solid organs such as the heart and kidney?
questions.explanation: Denaturation of structural proteins and enzymes preserves cellular outlines and tissue architecture in coagulative necrosis of solid-organ infarcts.
questions.imageAlt: Microscopic pattern of necrosis with retained cell outlines
questions.imageSourceLabel: Lecture 2 — Cell Injury and Death, PDF page 15
questions.sourceRef: Cell injury and death — Q3

questions.question: Why does hypoxic or ischemic cell death in the central nervous system characteristically result in liquefactive necrosis rather than coagulative necrosis?
options: Because the brain has an extensive dual blood supply with abundant collateral anastomoses
Because brain tissue has high lipid content and scant stroma, and dead cells are completely digested by hydrolytic enzymes
Because neurons lack all forms of intracellular lysosomes and structural proteins
Because the skull prevents any inflammatory cell recruitment into the cranial vault
questions.explanation: The brain undergoes liquefactive necrosis: its high lipid content and scant stroma accompany enzymatic digestion of dead tissue into a viscous mass.
questions.imageAlt: Features of liquefactive necrosis in neural tissue
questions.imageSourceLabel: Lecture 2 — Cell Injury and Death, PDF page 16
questions.sourceRef: Cell injury and death — Q4

questions.question: What gross and microscopic pathological features define caseous necrosis as classically seen in tuberculosis?
options: Bright pink amorphous protein deposits within blood vessel walls
Friable, white, cheese-like central debris surrounded by granulomatous inflammation with Langhans giant cells
Chalky white deposits resulting from enzymatic saponification of fat
Fluid-filled cystic cavities lined by reactive astrocytic glial scars
questions.explanation: Caseous necrosis has a cheese-like gross appearance and central acellular granular debris enclosed within a granulomatous rim.
questions.imageAlt: Gross and microscopic findings associated with caseous necrosis
questions.imageSourceLabel: Lecture 2 — Cell Injury and Death, PDF page 17
questions.sourceRef: Cell injury and death — Q5

questions.question: What biochemical mechanism produces the chalky white deposits of fat necrosis during acute pancreatitis?
options: Deposition of immune complexes and leaked serum fibrin
Saponification, in which liberated free fatty acids combine with calcium
Dystrophic calcification secondary to chronic hyperparathyroidism
Bacterial fermentation of subcutaneous adipose tissue lipids
questions.explanation: Pancreatic lipases release free fatty acids from fat; these bind calcium to form chalky white soap deposits by saponification.
questions.imageAlt: Fat necrosis and its gross appearance
questions.imageSourceLabel: Lecture 2 — Cell Injury and Death, PDF page 18
questions.sourceRef: Cell injury and death — Q6

questions.question: Which sequence accurately describes the nuclear changes of necrosis?
questions.explanation: The sequence is pyknosis (nuclear shrinkage and condensation), karyorrhexis (fragmentation), then karyolysis (fading through DNase digestion).
questions.imageAlt: Sequence of nuclear changes in necrosis
questions.imageSourceLabel: Lecture 2 — Cell Injury and Death, PDF page 14
questions.sourceRef: Cell injury and death — Q7

questions.question: What is the crucial clinical distinction between dry and wet gangrene?
options: Dry gangrene involves extensive bacterial sepsis, whereas wet gangrene is entirely sterile
Dry gangrene is ischemia alone with a clear demarcation line, whereas wet gangrene involves bacterial superinfection, swelling, and high sepsis risk requiring urgent debridement
Dry gangrene exclusively affects the bowel, while wet gangrene affects only the upper limbs
Wet gangrene can always be managed expectantly, whereas dry gangrene requires emergency amputation
questions.explanation: Wet gangrene is superinfected and carries high sepsis risk, so urgent surgical intervention is required; dry gangrene may sometimes be managed expectantly.
questions.imageAlt: Comparison of dry and wet gangrene
questions.imageSourceLabel: Lecture 2 — Cell Injury and Death, PDF page 20
questions.sourceRef: Cell injury and death — Q8

questions.question: What is the primary pathophysiological driver and surgical significance of gas gangrene caused by Clostridium perfringens?
options: Chronic venous stasis leading to painless pedal edema and skin ulceration
Bacterial toxins cause profound muscle necrosis and fermentation produces gas, making urgent debridement essential
Immune complex deposition inside small dermal arterioles results in fibrinoid vasculitis
Immediate activation of the extrinsic apoptotic pathway via Fas-ligand binding on myocytes
questions.explanation: Bacterial toxins cause muscle necrosis and fermentation produces gas; this rapidly progressive emergency requires urgent removal of dead tissue because antibiotics alone are inadequate.
questions.imageAlt: Clinical and pathologic features of gas gangrene
questions.imageSourceLabel: Lecture 2 — Cell Injury and Death, PDF page 21
questions.sourceRef: Cell injury and death — Q9

questions.question: How does apoptosis fundamentally differ from necrosis regarding energy requirements and inflammatory response?
options: Apoptosis is energy-independent and triggers severe surrounding inflammation
Apoptosis is energy-dependent and does not provoke an inflammatory response
Apoptosis results in massive cellular swelling and cell lysis
Apoptosis occurs only as a pathological consequence of severe ischemic injury
questions.explanation: Apoptosis is a regulated, ATP-requiring pathway that eliminates cells without inducing an inflammatory response.
questions.imageAlt: Comparison of necrosis and apoptosis
questions.imageSourceLabel: Lecture 2 — Cell Injury and Death, PDF page 25
questions.sourceRef: Cell injury and death — Q10

questions.question: Which proteolytic enzymes are central executioners in both the intrinsic and extrinsic pathways of apoptosis?
questions.explanation: Caspases are the main executioner proteases of apoptosis and degrade cellular proteins and DNA.
questions.imageAlt: Apoptosis pathways converging on execution caspases
questions.imageSourceLabel: Lecture 2 — Cell Injury and Death, PDF page 24
questions.sourceRef: Cell injury and death — Q11

questions.question: What sequence characterizes ischemia–reperfusion injury when blood supply returns to ischemic tissue?
options: Immediate restoration of normal cellular pH and complete resolution of oxidative stress
A burst of reactive oxygen species, neutrophil influx, complement activation, and mitochondrial permeability transition pore opening that worsens tissue damage
Permanent stabilization of cellular ATP stores and immediate closure of all calcium channels
Conversion of coagulative necrosis into benign fibrous scar tissue within minutes
questions.explanation: Reperfusion returns oxygen to tissue primed for oxidative damage, provoking ROS generation and inflammatory responses that add to the injury.
questions.imageAlt: Sequence of events in ischemia–reperfusion injury
questions.imageSourceLabel: Lecture 2 — Cell Injury and Death, PDF page 26
questions.sourceRef: Cell injury and death — Q12

questions.question: What distinguishes dystrophic calcification from metastatic calcification?
options: Dystrophic calcification occurs in normal, healthy tissues secondary to systemic hypercalcemia
Dystrophic calcification occurs in dead or damaged tissue with normal serum calcium, whereas metastatic calcification affects normal tissues secondary to hypercalcemia
Dystrophic calcification only affects the renal cortex and gastric mucosa
Metastatic calcification is exclusively found inside atherosclerotic plaques and tuberculous scars
questions.explanation: Dystrophic calcification occurs in injured or necrotic tissue despite normal serum calcium; metastatic calcification occurs in otherwise normal tissues with hypercalcemia.
questions.imageAlt: Comparison of dystrophic and metastatic calcification
questions.imageSourceLabel: Lecture 2 — Cell Injury and Death, PDF page 29
questions.sourceRef: Cell injury and death — Q13

questions.question: Which cellular changes underlie aging and reduced physiological reserve in elderly surgical patients?
options: Continuous elongation of chromosomal telomeres beyond normal mitotic thresholds
Accumulated uncorrected DNA damage, telomere shortening leading to replicative senescence, and misfolded protein buildup
Complete cessation of intracellular reactive oxygen species production
Hypertrophy of all cytoplasmic organelles and increased metabolic efficiency
questions.explanation: Cellular aging involves accumulated molecular damage, telomere shortening, and defective protein homeostasis, contributing to reduced reserve.
questions.imageAlt: Cellular mechanisms associated with aging
questions.imageSourceLabel: Lecture 2 — Cell Injury and Death, PDF page 30
questions.sourceRef: Cell injury and death — Q14

questions.question: According to the lecture, which cause is identified as the most common cause of cell injury?
questions.explanation: The lecture identifies hypoxia or ischemia, involving loss of oxygen or blood supply, as the most common cause of cell injury.
questions.imageAlt: Categories of causes of cell injury
questions.imageSourceLabel: Lecture 2 — Cell Injury and Death, PDF page 3
questions.sourceRef: Supplementary question derived from Lecture 2 slides, PDF page 3

questions.question: Which set consists entirely of cellular adaptations listed in the lecture?
options: ATP depletion, calcium influx, ROS, and membrane rupture
questions.explanation: The lecture lists hypertrophy, atrophy, hyperplasia, and metaplasia as forms of adaptation in the stress-response spectrum.
questions.imageAlt: Cellular stress-response spectrum
questions.imageSourceLabel: Lecture 2 — Cell Injury and Death, PDF page 4
questions.sourceRef: Supplementary question derived from Lecture 2 slides, PDF page 4

questions.question: How does failure of the Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase pump during ATP depletion lead to cellular swelling?
options: Na⁺ and water enter the cell
K⁺ and water leave the cell
Cytosolic calcium is converted into ATP
questions.explanation: The lecture states that Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase failure causes sodium and water to enter the cell, producing cellular swelling.
questions.imageAlt: Cellular consequences of ATP depletion
questions.imageSourceLabel: Lecture 2 — Cell Injury and Death, PDF page 7
questions.sourceRef: Supplementary question derived from Lecture 2 slides, PDF page 7

questions.question: In the intrinsic apoptotic pathway described in the lecture, what follows leakage of cytochrome c from damaged mitochondria?
options: Caspase-8 activation through a death receptor
questions.explanation: Mitochondrial cytochrome c release activates caspase-9 in the intrinsic apoptotic pathway.
questions.imageAlt: Mitochondrial damage and the intrinsic apoptosis pathway
questions.imageSourceLabel: Lecture 2 — Cell Injury and Death, PDF page 8
questions.sourceRef: Supplementary question derived from Lecture 2 slides, PDF page 8

questions.question: Which damaging enzyme activity is associated with sustained high cytosolic Ca²⁺ in injured cells?
questions.explanation: Sustained high Ca²⁺ activates phospholipases that degrade cell membranes; the lecture also describes activation of proteases, endonucleases, and ATPases.
questions.imageAlt: Calcium influx and downstream cellular effects
questions.imageSourceLabel: Lecture 2 — Cell Injury and Death, PDF page 9
questions.sourceRef: Supplementary question derived from Lecture 2 slides, PDF page 9

questions.question: Which is listed as a damage target of reactive oxygen species in oxidative stress?
options: Increased glycogen storage in all cells
questions.explanation: The lecture lists membrane lipid peroxidation, protein cross-linking and fragmentation, and DNA strand breaks as ROS damage targets.
questions.imageAlt: Sources and cellular targets of oxidative stress
questions.imageSourceLabel: Lecture 2 — Cell Injury and Death, PDF page 10
questions.sourceRef: Supplementary question derived from Lecture 2 slides, PDF page 10

questions.question: What is a direct consequence of lysosomal membrane damage in an injured cell?
options: Hydrolytic enzymes leak into the cytosol and cause autodigestion
Cytochrome c is returned to the mitochondria
The plasma membrane becomes impermeable to all ions
Telomeres lengthen and prevent cell death
questions.explanation: Damage to lysosomal membranes releases hydrolytic enzymes, including RNases, DNases, and proteases, into the cytosol and promotes autodigestion.
questions.imageAlt: Cellular effects of membrane damage
questions.imageSourceLabel: Lecture 2 — Cell Injury and Death, PDF page 11
questions.sourceRef: Supplementary question derived from Lecture 2 slides, PDF page 11

questions.question: Which description of fatty change in reversible injury matches the lecture?
options: Lipid vacuoles accumulate within the cytoplasm, especially in the liver, and the change can reverse if the cause is corrected
Calcium deposits replace all cytoplasmic lipids and cannot be reversed
It is a nuclear change caused by DNase digestion
It occurs only after tissue architecture is completely destroyed
questions.explanation: The lecture describes fatty change as cytoplasmic lipid-vacuole accumulation, particularly with hypoxic, toxic, or metabolic injury in the liver, and potentially reversible when the cause is corrected.
questions.imageAlt: Morphologic features of reversible injury and fatty change
questions.imageSourceLabel: Lecture 2 — Cell Injury and Death, PDF page 12
questions.sourceRef: Supplementary question derived from Lecture 2 slides, PDF page 12

questions.question: Which microscopic finding is associated with liquefactive necrosis in the lecture?
options: Amorphous debris, abundant neutrophils, and loss of cellular outlines
Preserved ghost outlines with loss of nuclei
Bright pink deposits confined to vessel walls
Intact cell outlines with mild chromatin clumping
questions.explanation: Liquefactive necrosis is described microscopically by amorphous debris, abundant neutrophils, and loss of cellular outlines after enzymatic digestion.
questions.imageAlt: Microscopic characteristics of liquefactive necrosis
questions.imageSourceLabel: Lecture 2 — Cell Injury and Death, PDF page 16
questions.sourceRef: Supplementary question derived from Lecture 2 slides, PDF page 16

questions.question: What produces the bright pink amorphous appearance of fibrinoid necrosis in a vessel wall on H&E staining?
options: Deposition of immune complexes, fibrin, and plasma proteins
Saponification of free fatty acids with calcium
Digestion of neural tissue by hydrolytic enzymes
questions.explanation: Fibrinoid necrosis features immune complexes together with leaked fibrin and plasma proteins deposited in vessel walls, producing a bright pink amorphous appearance.
questions.imageAlt: Fibrinoid material within a vessel wall
questions.imageSourceLabel: Lecture 2 — Cell Injury and Death, PDF page 19
questions.sourceRef: Supplementary question derived from Lecture 2 slides, PDF page 19

questions.question: Which trigger is associated with the extrinsic apoptosis pathway in the lecture?
options: External signals binding to death receptors such as Fas
Internal DNA damage activating mitochondrial membrane permeabilization
Failure of the Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase pump
Calcium binding to free fatty acids
questions.explanation: The extrinsic pathway is triggered by external signals binding death receptors such as Fas, which recruit adaptor proteins and activate caspases through receptor-mediated signaling.
questions.imageAlt: Intrinsic and extrinsic apoptosis pathways
questions.imageSourceLabel: Lecture 2 — Cell Injury and Death, PDF page 24
questions.sourceRef: Supplementary question derived from Lecture 2 slides, PDF page 24

questions.question: What happens to the plasma membrane during apoptosis, according to the lecture comparison?
options: It remains intact and blebs into apoptotic bodies
It undergoes complete dissolution before nuclear change
It is replaced by a lysosomal membrane
questions.explanation: In apoptosis, the plasma membrane remains intact while forming blebs that package cell fragments into apoptotic bodies; necrosis instead disrupts the membrane.
questions.imageAlt: Cellular features contrasting necrosis and apoptosis
questions.imageSourceLabel: Lecture 2 — Cell Injury and Death, PDF page 25
questions.sourceRef: Supplementary question derived from Lecture 2 slides, PDF page 25

questions.question: Which mediators are highlighted as primarily responsible for pain during acute inflammation?
questions.explanation: The lecture associates pain with PGE2 and bradykinin, as shown among the cardinal signs.
questions.imageAlt: Cardinal signs of inflammation and their associations
questions.sourceRef: Inflammation  — Question bank Q1

questions.question: Which sequence correctly orders the leukocyte recruitment steps during acute inflammation?
questions.explanation: Leukocytes move to the vessel periphery, roll, adhere, cross the endothelium, and then migrate toward injury.
questions.imageAlt: Ordered leukocyte recruitment steps
questions.sourceRef: Inflammation  — Question bank Q2

questions.question: Which adhesion molecules mediate leukocyte rolling along the vascular endothelium?
questions.explanation: The lecture identifies selectins as the mediators of rolling; integrins bind ICAM-1 and VCAM-1 during adhesion.
questions.imageAlt: Molecules involved in leukocyte recruitment
questions.sourceRef: Inflammation  — Question bank Q3

questions.question: Which description best distinguishes an inflammatory exudate from a transudate?
options: Exudate has low protein and low specific gravity due to non-inflammatory pressure imbalance.
Exudate is associated with inflammation and has protein above 3 g/dL and specific gravity above 1.020.
Transudate is a neutrophil-rich fluid caused by localized bacterial infection.
Transudate has specific gravity above 1.020 and a turbid appearance.
questions.explanation: The slide comparison describes exudate as inflammation-related, protein-rich, and having specific gravity above 1.020; transudate reflects hydrostatic/oncotic imbalance.
questions.imageAlt: Comparison of fluid features in exudate and transudate
questions.sourceRef: Inflammation  — Question bank Q4

questions.question: Which cells are described as first responders arriving 6–24 hours after acute inflammation begins?
questions.explanation: The lecture identifies neutrophils as first responders arriving within 6–24 hours.
questions.imageAlt: Neutrophil functions and selected inflammatory mediators
questions.sourceRef: Inflammation  — Question bank Q5

questions.question: Which complement-derived factors are listed as promoting opsonization and chemotaxis?
questions.explanation: The mediator table assigns opsonization and chemotaxis to complement C3a/C5a.
questions.imageAlt: Mediator table listing complement functions
questions.sourceRef: Inflammation  — Question bank Q6

questions.question: What management does the lecture specify for a localized abscess containing pus?
options: Antibiotics alone are sufficient to resolve the collection.
Drainage is required because antibiotics alone cannot resolve the walled-off collection.
Corticosteroids should be given to induce resolution.
Observation is appropriate because abscesses always restore normal tissue.
questions.explanation: The lecture states that a localized abscess requires drainage and cannot be resolved with antibiotics alone.
questions.imageAlt: Acute inflammation outcomes including localized pus collection
questions.sourceRef: Inflammation  — Question bank Q7

questions.question: Which combination characterizes chronic inflammation?
options: Predominantly short-lived neutrophils, little tissue damage, and immediate complete resolution
Mononuclear infiltrates, ongoing tissue destruction, and simultaneous repair by fibrosis and angiogenesis
Immune-complex deposition in vessel walls exclusively
Low-protein fluid accumulation without cellular infiltration
questions.explanation: Chronic inflammation combines mononuclear cell infiltration and tissue destruction with repair through fibrosis and angiogenesis.
questions.imageAlt: Definition and characteristic features of chronic inflammation
questions.sourceRef: Inflammation  — Question bank Q8

questions.question: Which cell is described as the central orchestrator of chronic inflammation, including phagocytosis, antigen presentation, and fibrogenic cytokine release?
questions.explanation: The lecture describes macrophages as central orchestrators and notes their role in phagocytosis, antigen presentation, cytokine release, and fibrosis activation.
questions.imageAlt: Hallmark cells and their roles in chronic inflammation
questions.sourceRef: Inflammation  — Question bank Q9

questions.question: Which chronic inflammation pattern features foamy, lipid-accumulating macrophages and may mimic malignancy?
questions.explanation: Xanthomatous inflammation is characterized by foamy macrophages and lipid accumulation and is noted as a surgical mimic of malignancy.
questions.imageAlt: Morphological patterns of chronic inflammation
questions.sourceRef: Inflammation  — Question bank Q10

questions.question: Which systemic complication can occur with prolonged chronic inflammatory disease and is associated with AA-type amyloid?
questions.explanation: The lecture lists amyloidosis of AA type among systemic effects of prolonged chronic inflammation.
questions.imageAlt: Systemic effects associated with prolonged chronic inflammation
questions.sourceRef: Inflammation  — Question bank Q11

questions.question: Which cytokine released by Th1 CD4+ T cells drives macrophage activation and epithelioid transformation in granuloma formation?
questions.explanation: The formation pathway shows Th1 cells releasing IFN-gamma, which activates macrophages and promotes epithelioid transformation.
questions.imageAlt: Granuloma formation pathway
questions.sourceRef: Inflammation  — Question bank Q12

questions.question: Which giant-cell type is associated in the lecture with caseating tuberculosis granulomas?
options: Foreign-body giant cells with haphazard nuclei
Langhans giant cells with peripheral horseshoe-shaped nuclei
Touton giant cells with lipid-laden borders
questions.explanation: The question-bank explanation associates Langhans giant cells with tuberculosis granulomas; the slide table also lists Langhans cells for tuberculosis.
questions.imageAlt: Granuloma types and giant-cell associations
questions.sourceRef: Inflammation  — Question bank Q13

questions.question: How do sarcoidosis and Crohn disease granulomas differ from the tuberculosis granuloma described in the lecture?
options: They have central caseous necrosis identical to tuberculosis.
They are non-caseating, without central necrosis.
They contain abundant neutrophils and frank pus.
They consist only of plasma cells and B lymphocytes.
questions.explanation: The slide table marks sarcoidosis and Crohn disease as having no necrosis, unlike caseating tuberculosis.
questions.imageAlt: Comparison of granuloma examples and necrosis status
questions.sourceRef: Inflammation  — Question bank Q14

questions.question: What surgical complication can result from fibrosis following chronic inflammation in Crohn disease?
questions.explanation: The lecture links fibrosis after chronic inflammation to intestinal stricture and obstruction, including in Crohn disease.
questions.imageAlt: Fibrosis-related clinical complications
questions.sourceRef: Inflammation  — Question bank Q15

questions.question: Which components are listed in the lecture as characteristic of the acute suppurative infiltrate in a surgical site infection?
options: Lymphocytes, caseous necrosis, and foreign-body giant cells
Epithelioid macrophages, plasma cells, and dense collagen
Foamy macrophages, cholesterol clefts, and hemosiderin
questions.explanation: The question bank identifies the suppurative infiltrate as neutrophils, fibrin, and bacteria; the slides describe pus as PMNs plus debris and list neutrophilic infiltrate, fibrin, and bacteria in wound infection.
questions.imageAlt: Pathological findings associated with surgical site infection
questions.sourceRef: Inflammation  — Question bank Q16

questions.question: What mechanism does the lecture associate with malignant transformation during chronic inflammation?
options: Reduced cellular turnover that protects DNA integrity
Mutagenic reactive oxygen species and pro-inflammatory cytokines
Immediate apoptosis of all precancerous cells
Permanent hypoplasia of the gastric mucosa
questions.explanation: The slides associate chronic inflammation with increased mutagenic ROS and cytokines, and cite H. pylori-related gastric malignancy.
questions.imageAlt: Chronic inflammation and long-term malignant risk
questions.sourceRef: Inflammation  — Question bank Q17

questions.question: What rule of thumb does the question bank give for interpreting a caseating granuloma?
options: All granulomas are sterile and need no microbiological culture.
Foreign-body granulomas contain Langhans cells with peripheral nuclei.
questions.explanation: The bank states that a caseating granuloma should be considered tuberculosis until proven otherwise; this is also a slide takeaway.
questions.imageAlt: Clinical takeaways for interpreting granulomatous inflammation
questions.sourceRef: Inflammation  — Question bank Q18

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of the inflammatory response described in the lecture?
options: Permanently destroy vascular integrity and induce shock
Destroy the causative agent and repair tissue damage
Replace normal parenchymal cells with adipose tissue
Suppress immune-cell recruitment and prevent antibody production
questions.explanation: The lecture defines inflammation as a protective response designed to destroy the causative agent and repair tissue damage.
questions.imageAlt: Definition and purpose of inflammation
questions.sourceRef: Inflammation  — Question bank Q19

questions.question: Why does the lecture recommend surveillance colonoscopy for patients with long-standing inflammatory bowel disease?
options: To monitor stricture formation and remove sutures
Because long-standing chronic inflammation in IBD carries increased colorectal cancer risk
To evaluate acute neutrophil degranulation inhibitors
To prevent caseating granulomas in the colon
questions.explanation: The lecture links chronic inflammation in IBD with colorectal cancer risk and specifies surveillance colonoscopy.
questions.imageAlt: Long-term clinical risk and surveillance in inflammatory bowel disease
questions.sourceRef: Inflammation  — Question bank Q20

questions.question: Which event occurs after vascular permeability increases in the sequence of acute inflammation presented in the slides?
options: Stasis, with slowed blood flow and leukocytes concentrating near the vessel wall
questions.explanation: The slide sequence places stasis after increased vascular permeability and describes leukocytes concentrating near the vessel wall during stasis.
questions.imageAlt: Sequence of vascular events in acute inflammation
questions.sourceRef: Supplementary question derived from Lecture 3 slides, PDF page 4

questions.question: Which set of intracellular mechanisms is listed for leukocyte killing after phagocytosis?
options: Nitric oxide, reactive oxygen species, and lysosomal enzymes
questions.explanation: The slide states that after engulfment leukocytes perform intracellular killing using NO, ROS, and lysosomal enzymes.
questions.imageAlt: Leukocyte activation and intracellular killing
questions.sourceRef: Supplementary question derived from Lecture 3 slides, PDF page 5

questions.question: According to the slides, which event helps terminate acute inflammation?
options: Neutrophils undergo apoptosis and macrophages clear debris and dead cells
questions.explanation: The termination and resolution steps include neutrophil apoptosis and macrophage clearance of debris and dead cells.
questions.imageAlt: Events involved in termination and resolution
questions.sourceRef: Supplementary question derived from Lecture 3 slides, PDF page 5

questions.question: Which condition is specified by the slides as necessary for complete restoration of normal tissue during resolution?
questions.explanation: The outcomes slide says resolution restores normal tissue and requires minimal injury with no necrosis.
questions.imageAlt: Contrasting outcomes of acute inflammation
questions.sourceRef: Supplementary question derived from Lecture 3 slides, PDF page 8

questions.question: Which is listed among the causes that can lead to chronic inflammation?
options: Persistent toxic exposure such as silica or asbestos
A brief stimulus that is completely eliminated
Normal tissue repair without ongoing stimulus
questions.explanation: The lecture lists prolonged toxic exposure, including silica and asbestos, among causes of chronicity.
questions.imageAlt: Examples of causes and hallmark cells of chronic inflammation
questions.sourceRef: Supplementary question derived from Lecture 3 slides, PDF page 10

questions.question: What architectural feature defines the follicular pattern of chronic inflammation in the slides?
questions.explanation: The slides define the follicular pattern by lymphoid follicles with germinal centres.
questions.imageAlt: Morphological patterns of chronic inflammation
questions.sourceRef: Supplementary question derived from Lecture 3 slides, PDF page 11

questions.question: Which sequence best matches the granuloma formation pathway described in the slides?
options: Failed antigen digestion by macrophage, Th1 release of IFN-gamma, macrophage activation and epithelioid transformation, giant-cell formation, then lymphocytes and fibrosis
Neutrophil apoptosis, mast-cell histamine release, plasma-cell formation, then vasodilation
Fibrosis first, followed by transudate formation and leukocyte margination
B-cell activation, antibody secretion, then disappearance of macrophages
questions.explanation: The slide pathway proceeds from a macrophage failing to digest antigen to Th1 IFN-gamma release, macrophage activation and epithelioid transformation, fusion into giant cells, and surrounding lymphocytes and fibrosis.
questions.imageAlt: Cellular sequence involved in granuloma formation
questions.sourceRef: Supplementary question derived from Lecture 3 slides, PDF page 12

title: Day 4 — Circulatory Disturbances & Neoplasia: Grade, Stage & Biomarkers
description: 80 pathology MCQs from Lectures 4–6: Circulatory Disturbances, Neoplasia, and Grading, Staging & Biological Markers. Supplementary items are derived only from the matching lecture slides.

references.label: Question bank — Cell injury and death (combined Lectures 2 and 4)
Lecture 5 — Neoplasia, Local Invasion & Metastasis slides PDF
Question bank — Neoplasia..grading and staging (combined Lectures 5 and 6)
Lecture 6 — Grading, Staging & Biological Markers slides PDF

questions.question: What fundamental hemodynamic difference separates Hyperemia from Congestion?
options: Hyperemia is an active process driven by arteriolar dilation increasing blood inflow, whereas congestion is a passive process caused by impaired venous outflow.
Hyperemia involves cyanotic cold tissues, while congestion produces warm, erythematous tissues.
Hyperemia results exclusively from right heart failure, while congestion results from physical exercise.
Hyperemia is a pathological process, whereas congestion is always a normal physiological response.
questions.explanation: Active hyperemia increases arterial inflow (e.g., exercise, inflammation), whereas passive congestion stems from impaired venous outflow (e.g., heart failure).
questions.imageAlt: Lecture summary comparing active hyperemia with passive congestion.
questions.sourceRef: Cell injury and death (combined bank: Circulatory Disturbances) — Question bank Q15

questions.question: What macroscopic and microscopic features characterize a "Nutmeg Liver" resulting from chronic passive hepatic congestion?
options: Uniform pale yellow discoloration throughout all hepatic lobules due to massive glycogen storage
Centrilobular congestion, hemorrhage, and necrosis with periportal fatty change, creating a mottled red-brown cut surface resembling a nutmeg kernel
Diffuse fibrosis of the portal triads with complete sparing of the central veins
Marked dilation of the hepatic artery branches with ischemic atrophy of Kupffer cells
questions.explanation: Chronic right heart failure causes centrilobular congestion and necrosis alongside periportal steatosis, giving the liver a nutmeg appearance.
questions.imageAlt: Slide showing the nutmeg liver pattern in chronic passive hepatic congestion.
questions.sourceRef: Cell injury and death (combined bank: Circulatory Disturbances) — Question bank Q16

questions.question: What are "Heart Failure Cells" found in chronic passive congestion of the lungs?
options: Hypertrophied cardiac myocytes shed into the pulmonary venous bloodstream
Hemosiderin-laden alveolar macrophages resulting from phagocytosis of extravasated red blood cells in chronic pulmonary congestion
Neoplastic alveolar epithelial cells seen in left-sided valvular tumors
Neutrophils undergoing apoptosis within alveolar exudates
questions.explanation: Left heart failure causes alveolar capillary engorgement and microhemorrhages; macrophages take up iron and become hemosiderin-laden "heart failure cells".
questions.imageAlt: Slide showing chronic passive lung congestion and heart-failure cells.
questions.sourceRef: Cell injury and death (combined bank: Circulatory Disturbances) — Question bank Q17

questions.question: How do Transudates differ from Exudates in fluid accumulation (edema/effusions)?
options: Transudates have high protein content (>3 g/dL) and high cellularity due to active inflammation.
Transudates are non-inflammatory ultrafiltrates of plasma with low protein content (<3 g/dL) and few cells, caused by Starling-force imbalances.
Exudates are caused exclusively by left ventricular heart failure and hepatic cirrhosis.
Exudates have a specific gravity of less than 1.012 and lack inflammatory cells entirely.
questions.explanation: Transudates result from Starling-force imbalances (low protein, non-inflammatory), while exudates stem from increased vascular permeability during inflammation.
questions.imageAlt: Slide comparing transudate and exudate.
questions.sourceRef: Cell injury and death (combined bank: Circulatory Disturbances) — Question bank Q18

questions.question: Which four primary physiological mechanisms account for the formation of clinical Edema?
options: Increased vascular hydrostatic pressure, decreased plasma oncotic pressure, lymphatic obstruction, and sodium/water retention
Decreased arterial blood pressure, increased plasma albumin synthesis, enhanced renal perfusion, and local vasoconstriction
Primary bone marrow failure, hypercoagulability, endothelial denudation, and stasis
Excessive red blood cell mass, platelet hyperactivity, increased capillary fragility, and rapid thrombolysis
questions.explanation: Edema is governed by Starling forces and fluid regulation: high hydrostatic pressure, low oncotic pressure, lymphatic blockage, and renal salt/water retention.
questions.imageAlt: Slide listing the four mechanisms of edema.
questions.sourceRef: Cell injury and death (combined bank: Circulatory Disturbances) — Question bank Q19

questions.question: What terminology describes pinpoint hemorrhages measuring 1–2 mm in the skin or mucosa, typically indicative of low platelet count or platelet dysfunction?
questions.explanation: Petechiae are tiny 1–2 mm hemorrhages linked to platelet defects, whereas purpura (>3 mm) and ecchymoses (1–2 cm bruises) are larger.
questions.imageAlt: Slide defining petechiae, purpura and ecchymoses.
questions.sourceRef: Cell injury and death (combined bank: Circulatory Disturbances) — Question bank Q20

questions.question: What is the single most important determinant of the clinical impact and severity of a Hemorrhage?
options: The anatomical color of the bruising on the skin surface
The total volume of blood lost and the rate at which it is lost
Whether the bleeding is classified as a transudate or an exudate
The patient's resting pulse rate prior to injury
questions.explanation: Volume lost and rate of loss dictate clinical severity; rapid loss of >20% of blood volume risks hemorrhagic shock.
questions.imageAlt: Lecture slide illustrating hemorrhage clinical significance
questions.sourceRef: Cell injury and death (combined bank: Circulatory Disturbances) — Q21

questions.question: What are the three components of Virchow's Triad that predispose to pathologic thrombosis?
options: Endothelial injury, abnormal blood flow (stasis or turbulence), and hypercoagulability
Platelet depletion, vitamin K deficiency, and excessive fibrinolysis
Increased cardiac output, arterial vasoconstriction, and lymphatic obstruction
questions.explanation: Virchow's triad comprises endothelial injury, abnormal blood flow, and hypercoagulability—all three of which surgery classically contributes to.
questions.imageAlt: Lecture slide illustrating Virchow triad
questions.sourceRef: Cell injury and death (combined bank: Circulatory Disturbances) — Q22

questions.question: What structural features distinguish an Arterial ("White") Thrombus from a Venous ("Red") Thrombus?
options: Arterial thrombi are erythrocyte-rich and form in deep leg vein valve pockets, while venous thrombi are platelet-rich and form on atherosclerotic plaques.
Arterial thrombi are platelet- and fibrin-rich with alternating "Lines of Zahn", whereas venous thrombi are erythrocyte-rich, resembling stagnant clotted blood.
Arterial thrombi never undergo organization or recanalization.
Venous thrombi exclusively cause myocardial infarction and acute stroke.
questions.explanation: Arterial white thrombi are platelet/fibrin-rich with Lines of Zahn at injury sites, while venous red thrombi are erythrocyte-rich clots formed in areas of stasis.
questions.imageAlt: Lecture slide illustrating arterial and venous thrombi
questions.sourceRef: Cell injury and death (combined bank: Circulatory Disturbances) — Q23

questions.question: What are the possible pathological fates of a newly formed thrombus within a blood vessel?
options: Propagation, embolization, dissolution, organization, and recanalization
Immediate transformation into a transudate effusion
Spontaneous conversion into an active hyperemic vascular bed
Encapsulation by adipose tissue and calcification without local effect
questions.explanation: Thrombi can propagate, dissolve via fibrinolysis, embolize, or undergo organization and recanalization to restore blood flow.
questions.imageAlt: Lecture slide illustrating thrombus fates
questions.sourceRef: Cell injury and death (combined bank: Circulatory Disturbances) — Q24

questions.question: What percentage of clinical pulmonary emboli originate from deep vein thrombosis in the lower extremities (femoral, popliteal, and iliac veins)?
options: Exactly 100% with no other known sources
questions.explanation: Over 95% of pulmonary thromboemboli originate from deep leg vein thrombi.
questions.imageAlt: Lecture slide illustrating pulmonary thromboembolism
questions.sourceRef: Cell injury and death (combined bank: Circulatory Disturbances) — Q25

questions.question: What is a Saddle Embolus, and what is its immediate clinical consequence?
options: A small fat globule lodged in a renal glomerulus causing microscopic hematuria
A large thromboembolus straddling the pulmonary artery bifurcation, capable of causing sudden death
An air bubble trapped in the right ventricular outflow tract during laparoscopy
A mural thrombus inside the left atrial appendage
questions.explanation: A saddle embolus occludes the main pulmonary artery bifurcation, leading to acute right heart failure and sudden death.
questions.imageAlt: Lecture slide illustrating saddle embolism
questions.sourceRef: Cell injury and death (combined bank: Circulatory Disturbances) — Q26

questions.question: What clinical presentation is characteristic of Fat Embolism Syndrome following long-bone fractures or major orthopedic surgery?
options: Immediate onset painless jaundice and hepatomegaly within 30 minutes
A classic triad of petechial rash, dyspnea, and neurologic symptoms developing 1–3 days after injury
Massive upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage from stress ulceration
Spontaneous arterial vasospasm and dry gangrene of all four limbs
questions.explanation: Fat embolism syndrome manifests 1–3 days post-trauma with pulmonary symptoms, neurological impairment, and a characteristic petechial rash.
questions.imageAlt: Lecture slide illustrating fat embolism
questions.sourceRef: Cell injury and death (combined bank: Circulatory Disturbances) — Q27

questions.question: What volume of intravenous air is generally estimated to be required to produce clinical air embolism symptoms in humans?
questions.explanation: Roughly 100 mL of air introduced into the circulation can produce significant clinical effects or a "gas lock" obstructing right ventricular outflow.
questions.imageAlt: Lecture slide illustrating air embolism
questions.sourceRef: Cell injury and death (combined bank: Circulatory Disturbances) — Q28

questions.question: How are Infarcts anatomically classified based on their gross appearance and underlying vascular supply?
options: Primary infarcts versus secondary metastatic infarcts
questions.explanation: Infarcts are classified as white (solid organs with end-arterial supply like heart/spleen) or red (loose tissues/dual supply like lung/intestine).
questions.imageAlt: Lecture slide illustrating infarct classification
questions.sourceRef: Cell injury and death (combined bank: Circulatory Disturbances) — Q29

questions.question: Why do tissues like the lung and small intestine characteristically develop Red (Hemorrhagic) Infarcts following vascular occlusion?
options: Because they possess a strict end-arterial supply with zero collateral vessels.
Because they feature loose tissue structure or dual blood supplies that permit blood to seep into the necrotic zone from anastomosing channels.
Because their cells are completely immune to hypoxic injury and oxidative stress.
Because venous drainage is always permanently unobstructed.
questions.explanation: Loose tissues and dual blood supplies allow blood to accumulate in the infarcted area, producing a red, hemorrhagic appearance.
questions.imageAlt: Lecture slide illustrating red infarcts
questions.sourceRef: Cell injury and death (combined bank: Circulatory Disturbances) — Q30

questions.question: Which tissue or organ demonstrates the highest sensitivity and shortest tolerance to complete ischemia (hypoxia)?
options: Brain neurons (tolerate only 3–4 minutes of ischemia)
questions.explanation: Neurons in the central nervous system tolerate only 3–4 minutes of ischemia, whereas myocardium tolerates 20–30 minutes and fibroblasts are more resistant.
questions.imageAlt: Lecture slide illustrating ischemia tolerance
questions.sourceRef: Cell injury and death (combined bank: Circulatory Disturbances) — Q31

questions.question: How does the healing process of an Infarct in the brain differ from infarcts in other solid organs (like the heart or kidney)?
options: Brain infarcts heal by forming a dense collagenous fibrous scar.
Brain tissue undergoes liquefactive necrosis which resolves into a fluid-filled cystic cavity rather than a fibrous scar.
Brain infarcts never undergo any structural remodeling or macrophage clearance.
Brain tissue regenerates entirely back to normal functional neurons.
questions.explanation: Unlike solid organs where infarcts are replaced by fibrous scars, liquefactive necrosis in the brain leaves behind a fluid-filled cystic space.
questions.imageAlt: Lecture slide illustrating infarct healing
questions.sourceRef: Cell injury and death (combined bank: Circulatory Disturbances) — Q32

questions.question: What is the primary definition of Shock in circulatory pathology?
options: Transient local arterial vasospasm resulting in localized tissue blanching
Systemic hypoperfusion leading to cellular hypoxia and, if uncorrected, cell death
Acute hypertension driven by excessive catecholamine release during surgery
Localized venous congestion due to deep vein thrombosis
questions.explanation: Shock is systemic hypoperfusion causing widespread cellular hypoxia and organ dysfunction.
questions.imageAlt: Lecture slide illustrating shock definition
questions.sourceRef: Cell injury and death (combined bank: Circulatory Disturbances) — Q33

questions.question: What are the primary etiologic categories of Shock?
options: Cardiogenic, hypovolemic, septic, anaphylactic, and neurogenic
Ischemic, metabolic, toxic, traumatic, and genetic
questions.explanation: Shock is classified into cardiogenic, hypovolemic, septic, anaphylactic, and neurogenic types based on underlying pathophysiology.
questions.imageAlt: Lecture slide illustrating shock classification
questions.sourceRef: Cell injury and death (combined bank: Circulatory Disturbances) — Q34

questions.question: What pathophysiological mechanisms operate in Septic Shock?
options: Primary failure of the cardiac pacemaker node without peripheral vasodilation
Endotoxin and cytokine release causing systemic vasodilation, increased vascular permeability, myocardial depression, and often disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)
Acute IgE-mediated bronchospasm without endothelial activation
Complete loss of spinal sympathetic outflow following local anesthetic administration
questions.explanation: Septic shock involves microbial mediators triggering widespread vasodilation, capillary leak, myocardial dysfunction, and coagulopathy.
questions.imageAlt: Lecture slide illustrating septic shock mechanisms
questions.sourceRef: Cell injury and death (combined bank: Circulatory Disturbances) — Q35

questions.question: What clinical and physiological events characterize the Nonprogressive (Compensated) stage of Shock?
options: Reflex compensatory mechanisms (tachycardia, peripheral vasoconstriction, renal fluid conservation) maintain adequate perfusion of vital organs.
Complete failure of blood pressure with irreversible multi-organ system failure
Massive peripheral vasodilation and warm, flushed extremities without tachycardia
Immediate cessation of all neuroendocrine stress hormone output
questions.explanation: In compensated shock, neurohormonal reflexes sustain blood pressure and perfusion to vital organs before decompensation occurs.
questions.imageAlt: Lecture slide illustrating shock stages
questions.sourceRef: Cell injury and death (combined bank: Circulatory Disturbances) — Q36

questions.question: Which organs are classically designated as "Shock Organs" displaying characteristic pathological lesions during prolonged systemic hypoperfusion?
options: Kidneys (acute tubular necrosis), Lungs (ARDS/diffuse alveolar damage), Brain (ischemic encephalopathy), Heart, and Gastrointestinal tract
Thyroid gland, skeletal muscles, and skin epidermis exclusively
Gallbladder, spleen, and pancreas with complete sparing of the kidneys
Large conducting arteries and peripheral nerve trunks
questions.explanation: Prolonged shock targets vulnerable organs, producing acute tubular necrosis in kidneys, ARDS in lungs, and ischemic injury in the brain, heart, and gut.
questions.imageAlt: Lecture slide illustrating shock organs
questions.sourceRef: Cell injury and death (combined bank: Circulatory Disturbances) — Q37

questions.question: Why does Testicular Torsion represent a surgical emergency regarding circulatory disturbances?
options: It causes immediate systemic anaphylaxis through antigen release.
It causes venous outflow obstruction followed by arterial compromise, leading to a time-critical hemorrhagic (red) infarction of the gonad.
It triggers dry gangrene that can be managed safely with observation alone.
It induces metastatic calcification of the spermatic cord.
questions.explanation: Testicular torsion compromises venous drainage first and then arterial inflow, producing a red infarction that requires urgent surgical detorsion.
questions.imageAlt: Lecture slide illustrating infarction surgical relevance
questions.sourceRef: Cell injury and death (combined bank: Circulatory Disturbances) — Q38

questions.question: What is the primary surgical rationale for Damage-Control Surgery in severe trauma patients presenting with hemorrhagic shock?
options: To complete all definitive anatomical reconstructions and cosmetic closures in a single 8-hour operation
To prioritize rapid hemorrhage and contamination control over definitive repair, preventing the lethal triad of hypothermia, acidosis, and coagulopathy
To avoid administering any blood products or intravenous crystalloids
To delay all surgical intervention until laboratory clotting parameters are 100% normal
questions.explanation: Damage-control surgery prioritizes arresting bleeding and containing contamination quickly in unstable patients before physiological exhaustion occurs.
questions.imageAlt: Lecture slide illustrating hemorrhage management
questions.sourceRef: Cell injury and death (combined bank: Circulatory Disturbances) — Q39

questions.question: How does Ischemia-Reperfusion Injury impact organ transplantation and vascular surgery?
options: Releasing the vascular clamp or restoring blood flow delivers oxygen that triggers a burst of ROS and inflammation, paradoxically worsening tissue damage in the graft or limb.
It guarantees 100% immediate cell survival and instant tissue regeneration.
It converts all ischemic tissue into stable fibrous scar tissue within seconds.
It prevents any post-operative thrombosis or edema formation.
questions.explanation: Reperfusion injury is critical in transplantation and vascular clamping because returning blood flow paradoxically exacerbates cellular injury via oxidative stress and inflammation.
questions.imageAlt: Lecture slide illustrating reperfusion injury
questions.sourceRef: Cell injury and death (combined bank: Circulatory Disturbances) — Q40

questions.question: What presentation is described for amniotic fluid embolism?
options: Gradual leg swelling followed by chronic pulmonary hypertension
Sudden dyspnea, cyanosis, and shock, often followed by disseminated intravascular coagulation
Petechial rash and neurologic symptoms 1–3 days after a long-bone fracture
A confined collection of blood within a body cavity
questions.explanation: Amniotic fluid embolism is described with sudden dyspnea, cyanosis, and shock, often followed by DIC.
questions.imageAlt: Slide describing amniotic fluid embolism
questions.sourceRef: Supplementary question derived from Lecture 4 slides, PDF page 46

questions.question: Which core characteristic defines neoplasia and distinguishes it from a normal hyperplastic response?
options: Coordinated, reversible growth driven by continuous hormonal stimulation.
Uncoordinated, autonomous growth that persists in the same excessive manner after the initiating stimulus is withdrawn.
Multiclonal proliferation originating from multiple independent transformed parent cells.
Complete absence of heritable genetic alterations within the proliferating cell population.
questions.explanation: Neoplasia is uncoordinated, autonomous, clonal tissue growth that continues after the inciting stimulus is removed.
questions.imageAlt: Slide defining neoplasia and summarizing its core properties

questions.question: Which pair names a benign tumor arising from glandular epithelium and its malignant counterpart?

questions.question: What distinguishes a hamartoma from a true neoplasm?
options: It is a malignant mesenchymal tumor with high mitotic activity.
It is a developmental malformation of disorganized but mature native tissue, rather than a true neoplasm.
It arises from more than one germ cell layer via totipotent cells.
It always metastasizes exclusively by hematogenous spread.
questions.explanation: The source describes a hamartoma as disorganized but mature native tissue forming a developmental malformation, not a true neoplasm.
questions.imageAlt: Slide comparing special tumor categories, including hamartoma

questions.question: Which set of microscopic findings is characteristic of malignant anaplasia?
options: Uniform cell size, preserved polarity, and rare normal mitoses
Pleomorphism, enlarged hyperchromatic nuclei, a high N:C ratio, and atypical mitoses
Well-formed glandular tubules with abundant mucin and low growth fraction
Intact basement membranes separating epithelial nests from stroma
questions.explanation: Anaplasia is characterized by variation in cell size and shape, hyperchromatic enlarged nuclei, a high N:C ratio, abnormal mitoses, and loss of polarity.

questions.question: How does local growth of a malignant tumor differ from that of a benign tumor, as described in the source?
options: Benign tumors often form a fibrous capsule and push surrounding tissue; malignant tumors lack a capsule and infiltrate and destroy surrounding tissue.
Malignant tumors rely on encapsulation to compress adjacent organs.
Benign tumors actively degrade basement membranes with matrix metalloproteinases.
Malignant invasion is driven by increased intercellular adhesion through E-cadherin.
questions.explanation: The source contrasts expansile, often encapsulated benign growth with unencapsulated malignant growth that penetrates and destroys neighboring tissue.

questions.question: Which molecular and cellular changes facilitate tumor-cell invasion through the extracellular matrix?
options: Increased E-cadherin and suppression of cellular motility
Reduced intercellular adhesion, protease-mediated matrix degradation, and acquisition of motility
Synthesis of thick basement membranes around individual cells
Permanent arrest of proteolytic enzyme transcription
questions.explanation: The slide lists loss of intercellular adhesion, extracellular-matrix degradation by proteases such as matrix metalloproteinases, and acquisition of tumor-cell motility as key mechanisms.

questions.question: What is the single most reliable feature distinguishing malignant from benign neoplasms?
options: A high mitotic rate and cellular pleomorphism
Metastasis, meaning secondary tumor deposits discontinuous with the primary
Elevated serum CA-125 and CEA levels
A primary tumor larger than 10 centimeters
questions.explanation: The source defines metastasis as discontinuous secondary tumor deposits and identifies it as the most reliable distinction between malignant and benign tumors.

questions.question: Which three routes of metastatic spread are described in the lecture?
options: Direct seeding of body cavities, lymphatic spread, and hematogenous spread
Perineural tracking, trans-epithelial migration, and airborne transmission
Arterial embolism, ductal reflux, and osmotic diffusion
Superficial ulceration, mechanical pressure, and thermal conduction
questions.explanation: The lecture enumerates direct seeding, lymphatic spread, and hematogenous spread as the three routes.

questions.question: Which route of metastasis is favored by carcinomas compared with sarcomas in the lecture?
options: Carcinomas favor hematogenous spread; sarcomas favor direct cavity seeding.
Carcinomas favor lymphatic spread; sarcomas favor hematogenous spread.
questions.explanation: The lecture identifies lymphatic spread as favored by carcinomas and hematogenous spread as favored by sarcomas.

questions.question: Why is the metastatic cascade described as intrinsically inefficient?
options: Tumor cells cannot enter blood vessels.
Only a small fraction of circulating tumor cells survive shear stress and immune attack and establish a significant deposit.
All metastatic cells undergo immediate apoptosis inside lymph nodes.
Host tissues inhibit angiogenesis throughout the body.
questions.explanation: The slide states that most tumor cells entering circulation are destroyed by shear stress or immune attack, and only a small fraction establish a clinically significant deposit.
questions.imageAlt: Slide outlining stages and inefficiency of the metastatic cascade

questions.question: What does the lecture identify as a basis for tumors preferentially colonizing particular organs?
options: Organotropism involving adhesion-molecule expression and a favorable local seed-and-soil microenvironment
Absence of capillary beds in all non-target organs
Mechanical trapping of large clusters in renal glomeruli
questions.explanation: The slide attributes organotropism to adhesion-molecule expression and a favorable target-organ microenvironment, not merely vascular anatomy.

questions.question: Which functional gene classes are identified as central to the molecular basis of cancer?
options: Structural collagen, keratin, and hemoglobin genes
Proto-oncogenes, tumor suppressor genes, DNA repair genes, and apoptosis-regulating genes
Ribosomal RNA and mitochondrial transfer genes
questions.explanation: The lecture lists these four classes as governing growth, survival, and genomic integrity in cancer.

questions.question: How do proto-oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes differ in the mutation patterns described?
options: Proto-oncogenes undergo loss of function, while tumor suppressors undergo gain of function.
Proto-oncogenes can acquire gain-of-function changes that drive proliferation, while tumor suppressors can lose function and remove cell-cycle brakes.
Proto-oncogenes regulate DNA repair exclusively, while tumor suppressors control respiration.
Tumor suppressors are viral genes, while proto-oncogenes are strictly inherited.
questions.explanation: The source describes gain-of-function activation of proto-oncogenes and loss of function in tumor suppressors, removing normal restraints on the cell cycle.

questions.question: What distinguishes direct-acting from indirect-acting chemical carcinogens in the lecture?
options: Direct-acting agents require liver activation; indirect-acting agents do not.
Direct-acting agents need no metabolic conversion, whereas indirect-acting agents require metabolic activation.
Direct-acting agents cause only benign tumors, whereas indirect agents cause sarcomas.
Direct-acting agents are plant alkaloids, whereas indirect agents are radiation.

options: Increasing normal self-antigen expression to trigger T-cell expansion
Reducing antigen presentation, secreting immunosuppressive factors, and co-opting immune checkpoints
Destroying all regional lymph nodes before primary tumor growth

questions.question: How does cancer cachexia manifest clinically in the lecture?
options: Rapid weight gain and marked visceral fat accumulation
Progressive weight loss, muscle atrophy, and weakness disproportionate to tumor bulk
Loss of appetite solely from mechanical esophageal obstruction
Acute fluid retention identical to nephrotic syndrome
