questions.question: What clinical significance of paraneoplastic syndromes is noted in the lecture?
options: They are caused exclusively by direct compression of local nerve roots.
They may be the first clue to an occult malignancy, even when a tumor is too small to cause local symptoms.
They occur only in patients with benign adenomas.

Lymph-node colonization, primary tumor regression, and local encapsulation

Angiogenesis, immune surveillance, and formation of a fibrous capsule

They drain only to regional lymph nodes through natural channels.

questions.question: According to the lecture, how do tumor cells spread through lymphatic channels?

They enter a body cavity and implant on serosal surfaces.
They travel through veins directly to the first capillary bed.

Directly to serosal surfaces within the peritoneal cavity
Back into the primary tumor through lymphatic channels

The tumor is surrounded by a thick capsule that cannot be opened.

questions.question: What components make up the core TNM Staging Classification framework?
options: Total tumor weight (T), number of mitoses (N), and margin status (M).
Size/local extent of primary tumor (T), regional lymph node involvement (N), and presence of distant metastasis (M).
Tissue differentiation (T), necrosis percentage (N), and vascular invasion (M).
Translocation status (T), nuclear grade (N), and molecular profile (M).

questions.question: What distinguishes Clinical Staging (cTNM) from Pathologic Staging (pTNM)?
options: Clinical staging relies on physical exams, imaging, and pre-treatment biopsy, whereas pathologic staging relies on histologic examination of surgically resected tissues.
Clinical staging is only performed post-mortem during autopsy.
Pathologic staging never evaluates regional lymph nodes or surgical margins.
Clinical staging is completely independent of the TNM framework.
questions.explanation: cTNM uses pre-treatment examination, imaging, and biopsy; pTNM uses histology from resected tissue, including nodes and margins.

questions.question: Which specialized staging system is universally applied to Lymphomas based on the number and location of involved lymph node regions relative to the diaphragm?

questions.question: What is the clinical utility of a Sentinel Lymph Node Biopsy?
options: To completely remove all lymphatic chains in the body to prevent primary tumor initiation.
To identify and assess the first-draining lymph node for regional spread with significantly less morbidity than full nodal dissection.
To measure circulating serum PSA and CEA levels pre-operatively.
To deliver targeted radiation directly to distant bone metastases.
questions.explanation: It identifies the first-draining node to assess regional spread while causing less morbidity than full nodal dissection.

It indicates benign biological behavior and eliminates the need for chemotherapy.

questions.question: What clinical implication is associated with KRAS mutations in Colorectal Carcinoma?

They predict primary resistance to anti-EGFR antibody therapy.

questions.question: What advantage does a 'Liquid Biopsy' (measuring ctDNA or CTCs) offer over traditional tissue biopsy?
options: It provides exact 3D architectural tissue orientation and surgical margin status.
It is minimally invasive, easily repeatable over time, and captures tumor heterogeneity across multiple metastatic sites.
It completely replaces the need for any microscopic pathology or clinical staging.
It has 100% specificity with zero risk of false-positive elevations.

questions.question: What are the primary limitations associated with serum tumor markers in clinical oncology?
options: 100% sensitivity and specificity across all early-stage cancers.
Limited sensitivity and specificity, potential false positives from benign conditions, and inability to serve as standalone diagnostic tools.
Complete instability when exposed to standard laboratory storage temperatures.
Inability to be measured via automated blood analyzers.
questions.explanation: Markers may be absent in some tumors, elevated in benign conditions or other cancers, and cannot replace histologic diagnosis.

questions.topic: Clinical Integration of Grade, Stage & Biomarkers
questions.question: How are Grade, Stage, and Biomarkers integrated in clinical oncology decision-making?
options: They are evaluated in isolation, where stage alone determines all medical and surgical treatment protocols.
They answer distinct questions (aggressiveness, spread, molecular profile) and are integrated together to form an individualized prognosis and multi-modal treatment plan.
Biomarkers completely replace histological grading and anatomical staging in modern practice.
Grading is utilized exclusively for epidemiological statistics rather than patient care.
questions.explanation: Optimal prognosis and personalized treatment planning require integrating grade, stage, and biological markers together.
questions.imageAlt: Slide showing how grade, stage and biological markers combine in clinical decision-making.

questions.question: Which antibiogram practice does the lecture recommend when selecting empiric therapy?
options: Choose therapy only from the broadest available drug class.
Use the same national resistance estimate for every setting.
Use the local antibiogram rather than memorizing national data.
Ignore the antibiogram until the full treatment course is complete.
questions.explanation: The lecture's take-points say to know the local antibiogram and not memorize national data.
questions.imageAlt: Antimicrobial Resistance, slide 51; related topic: Antibiogram and empiric therapy
questions.sourceRef: Supplementary — Lecture 2 slides, slide 51

questions.question: Which description best matches an emerging infectious disease (EID) as defined in the lecture?
options: Any infection that is transmitted only by airborne droplets
An infection caused only by a pathogen never seen in animals
An infection that has disappeared permanently from every region
An infection caused by a novel pathogen or one increasing in incidence, expanding geographically, or acquiring new transmission dynamics
questions.explanation: The lecture defines EIDs to include novel pathogens and known pathogens with increased incidence, geographic expansion, or new transmission dynamics.
questions.imageAlt: Emerging Pathogens, slide 5; related topic: Emerging infectious diseases
questions.sourceRef: Supplementary — Lecture 3 slides, slide 5

questions.question: What distinguishes a re-emerging infectious disease in the lecture?
options: It is an infection that appears after a significant decline in incidence
It is always caused by a newly discovered virus
It is an infection that has never caused an outbreak
It is an infection restricted to animals
questions.explanation: Re-emerging infections return after their incidence has significantly declined and may reappear in epidemic proportions.
questions.imageAlt: Emerging Pathogens, slide 10; related topic: Emerging versus re-emerging diseases
questions.sourceRef: Supplementary — Lecture 3 slides, slide 10

questions.question: Which set contains only drivers of emergence named in the lecture introduction?
options: Reduced travel, lower antibiotic use, and stable ecosystems
Increased travel and trade, antibiotic overuse, environmental changes, and pathogen evolution
Declining urbanization, reduced food processing, and vector elimination
questions.explanation: The introduction lists increased travel and trade, antibiotic overuse, environmental changes, and evolving pathogens as drivers.
questions.imageAlt: Emerging Pathogens, slide 3; related topic: Drivers of emergence
questions.sourceRef: Supplementary — Lecture 3 slides, slide 3

questions.question: How can deforestation contribute to the emergence of zoonotic infections?
options: It prevents people from encountering animal reservoirs
It increases human intrusion into wildlife habitats and contact with animal reservoirs
questions.explanation: The lecture explains that human intrusion into wildlife habitats through deforestation can increase contact with animal reservoirs and facilitate cross-species transmission.
questions.imageAlt: Emerging Pathogens, slide 12; related topic: Zoonotic spillover
questions.sourceRef: Supplementary — Lecture 3 slides, slide 12

questions.question: According to the lecture, how can climate change help vector-borne pathogens emerge in new regions?
options: By restricting vectors to tropical regions
By expanding the geographic range of mosquitoes and ticks
By making all vectors unable to reproduce
questions.explanation: Rising temperatures and altered rainfall can expand the range of arthropod vectors, allowing pathogens such as dengue, Zika, and malaria to emerge in previously temperate regions.
questions.imageAlt: Emerging Pathogens, slide 12; related topic: Climate and vectors
questions.sourceRef: Supplementary — Lecture 3 slides, slide 12

questions.question: Why can rapid global travel and trade accelerate pathogen spread?
options: They remove the need for disease surveillance
They confine pathogens to rural locations
They can move an infectious agent from a remote epicenter to global cities within hours
They prevent transmission across geographical boundaries
questions.explanation: High-volume air travel and interconnected supply chains can carry an agent to major cities quickly, outpacing traditional containment measures.
questions.imageAlt: Emerging Pathogens, slide 13; related topic: Global travel and trade
questions.sourceRef: Supplementary — Lecture 3 slides, slide 13

questions.question: What feature of RNA viruses is highlighted as enabling rapid changes in pathogen properties?
options: High mutation rates and recombination capabilities
questions.explanation: The lecture notes that RNA viruses can mutate and recombine rapidly, potentially acquiring immune evasion, increased transmissibility, or enhanced virulence.
questions.imageAlt: Emerging Pathogens, slide 13; related topic: Microbial evolution
questions.sourceRef: Supplementary — Lecture 3 slides, slide 13

questions.question: Which practice is identified as driving selection of antimicrobial-resistant strains?
options: Overuse and misuse of antibiotics and antivirals in humans and livestock
questions.explanation: The lecture links overuse and misuse of antibiotics and antivirals in humans and livestock to selection for resistant strains such as MRSA and drug-resistant TB.
questions.imageAlt: Emerging Pathogens, slide 14; related topic: Antimicrobial resistance
questions.sourceRef: Supplementary — Lecture 3 slides, slide 14

questions.question: How can intensive agricultural and food production practices promote pathogen emergence?
options: High-density farming and indiscriminate growth-promoter use can create mixing vessels and bridges from livestock to people
They reduce all contact between livestock and humans
They prevent pathogens from mixing between hosts
They eliminate the possibility of genetic reassortment
questions.explanation: The lecture describes high-density factory farming and wet markets as settings that can facilitate pathogen mixing and provide a bridge from livestock to human populations.
questions.imageAlt: Emerging Pathogens, slide 14; related topic: Food production and emergence
questions.sourceRef: Supplementary — Lecture 3 slides, slide 14

questions.question: Which conditions can amplify fecal-oral and respiratory transmission in cities?
options: Overcrowding combined with inadequate water and sewage systems
Reduced human mobility and strong infection control
Low population density and reliable sewage systems
High laboratory capacity and rapid reporting
questions.explanation: The lecture states that overcrowded megacities with inadequate water and sewage systems can amplify fecal-oral and respiratory spread.
questions.imageAlt: Emerging Pathogens, slide 15; related topic: Urbanization and sanitation
questions.sourceRef: Supplementary — Lecture 3 slides, slide 15

questions.question: Why can weak public health surveillance and laboratory capacity increase outbreak risk?
options: They ensure that quarantine always begins before transmission
They guarantee immediate identification of unusual cases
Delayed detection and inadequate reporting can allow silent community spread before an outbreak is identified
questions.explanation: Insufficient diagnostics, genomic sequencing, and reporting can delay identification and create a window for silent spread.
questions.imageAlt: Emerging Pathogens, slide 15; related topic: Surveillance capacity
questions.sourceRef: Supplementary — Lecture 3 slides, slide 15

questions.question: Which disease is listed in the lecture as an example of an emerging infection?
questions.explanation: HIV infection is among the lecture's examples of emerging infections, alongside Ebola, SARS, and others.
questions.imageAlt: Emerging Pathogens, slide 8; related topic: Examples of emerging infections
questions.sourceRef: Supplementary — Lecture 3 slides, slide 8

questions.question: Which explanation does the lecture give for cholera reappearing in places where it had previously disappeared?
options: Deterioration of water and sanitation systems
The elimination of contaminated food and water
questions.explanation: The lecture links cholera's reintroduction and spread to deteriorated water and sanitation systems.
questions.imageAlt: Emerging Pathogens, slide 10; related topic: Examples of re-emergence
questions.sourceRef: Supplementary — Lecture 3 slides, slide 10

questions.question: Which description best distinguishes droplet spread from airborne transmission in the lecture?
options: Droplets travel only through food, while airborne pathogens require ticks
Droplet spread requires a contaminated object, while airborne spread requires direct skin contact
Heavy respiratory droplets travel a short distance before falling, while tiny droplet nuclei can remain suspended for long periods
Both routes are defined as transmission by mosquitoes
questions.explanation: The lecture describes droplets from coughing, sneezing, or talking as heavy and short-range; airborne droplet nuclei are tiny and can remain suspended for long periods.
questions.imageAlt: Emerging Pathogens, slide 45; related topic: Transmission routes
questions.sourceRef: Supplementary — Lecture 3 slides, slide 45

questions.question: Which is a vehicle-borne route of transmission described in the lecture?
options: Spread through contaminated food or water
Spread by a mosquito carrying a pathogen
Spread through tiny nuclei suspended in air
questions.explanation: Vehicle-borne transmission involves an intermediary such as contaminated food, water, blood, or bedding; contaminated food or water can transmit infection by the fecal-oral route.
questions.imageAlt: Emerging Pathogens, slide 45; related topic: Vehicle-borne transmission
questions.sourceRef: Supplementary — Lecture 3 slides, slide 45

questions.question: Which factor can make an epidemic harder to detect and contain?
questions.explanation: Asymptomatic transmission can occur before symptoms appear, making detection and containment more difficult.
questions.imageAlt: Emerging Pathogens, slide 51; related topic: Epidemic potential
questions.sourceRef: Supplementary — Lecture 3 slides, slide 51

questions.question: What does the One Health approach integrate to address emerging infectious diseases?
options: Only hospital treatment and pharmaceutical manufacturing
Only wildlife protection, excluding human health
questions.explanation: The lecture presents One Health as a framework connecting human, animal, and environmental health through cross-sector collaboration.
questions.imageAlt: Emerging Pathogens, slide 56; related topic: One Health and control
questions.sourceRef: Supplementary — Lecture 3 slides, slide 56

questions.question: Which set of measures is included in the lecture's infection prevention and vector-control strategies?
options: Using antibiotics without stewardship and ending contact tracing
Stopping surveillance and avoiding protective equipment
Vector control, isolation, quarantine, contact tracing, hand hygiene, and protective equipment
Replacing vaccination with unrestricted exposure to vectors
questions.explanation: The lecture recommends vector control and healthcare infection-prevention measures including isolation, quarantine, contact tracing, hand hygiene, and appropriate protective equipment.
questions.imageAlt: Emerging Pathogens, slide 57; related topic: Prevention and response
questions.sourceRef: Supplementary — Lecture 3 slides, slide 57

questions.question: What is a key concern about H5N1 described in the lecture's case study?
options: Humans have no preexisting immunity against the strain, and spillover may give it opportunities to adapt
The virus is unable to infect animals other than birds
Sustained human-to-human transmission has already been confirmed
It has stopped evolving into genetically diverse clades
questions.explanation: The lecture notes a lack of preexisting human immunity and concern that spillover events provide opportunities for adaptation, while sustained human-to-human transmission had not yet occurred.
questions.imageAlt: Emerging Pathogens, slide 58; related topic: H5N1 case study
questions.sourceRef: Supplementary — Lecture 3 slides, slide 58

questions.question: What does the lecture identify as the most sustainable way to address infectious diseases?
options: Reducing information sharing between health systems
Waiting until an outbreak becomes widespread
Relying solely on treatment after transmission peaks
questions.explanation: The conclusion identifies early detection and rapid response as the most sustainable way to deal with infectious diseases.
questions.imageAlt: Emerging Pathogens, slide 75; related topic: Preparedness and response
questions.sourceRef: Supplementary — Lecture 3 slides, slide 75

questions.question: What is the defining characteristic of an antigen or immunogen?
options: A substance capable of stimulating the human immune system to produce an immune response.
A carbohydrate molecule found only on the cell walls of fungi.
Any protein synthesized exclusively by plasma B-lymphocytes.
A cellular enzyme responsible for complement fixation in serum.
questions.explanation: An antigen is a substance capable of stimulating the immune system to produce an immune response against it.
questions.imageAlt: Immunology and Serology, slide 4; related topic: Antigens
questions.sourceRef: Immunology and Serology question bank — Q1

questions.question: Which historical milestone in immunology was achieved by Louis Pasteur in 1885?
options: The global eradication of smallpox through variolation.
The description of serum globulin electrophoresis fractions by Tiselius.
The administration of the first attenuated rabies vaccine to a human, Joseph Meister.
The discovery of complement proteins in human serum.
questions.explanation: Pasteur demonstrated that a weakened pathogen could be administered as a vaccine and gave his first human vaccine to a boy bitten by a rabid dog in 1885.
questions.imageAlt: Immunology and Serology, slide 6; related topic: History of immunology
questions.sourceRef: Immunology and Serology question bank — Q2

questions.question: Which features distinguish the adaptive immune response?
options: No time lag, broad response, and absence of memory.
Immediate response through physical barriers only.
questions.explanation: The lecture identifies specificity, diversity, and memory as cardinal features of adaptive immunity.
questions.imageAlt: Immunology and Serology, slide 18; related topic: Adaptive immunity
questions.sourceRef: Immunology and Serology question bank — Q3

questions.question: Where do T-lymphocytes mature, and what type of immunity do they mediate?
questions.explanation: T cells mature in the thymus and mediate cellular, or cell-mediated, immunity.
questions.imageAlt: Immunology and Serology, slide 23; related topic: T lymphocytes
questions.sourceRef: Immunology and Serology question bank — Q4

questions.question: In Tiselius's serum protein electrophoresis description, in which protein fraction are antibodies primarily located?
questions.explanation: The lecture states that antibodies are located in the gamma-globulin fraction and were therefore termed immunoglobulins.
questions.imageAlt: Immunology and Serology, slide 27; related topic: Immunoglobulins
questions.sourceRef: Immunology and Serology question bank — Q5

questions.question: What is the basic structural composition of a monomeric immunoglobulin molecule?
options: A pentameric ring of heavy chains surrounding a central J-chain.
Two identical heavy chains and two identical light chains joined by disulfide bonds.
Four identical polypeptide chains, each with a molecular weight of 50,000 Da.
A single secretory component linked to three light chains.
questions.explanation: An antibody has two identical light chains and two identical heavy chains, joined by disulfide bonds and other interactions.
questions.imageAlt: Immunology and Serology, slide 28; related topic: Antibody structure
questions.sourceRef: Immunology and Serology question bank — Q6

questions.question: Which immunoglobulin class is most abundant in human serum and can cross the placenta?
questions.explanation: IgG is the most abundant serum antibody and crosses the placenta, providing natural immunity to the fetus and neonate.
questions.imageAlt: Immunology and Serology, slide 32; related topic: IgG
questions.sourceRef: Immunology and Serology question bank — Q7

questions.question: What structural feature characterizes secretory IgA in mucosal secretions, milk, saliva, and tears?
options: A pentameric structure bound by a single hexameric J-chain.
A dimer of two monomeric units joined by a J-chain and associated with a secretory component.
A monomeric structure with high carbohydrate content.
questions.explanation: Secretory IgA is dimeric; its monomers are joined by a J-chain and it has a secretory component.
questions.imageAlt: Immunology and Serology, slide 36; related topic: Secretory IgA
questions.sourceRef: Immunology and Serology question bank — Q8

questions.question: Which immunoglobulin is the largest, appears first during an initial infection, and activates complement?
questions.explanation: IgM is the largest immunoglobulin, is the first antibody to appear after initial antigen exposure, and can activate complement.
questions.imageAlt: Immunology and Serology, slide 38; related topic: IgM
questions.sourceRef: Immunology and Serology question bank — Q9

questions.question: Which antibody class has the lowest serum concentration, is heat-labile, and mediates type I hypersensitivity?
questions.explanation: IgE has the lowest serum concentration, is inactivated by heat at 56°C, and mediates type I hypersensitivity reactions.
questions.imageAlt: Immunology and Serology, slide 42; related topic: IgE
questions.sourceRef: Immunology and Serology question bank — Q10

questions.question: What is the known primary function of Immunoglobulin D (IgD)?
options: Acting as a membrane-bound B-cell receptor alongside IgM.
Neutralizing toxins within the intestinal lumen.
Crossing the placental barrier to protect fetuses.
questions.explanation: IgD is found on B-cell surfaces as a membrane immunoglobulin and acts as a B-cell receptor along with IgM.
questions.imageAlt: Immunology and Serology, slide 44; related topic: IgD
questions.sourceRef: Immunology and Serology question bank — Q11

questions.question: How does the secondary immune response compare with the primary response?
options: It is more rapid and larger than the primary response after re-exposure to the same antigen.
It relies exclusively on memory T cells and produces no antibodies.
It is slower and produces lower antibody levels than the primary response.
It has a shorter lag phase and produces massive levels of IgG during the first exposure.
questions.explanation: The lecture states that responses to second and subsequent exposure to the same antigen are usually more rapid and larger.
questions.imageAlt: Immunology and Serology, slide 19; related topic: Primary and secondary responses
questions.sourceRef: Immunology and Serology question bank — Q12

questions.question: How can passive immunization be achieved, and what is its primary limitation?
options: By administering live-attenuated vaccines; its protection is permanent.
By transferring memory cells; it prevents all future infections.
By natural infection; it always produces lifelong protection.
By transferring or injecting preformed antibodies; its protection is temporary.
questions.explanation: Passive immunization transfers preformed antibodies, such as maternal antibodies or immune globulins, and its effects are temporary.
questions.imageAlt: Immunology and Serology, slide 51; related topic: Passive immunization
questions.sourceRef: Immunology and Serology question bank — Q13

questions.question: What is a major disadvantage of attenuated bacterial or viral vaccines?
options: They cannot replicate within host cells.
They provide no exposure to the immune system.
The attenuated organism may revert to a virulent form.
They are non-antigenic and cannot stimulate immunity.
questions.explanation: The lecture identifies possible reversion as a major disadvantage of attenuated vaccines.
questions.imageAlt: Immunology and Serology, slide 57; related topic: Attenuated vaccines
questions.sourceRef: Immunology and Serology question bank — Q14

questions.question: What results from active immunization by natural infection or vaccination, according to the lecture?
options: Proliferation of T and B cells and formation of effector and memory cells.
questions.explanation: Natural infection or vaccination stimulates proliferation of T and B cells, resulting in effector and memory cells.
questions.imageAlt: Immunology and Serology, slide 52; related topic: Active immunization
questions.sourceRef: Supplementary — Lecture 4 slides, slide 52

questions.question: What is the principle of immunofluorescence (IFA)?
options: Enzyme-labeled antibodies cause a measurable color change.
Antibodies bind to inert particles to produce visible clumping.
Chemical reactions emit light proportional to the analyte concentration.
Fluorescently labeled antibodies are viewed under a fluorescence microscope.
questions.explanation: IFA uses fluorescently labeled antibodies that are viewed under a fluorescence microscope.
questions.imageAlt: Immunology and Serology, slide 75; related topic: Immunofluorescence
questions.sourceRef: Supplementary — Lecture 4 slides, slide 75

questions.question: What signal is measured in a chemiluminescence immunoassay (CLIA)?
options: Fluorescent antibody staining viewed only in tissue sections.
Light emitted by a chemical reaction after target binding.
questions.explanation: CLIA uses light-emitting chemical markers; target binding triggers a chemical reaction whose emitted light is measured.
questions.imageAlt: Immunology and Serology, slide 79; related topic: Chemiluminescence immunoassays
questions.sourceRef: Supplementary — Lecture 4 slides, slide 79

questions.question: What is the diagnostic principle of indirect (passive) agglutination tests such as latex agglutination?
options: Photon emission triggered by a chemiluminescent substrate.
Visible clumping when target antigens bind to antibodies coated on inert carrier particles.
Direct precipitation of soluble toxins in agar.
questions.explanation: The lecture describes latex beads coated with specific antibodies that bind bacterial antigens and create visible clumping.
questions.imageAlt: Immunology and Serology, slide 68; related topic: Agglutination tests
questions.sourceRef: Immunology and Serology question bank — Q18

questions.question: What is the principle and a key advantage of ELISA?
options: Light emission replaces antibody binding and provides no quantitative results.
Ultraviolet microscopy visualizes unstained organisms with no reagents.
Radioactive decay produces a measurable signal with no antigen-antibody binding.
Enzyme-labeled antibodies produce a color change; the method has high sensitivity and specificity.
questions.explanation: ELISA uses enzyme-labeled antibodies to produce a color change and offers high sensitivity, specificity, and quantitative results.
questions.imageAlt: Immunology and Serology, slide 71; related topic: ELISA
questions.sourceRef: Immunology and Serology question bank — Q19

questions.question: Which finding in paired acute and convalescent serum samples indicates recent infection?
options: A fourfold rise in IgG titer between the samples.
Absence of IgM in the acute sample.
A negative result in both samples.
An unchanged IgG titer in both samples.
questions.explanation: A fourfold rise in IgG titer between acute and convalescent samples indicates recent infection.
questions.imageAlt: Immunology and Serology, slide 81; related topic: Paired sera
questions.sourceRef: Immunology and Serology question bank — Q20

questions.question: What is cilastatin's role when given with imipenem?

It blocks imipenem entry into the cerebrospinal fluid
It prevents imipenem metabolism in the liver
It inhibits renal dipeptidase that hydrolyses imipenem

questions.question: Which statement about aztreonam and penicillin allergy is given in the lecture?
options: It cross-reacts with penicillins in all cases
It is a glycopeptide with no beta-lactam ring
It has no cross-allergenicity with penicillins, though ceftazidime is an exception
It is ineffective against aerobic Gram-negative rods

questions.question: What precaution does the lecture give for administering aminoglycosides with penicillins?
options: Mix them in the same ampoule to improve synergy
Do not mix them in the same ampoule, injection, or line because they complex in vitro
Give both only by the oral route
Separate them by at least two hours because of calcium binding
questions.explanation: The lecture warns that mixing these drugs in the same container or line causes in-vitro complexing.

It is active only in acidic urine
It is eliminated exclusively through the lungs

It is absorbed systemically and used for Pseudomonas bacteremia
It is used as endocarditis prophylaxis
It is a first-line eradication agent for H. pylori

options: It is an oral agent used only for uncomplicated cystitis
It is a monobactam used for Gram-positive anaerobes
It is a macrolide used for H. pylori eradication
It is a minocycline derivative reserved for complicated skin/soft-tissue, intra-abdominal, and community-acquired pneumonia infections and is given by IV infusion

questions.question: How is a wound defined in surgical pathology?

Any localized collection of blood outside blood vessels.
An avascular scar resulting from chronic inflammation.
Primary epithelial hyperplasia without basement membrane disruption.
questions.explanation: A wound is defined as a disruption of normal anatomical structure and function

questions.question: What is the clinical distinction between a hypertrophic scar and a keloid?
options: Hypertrophic scars extend far beyond the original boundaries of the wound, whereas keloids remain strictly confined.
Keloids extend beyond the original boundaries of the original wound and rarely regress spontaneously, whereas hypertrophic scars remain confined to the wound borders.
Hypertrophic scars occur exclusively on the lower extremities, while keloids occur only on mucosal surfaces.
Keloids contain no collagen, whereas hypertrophic scars consist entirely of elastin.
questions.explanation: Keloids grow beyond the original wound margins and do not regress on their own, unlike hypertrophic scars which stay within the wound boundaries.

questions.question: How is sterilization defined in surgical and microbiological terms?
options: Destruction of micro-organisms in all forms including spores.
Reduction of a population of pathological micro-organisms without killing spores.
Killing of vegetative bacteria only while preserving viruses.
Chemical inactivation of surface pyrogens and endotoxins.
questions.explanation: Sterilization is the complete destruction or elimination of all forms of microbial life, including highly resistant bacterial spores.

questions.question: What is the clinical definition of disinfection?
options: Total elimination of prions and bacterial spores from metallic instruments.
Reduction of a population of pathological micro-organisms or killing the vegetative forms without killing spores.
Radiation-based sterilization of single-use pharmaceutical packaging.
Ultrasonic removal of bioburden prior to autoclaving.

title: Day 9 — Metabolic, Nutrition, VTE & Acid–Base
description: 80 MCQs on perioperative metabolism, nutrition, VTE, and acid–base balance. Each question links to its source bank; a lecture image is shown only when a matching slide page is available. Day 6 anticoagulant pharmacology questions are excluded.

questions.question: How long does the ebb phase of the metabolic response to injury typically last?
questions.explanation: The ebb phase is the period of shock immediately following the insult, lasting roughly 24–48 hours, and is characterized by a decrease in metabolic rate and oxygen consumption.
questions.sourceRef: Metabolic & Nutrition — Q1
questions.sourceEvidence: Bank Q1 marks “24 to 48 hours (hours to 2 days)” as correct and explains: The ebb phase is the period of shock immediately following the insult, lasting roughly 24–48 hours, and is characterized by a decrease in metabolic rate and oxygen consumption.
questions.imageAlt: Metabolic Response to Trauma.pptx, Slide 17; related to Metabolic Response & Nutrition

questions.question: Which of the following physiological changes occurs during the flow phase of the trauma stress response?
options: Increase in body weight due to severe fluid retention
questions.explanation: The flow phase (lasting 2 to 7+ days) is characterized by hyper-metabolism, increased basal metabolic rate (BMR), increased cardiac output, and hyperthermia (SIRS features).
questions.sourceRef: Metabolic & Nutrition — Q2
questions.sourceEvidence: Bank Q2 marks “Increase in basal metabolic rate (hyper-metabolism)” as correct and explains: The flow phase (lasting 2 to 7+ days) is characterized by hyper-metabolism, increased basal metabolic rate (BMR), increased cardiac output, and hyperthermia (SIRS features).
questions.imageAlt: Metabolic Response to Trauma.pptx, Slide 17; related to Metabolic Response & Nutrition

questions.question: Peripheral insulin resistance following major trauma directly contributes to which metabolic abnormality?
questions.explanation: Insulin resistance reduces cellular glucose uptake, leading to stress-induced hyperglycemia immediately after injury.
questions.sourceRef: Metabolic & Nutrition — Q3
questions.sourceEvidence: Bank Q3 marks “Hyperglycemia” as correct and explains: Insulin resistance reduces cellular glucose uptake, leading to stress-induced hyperglycemia immediately after injury.

questions.question: Which cytokine is considered a key mediator in the systemic inflammatory and acute-phase response to injury?
questions.explanation: Along with IL-1 and TNF-alpha, IL-6 serves as a central cytokine driving the acute-phase protein response and systemic inflammation.
questions.sourceRef: Metabolic & Nutrition — Q4
questions.sourceEvidence: Bank Q4 marks “Interleukin-6 (IL-6)” as correct and explains: Along with IL-1 and TNF-alpha, IL-6 serves as a central cytokine driving the acute-phase protein response and systemic inflammation.

questions.question: The metabolic response after major surgery is classically associated with which of the following?
questions.explanation: During the flow phase, hyper-metabolism drives up oxygen consumption, cardiac index, and body temperature (pyrexia).
questions.sourceRef: Metabolic & Nutrition — Q5
questions.sourceEvidence: Bank Q5 marks “Increase in oxygen consumption” as correct and explains: During the flow phase, hyper-metabolism drives up oxygen consumption, cardiac index, and body temperature (pyrexia).
questions.imageAlt: Metabolic Response to Trauma.pptx, Slide 19; related to Metabolic Response & Nutrition

questions.question: Which of the following substances does NOT contribute to the neuroendocrine or inflammatory response to surgery?
questions.explanation: The primary drivers of the response include the sympathetic system, HPA axis (stress hormones like catecholamines, cortisol, GH, ACTH), and cytokines, whereas somatostatin is not a primary mediator of the response.
questions.sourceRef: Metabolic & Nutrition — Q6
questions.sourceEvidence: Bank Q6 marks “Somatostatin” as correct and explains: The primary drivers of the response include the sympathetic system, HPA axis (stress hormones like catecholamines, cortisol, GH, ACTH), and cytokines, whereas somatostatin is not a primary mediator of the response.
questions.imageAlt: Metabolic Response to Trauma.pptx, Slide 19; related to Metabolic Response & Nutrition

questions.question: Which factor does NOT typically alter or affect the magnitude of the metabolic response to surgery and trauma?
questions.explanation: Severity of injury, age, pre-existing conditions (malnutrition, diabetes), infection, and medications affect the response, whereas race is not a listed determinant.
questions.sourceRef: Metabolic & Nutrition — Q7
questions.sourceEvidence: Bank Q7 marks “Race” as correct and explains: Severity of injury, age, pre-existing conditions (malnutrition, diabetes), infection, and medications affect the response, whereas race is not a listed determinant.
questions.imageAlt: Metabolic Response to Trauma.pptx, Slide 20; related to Metabolic Response & Nutrition

questions.question: Which system does NOT contribute directly to the physiological control mechanisms of the response to surgery and trauma?
questions.explanation: The response is controlled by the sympathetic system, endocrine/HPA axis, vascular endothelial system, and the acute-phase/cytokine system.
questions.sourceRef: Metabolic & Nutrition — Q8
questions.sourceEvidence: Bank Q8 marks “Parasympathetic nervous system” as correct and explains: The response is controlled by the sympathetic system, endocrine/HPA axis, vascular endothelial system, and the acute-phase/cytokine system.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT classified as a primary stress hormone driving the metabolic response?

questions.question: What causes the dilutional hyponatremia frequently observed following severe trauma or surgery?

It is significantly cheaper and easier to administer without any monitoring.
It completely eliminates the risk of hyperglycemia.
It stops all forms of muscle proteolysis instantly.

questions.explanation: Metabolic alkalosis is commonly associated with hypokalemia (due to renal H+/K+ exchange shifts and renal potassium wasting) and hypochloremia.
questions.sourceRef: VTE&acid&base balance  — Q36
questions.sourceEvidence: Bank Q36 marks “Hypokalemia and hypochloremia” as correct and explains: Metabolic alkalosis is commonly associated with hypokalemia (due to renal H+/K+ exchange shifts and renal potassium wasting) and hypochloremia.

questions.question: What is the immediate physiological consequence of acute hyperventilation (e.g., panic attack or mechanical over-ventilation)?
options: Respiratory acidosis due to CO2 trapping
Respiratory alkalosis due to excessive elimination of carbon dioxide
questions.explanation: Rapid blowing off of CO2 decreases PaCO2, raising blood pH and causing acute respiratory alkalosis.
questions.sourceRef: VTE&acid&base balance  — Q37
questions.sourceEvidence: Bank Q37 marks “Respiratory alkalosis due to excessive elimination of carbon dioxide” as correct and explains: Rapid blowing off of CO2 decreases PaCO2, raising blood pH and causing acute respiratory alkalosis.

questions.question: Which buffer system is considered the primary and most important extracellular chemical buffer in human blood?
questions.explanation: The extracellular bicarbonate-carbonic acid buffer system works rapidly alongside lungs and kidneys to maintain blood pH homeostasis.
questions.sourceRef: VTE&acid&base balance  — Q38
questions.sourceEvidence: Bank Q38 marks “Bicarbonate-carbonic acid buffer system” as correct and explains: The extracellular bicarbonate-carbonic acid buffer system works rapidly alongside lungs and kidneys to maintain blood pH homeostasis.

questions.question: In renal failure (uremia), failing glomerular filtration leads to the accumulation of organic acids (sulfates, phosphates, organic anions), resulting in:
questions.explanation: Decreased renal excretion of unmeasured anions and organic acids causes high anion gap metabolic acidosis in uremia.
questions.sourceRef: VTE&acid&base balance  — Q39
questions.sourceEvidence: Bank Q39 marks “High Anion Gap Metabolic Acidosis” as correct and explains: Decreased renal excretion of unmeasured anions and organic acids causes high anion gap metabolic acidosis in uremia.

questions.question: What term describes a mixed acid-base disorder where both metabolic acidosis and metabolic alkalosis occur simultaneously, resulting in a nearly normal blood pH but abnormal HCO3- and anion gap?
options: Concomitant metabolic acidosis and metabolic alkalosis (e.g., vomiting in a patient with uremic acidosis or DKA)
questions.explanation: Patients can have opposing primary metabolic processes (such as vomiting causing alkalosis combined with renal failure causing acidosis), yielding a normal pH with abnormal individual parameters.
questions.sourceRef: VTE&acid&base balance  — Q40
questions.sourceEvidence: Bank Q40 marks “Concomitant metabolic acidosis and metabolic alkalosis (e.g., vomiting in a patient with uremic acidosis or DKA)” as correct and explains: Patients can have opposing primary metabolic processes (such as vomiting causing alkalosis combined with renal failure causing acidosis), yielding a normal pH with abnormal individual parameters.

questions.question: How do the kidneys respond to chronic metabolic alkalosis?
options: By decreasing glomerular filtration rate to zero
By excreting excess bicarbonate ions in the urine
questions.explanation: The kidneys compensate for metabolic alkalosis by reducing renal bicarbonate reabsorption and actively excreting bicarbonate in alkaline urine.
questions.sourceRef: VTE&acid&base balance  — Q41
questions.sourceEvidence: Bank Q41 marks “By excreting excess bicarbonate ions in the urine” as correct and explains: The kidneys compensate for metabolic alkalosis by reducing renal bicarbonate reabsorption and actively excreting bicarbonate in alkaline urine.
questions.imageAlt: __Fluids and Electrolytes - نسخة.pdf, PDF page 21; related to VTE & Acid–Base Balance

questions.question: Which clinical condition can lead to chloride-responsive metabolic alkalosis?
options: Severe potassium depletion resistant to saline
Gastric vomiting or nasogastric suction (responsive to normal saline administration)
questions.explanation: Saline-responsive metabolic alkalosis is driven by volume contraction and chloride depletion, correctable with isotonic saline and potassium repletion.
questions.sourceRef: VTE&acid&base balance  — Q42
questions.sourceEvidence: Bank Q42 marks “Gastric vomiting or nasogastric suction (responsive to normal saline administration)” as correct and explains: Saline-responsive metabolic alkalosis is driven by volume contraction and chloride depletion, correctable with isotonic saline and potassium repletion.
questions.imageAlt: __Fluids and Electrolytes - نسخة.pdf, PDF page 17; related to VTE & Acid–Base Balance

questions.question: What is the primary compensatory mechanism for a primary metabolic alkalosis?
options: Renal retention of hydrogen ions and excretion of bicarbonate
Alveolar hypoventilation leading to an increase in PaCO2 (though limited by hypoxia drive)
questions.explanation: The respiratory system compensates for metabolic alkalosis by reducing ventilation, raising PaCO2 to retain carbonic acid, though respiratory compensation is restricted by hypoxic limits.
questions.sourceRef: VTE&acid&base balance  — Q43
questions.sourceEvidence: Bank Q43 marks “Alveolar hypoventilation leading to an increase in PaCO2 (though limited by hypoxia drive)” as correct and explains: The respiratory system compensates for metabolic alkalosis by reducing ventilation, raising PaCO2 to retain carbonic acid, though respiratory compensation is restricted by hypoxic limits.

questions.question: What is the primary pathological mechanism of Type 1 Distal Renal Tubular Acidosis (RTA)?
options: Excess loss of bicarbonate in the proximal tubule
Overproduction of lactic acid by skeletal muscle
Complete shutdown of renal blood flow
Inability of the distal renal tubules to secrete hydrogen ions properly, resulting in a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis
questions.explanation: Distal RTA (Type 1) features an inability to secrete H+ in the distal nephron, leading to a hyperchloremic normal anion gap metabolic acidosis with alkaline urine (pH > 5.5).
questions.sourceRef: VTE&acid&base balance  — Q44
questions.sourceEvidence: Bank Q44 marks “Inability of the distal renal tubules to secrete hydrogen ions properly, resulting in a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis” as correct and explains: Distal RTA (Type 1) features an inability to secrete H+ in the distal nephron, leading to a hyperchloremic normal anion gap metabolic acidosis with alkaline urine (pH > 5.5).
questions.imageAlt: __Fluids and Electrolytes - نسخة.pdf, PDF page 17; related to VTE & Acid–Base Balance

questions.question: What is the hallmark laboratory finding of Type 2 Proximal Renal Tubular Acidosis?
options: Elevated serum anion gap above 25 mEq/L
Impaired proximal tubular reabsorption of filtered bicarbonate, leading to bicarbonate wasting in urine and normal anion gap metabolic acidosis
questions.explanation: Proximal RTA (Type 2) results from defective bicarbonate reabsorption in the proximal tubule, causing urinary bicarbonate wasting and systemic metabolic acidosis.
questions.sourceRef: VTE&acid&base balance  — Q45
questions.sourceEvidence: Bank Q45 marks “Impaired proximal tubular reabsorption of filtered bicarbonate, leading to bicarbonate wasting in urine and normal anion gap metabolic acidosis” as correct and explains: Proximal RTA (Type 2) results from defective bicarbonate reabsorption in the proximal tubule, causing urinary bicarbonate wasting and systemic metabolic acidosis.

questions.question: In aspirin (salicylate) toxicity, patients frequently present with a complex mixed acid-base disturbance. What is the typical combination?
options: Pure metabolic alkalosis and respiratory alkalosis
Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis alone
Primary respiratory alkalosis (direct stimulation of the respiratory center) combined with high anion gap metabolic acidosis (salicylate uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation)
questions.explanation: Salicylate overdose stimulates the brainstem respiratory center (causing respiratory alkalosis) while simultaneously disrupting cellular metabolism to generate organic acids (causing HAGMA).
questions.sourceRef: VTE&acid&base balance  — Q46
questions.sourceEvidence: Bank Q46 marks “Primary respiratory alkalosis (direct stimulation of the respiratory center) combined with high anion gap metabolic acidosis (salicylate uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation)” as correct and explains: Salicylate overdose stimulates the brainstem respiratory center (causing respiratory alkalosis) while simultaneously disrupting cellular metabolism to generate organic acids (causing HAGMA).

questions.question: Which cellular adaptation term describes a "bad formation" characterized by an abnormality of development with alteration in the size, shape, and organization of cells?

options: To stimulate rapid cellular division during embryonic growth only.
To induce permanent vascular endothelial growth factor production.
To suppress the proliferation of cells and destroy genetically abnormal cells.
To convert normal tissues into metaplasia.

options: Routine blood count followed by immediate surgery without biopsy
Plain abdominal radiography and trial of antibiotics
Triple assessment (Clinical assessment, Imaging, and Cytohistopathology)

Carcinoma in situ restricted to the epithelium

The physical size of the primary tumor mass.
The presence or absence of distant metastasis in bones or liver.
The exact age and performance status of the patient.

options: The percentage of people who are alive five years after their initial cancer diagnosis.
The exact percentage of patients who will live for precisely 5 years and die on the exact day of the 5th anniversary.
The proportion of tumors that spontaneously shrink within 60 months.
The time required for a tumor to double in volume five times.

Tumor size, grade of tumor, and lymph node stage
Presence of liver metastasis, smoking history, and CEA level
Body mass index and hormone receptor status alone

options: To improve the patient's quality of life by controlling symptoms (e.g., pain, obstruction, bleeding).
To completely eradicate micro-metastases using high-dose chemotherapy.
To induce permanent cellular differentiation of grade IV tumors.
To accelerate the catabolic flow phase of metabolism.
questions.explanation: Palliative care focuses on maximizing quality of life, relieving pain, managing obstruction or bleeding, and controlling distressing symptoms when cure is impossible

options: The law is based on religion, whereas ethics is based strictly on hospital bylaws.
Ethics prescribes higher standards of behavior than does the law.
Ethics carries immediate prison sentences, whereas legal violations result in fines.
There is no overlap between legal obligations and ethical dutie

questions.question: Which ethical theory judges an act as morally permissible if it produces the greatest amount of good for the greatest number of persons affected?

Adhering strictly to universal rules regardless of outcomes.
Distributing healthcare resources equitably across society
Judging a person by their character and traits (such as honesty) rather than solely by isolated actions.

Universal utility and maximum societal pleasure.

questions.question: What does the principle of Beneficence require of a physician?

To remain completely neutral regarding treatment outcomes.
To distribute medical resources solely based on social status.
To prioritize patient welfare above all and act with the intent of doing good.

Absolute financial transparency with hospital administration.
Strict patient confidentiality under all criminal investigations.
Protection of public health data over individual rights.

questions.question: How does Islamic medical ethics view the sanctity of human life?

Life is sacred, and Islam places profound emphasis on preserving, protecting, and respecting life in all its stages.

Medical intervention is prohibited when illness strikes.

options: The surgeon faces no penalty because the intent was therapeutic.
The hospital administration assumes financial liability.
Qisas (retribution/liability) is mandatory upon the surgeon because they acted as a transgressor (muta'addi).
Only a minor reprimand is issued by the medical syndicate.

questions.question: What distinguishes "Morals" from "Ethics" according to the lecture classifications?
options: Morals are internal values related to religion, culture, and personal beliefs, whereas ethics represent structured guidelines, professional standards, and character.
Morals change rapidly with scientific development, whereas ethics are fixed.
Ethical violations carry no legal consequences, whereas moral violations result in imprisonment.
Morals are determined by hospital committees, while ethics are private matters.

questions.question: What does the principle of Justice (Equity) in medical ethics dictate?

Equitable distribution of health resources, benefits, and burdens irrespective of sex, religion, ethnicity, or social status.
Allocating advanced surgical care exclusively to high-paying individuals.
Prioritizing younger patients over older patients in every healthcare scenario.

questions.question: When is a physician legally and ethically justified in breaking patient confidentiality?

Whenever a family member demands details about an adult patient.
When required by law (e.g., reporting certain communicable diseases or child abuse) or to prevent imminent serious harm to others with patient consent where possible.
To publish case reports on social media without patient identifiers removed.
questions.explanation: Confidentiality must be maintained, but exceptions exist for public safety, statutory legal requirements, and prevention of severe harm

questions.question: Which principle supports a competent adult patient's right to refuse life-saving medical treatment?

questions.question: What is the primary role of ethical codes such as the Declaration of Geneva and the Helsinki Declaration?
options: To provide systematic ethical standards and guidelines for medical practice and clinical research.
To replace national civil laws entirely.
To dictate hospital billing structures and insurance tariffs.
To restrict technological advancements in surgery.
questions.explanation: Declarations like Geneva and Helsinki serve as essential ethical benchmarks for medical professionalism and research integrity worldwide
questions.sourceRef: Ethics&consent &breaking bad news — Q16
questions.sourceEvidence: medical ethics slide, PDF page 30: supports the tested concept.
questions.imageAlt: medical ethics (1).pptx, Slide 30; related to Ethics

questions.question: Why is the study of diverse ethical theories vital for clinicians?
options: Because ethical dilemmas have a single mathematical solution.
Because ethical dilemmas have no single right answer, and clinicians must navigate complex choices respecting patient dignity and autonomy without relying on rigid, single-minded rules.
To eliminate the need for hospital ethics committees.
To ensure doctors never face malpractice litigation.
questions.explanation: Ethics is not a rigid prescription; recognizing multiple ethical frameworks helps clinicians rationally resolve complex moral dilemmas. Part 2: Consent & Capacity (Q18–Q34)
