questions.question: How is medical consent formally defined?
options: A financial contract binding the patient to hospital fees.
A legal waiver transferring all medical liability from the doctor to the patient.
Permission or agreement given by a person to receive any type of medical treatment, test, examination, or communication.
A verbal agreement required only before major abdominal surgery.
questions.explanation: Consent is permission or agreement given for any medical examination, investigation, treatment, or procedure
questions.sourceRef: Ethics&consent &breaking bad news — Q18
questions.sourceEvidence: consent slide, PDF page 3: supports the tested concept.
questions.imageAlt: consent - Copy.pptx, Slide 3; related to Consent

questions.question: At what stage of a patient encounter is consent required?
options: Exclusively prior to general anesthesia and skin incisions.
Only when prescribing high-risk experimental medications.
In any clinical encounter, including history taking, physical examination, investigations, and procedures.
questions.explanation: Consent is required across all clinical interactions, from basic history taking and physical examination to diagnostic tests and surgical interventions
questions.sourceRef: Ethics&consent &breaking bad news — Q19
questions.sourceEvidence: consent slide, PDF page 8: supports the tested concept.
questions.imageAlt: consent - Copy.pptx, Slide 8; related to Consent

questions.question: What are the essential core elements required for a valid informed consent?
options: Comprehension, Voluntariness, Being Informed, and Capacity.
Written signature, notary verification, and witness approval.
Financial clearance, age above 21, and family consensus.
Complete absence of surgical risk and guaranteed clinical success.
questions.explanation: A valid consent requires patient comprehension, voluntary choice (free of pressure), full disclosure of information (informed), and decision-making capacity
questions.sourceRef: Ethics&consent &breaking bad news — Q20
questions.sourceEvidence: consent slide, PDF page 10: supports the tested concept.
questions.imageAlt: consent - Copy.pptx, Slide 10; related to Consent

questions.question: How is patient "Capacity" defined in the context of medical consent?
options: The legal status of being over 18 years of age.
The ability of an individual to understand, retain, and use information to make a healthcare decision and communicate that decision.
The physical stamina required to withstand general anesthesia.
The financial capability to pay for private medical treatment.
questions.explanation: Capacity refers to a person's functional mental ability to process information, weigh options, make a decision, and communicate it at the time consent is needed
questions.sourceRef: Ethics&consent &breaking bad news — Q21
questions.sourceEvidence: consent slide, PDF page 11: supports the tested concept.
questions.imageAlt: consent - Copy.pptx, Slide 11; related to Consent

questions.question: Who is authorized to assess a patient's capacity to consent?
options: Only a certified psychiatrist or legal judge.
An appropriately trained and experienced healthcare professional who is either recommending or involved in carrying out the treatment or intervention.
Any family member designated by the household elder.
questions.explanation: Capacity should be assessed at the time consent is required by an appropriately trained clinician involved in the patient's care
questions.sourceRef: Ethics&consent &breaking bad news — Q22
questions.sourceEvidence: consent slide, PDF page 22: supports the tested concept.
questions.imageAlt: consent - Copy.pptx, Slide 22; related to Consent

questions.question: Under which of the following circumstances is consent NOT legally required?
options: Elective cosmetic plastic surgery in a fully conscious adult.
Outpatient physical therapy for chronic back pain.
Diagnostic blood tests during a routine annual check-up.
Emergency treatment required immediately to save a life or in unconscious patients where delay would cause permanent harm.
questions.explanation: Emergency life-saving treatment in unconscious patients or immediate intraoperative life-saving procedures do not require prior formal consent
questions.sourceRef: Ethics&consent &breaking bad news — Q23
questions.sourceEvidence: consent slide, PDF page 18: supports the tested concept.
questions.imageAlt: consent - Copy.pptx, Slide 18; related to Consent

questions.question: Who typically holds parental responsibility to give consent for medical treatment on behalf of a child aged under 16–18 years?
options: The child, mother, appointed guardian, or court.
Any adult neighbor living in the same building.
questions.explanation: Consent for minors is provided by individuals with parental responsibility, such as parents, legal guardians, or the court
questions.sourceRef: Ethics&consent &breaking bad news — Q24
questions.sourceEvidence: consent slide, PDF page 20: supports the tested concept.
questions.imageAlt: consent - Copy.pptx, Slide 20; related to Consent

questions.question: What legal recourse is available if a parent refuses life-saving treatment for their child?
options: The physician must discharge the child immediately.
The decision can be overruled by a court order to prevent death or severe permanent injury.
The nurse must perform the procedure without documentation.
Treatment cannot be rendered under any circumstance.
questions.explanation: When parental refusal threatens a child's life or risks permanent injury, the court can overrule the refusal to allow necessary medical care
questions.sourceRef: Ethics&consent &breaking bad news — Q25
questions.sourceEvidence: consent slide, PDF page 20: supports the tested concept.
questions.imageAlt: consent - Copy.pptx, Slide 20; related to Consent

questions.question: Which of the following conditions can impair or disturb a person's mental capacity?
options: Mild routine fatigue after a normal night's sleep.
Acute intoxication caused by alcohol or drugs.
questions.explanation: Impairment of the mind due to mental health conditions, dementia, learning disabilities, brain damage, or drug/alcohol intoxication affects capacity
questions.sourceRef: Ethics&consent &breaking bad news — Q26
questions.sourceEvidence: consent slide, PDF page 21: supports the tested concept.
questions.imageAlt: consent - Copy.pptx, Slide 21; related to Consent

questions.question: Can a person's capacity to consent fluctuate or change over time?
options: No, capacity is a permanent legal attribute established at birth.
Capacity only changes if confirmed by a supreme court judge.
Once impaired, capacity can never be recovered.
Yes, capacity can change; individuals may manage simple decisions but lack capacity for complex long-term treatments, or have temporary impairments due to shock, panic, or psychosis.
questions.explanation: Capacity is decision-specific and time-dependent; it can fluctuate due to medical states, psychiatric episodes, shock, or medications
questions.sourceRef: Ethics&consent &breaking bad news — Q27
questions.sourceEvidence: consent slide, PDF page 24: supports the tested concept.
questions.imageAlt: consent - Copy.pptx, Slide 24; related to Consent

questions.question: What is required when discussing alternative treatments during the informed consent process?
options: Explaining any alternative treatments along with their risks, benefits, and expected outcomes.
Explaining only the most expensive surgical alternative.
Discouraging patients from considering second opinions.
Focusing exclusively on the risks of refusing the doctor's preferred method.
questions.explanation: Informed consent mandates discussing alternative treatment options, their respective risks, benefits, and outcomes, alongside the consequences of refusing treatment
questions.sourceRef: Ethics&consent &breaking bad news — Q28
questions.sourceEvidence: consent slide, PDF page 15: supports the tested concept.
questions.imageAlt: consent - Copy.pptx, Slide 15; related to Consent

questions.question: At what point can a patient withdraw their consent for a medical procedure?
options: Only before signing the paper consent form.
At any time before the start of the intervention or treatment.
Only after consulting hospital legal counsel.
Patients cannot withdraw consent once documentation is filed.
questions.explanation: A patient retains the right to withdraw consent at any point prior to the commencement of the procedure or treatment
questions.sourceRef: Ethics&consent &breaking bad news — Q29
questions.sourceEvidence: consent slide, PDF page 16: supports the tested concept.
questions.imageAlt: consent - Copy.pptx, Slide 16; related to Consent

questions.question: How should decisions regarding stopping life-support for an incapacitated patient be handled?
options: The attending physician decides unilaterally without consulting anyone.
Life support must be maintained indefinitely regardless of condition or cost.

Treatment can be stopped if there is agreement among the healthcare team and relatives/friends that continuing is not in the patient's best interest, with court referral if agreement cannot be reached.
Family members have sole legal authority without clinical input.
questions.explanation: Stopping life support requires consensus on the patient's best interest involving family and medical staff, or judicial referral if disputes arise or for long-term impaired consciousness
questions.sourceRef: Ethics&consent &breaking bad news — Q30
questions.sourceEvidence: consent slide, PDF page 18: supports the tested concept.
questions.imageAlt: consent - Copy.pptx, Slide 18; related to Consent

questions.question: What constitutes a common issue of concern or pitfall regarding informed consent in clinical practice?
options: Excessive patient comprehension and complete medical literacy.
Over-abundance of time for patient reflection.
Complete transparency and zero information gaps.
Language barriers, cultural differences, time pressures, and inadequate documentation.
questions.explanation: Pitfalls in consent include language barriers, cultural disparities, time constraints, incomplete disclosure, and treating patients with impaired decision-making
questions.sourceRef: Ethics&consent &breaking bad news — Q31
questions.sourceEvidence: consent slide, PDF page 18: supports the tested concept.
questions.imageAlt: consent - Copy.pptx, Slide 18; related to Consent

questions.question: What must be communicated regarding the risks and complications during informed consent?
options: The specific risks and complications associated with the treatment or intervention, alongside expected benefits and outcomes.
Only risks that have a 100% probability of occurring.
Only minor bruising to avoid frightening the patient.
No risks should be mentioned to prevent patient anxiety.
questions.explanation: Patients must receive clear explanations regarding the necessity of treatment, anticipated outcomes, benefits, and potential risks or complications
questions.sourceRef: Ethics&consent &breaking bad news — Q32
questions.sourceEvidence: consent slide, PDF page 10: supports the tested concept.
questions.imageAlt: consent - Copy.pptx, Slide 10; related to Consent

questions.question: What role do relatives play when obtaining consent for an adult patient with full capacity?
options: Relatives hold absolute veto power over the patient's independent medical choices.
Relatives can be consulted for discussion if the patient allows, but a competent adult makes their own autonomous decisions.
Relatives must sign all consent forms on behalf of the patient.
Relatives are legally prohibited from entering the consultation room.
questions.explanation: Competent adults have self-determination; while they can discuss options with relatives or friends, the final decision rests with them
questions.sourceRef: Ethics&consent &breaking bad news — Q33
questions.sourceEvidence: consent slide, PDF page 12: supports the tested concept.
questions.imageAlt: consent - Copy.pptx, Slide 12; related to Consent

questions.question: What is the primary legal and professional function of a signed written consent form?
options: To serve as an absolute shield against medical malpractice lawsuits.
To transfer all surgical risks onto the insurance company.
To provide a documentary record showing that the patient was informed and agreed to the examination, test, treatment, or intervention.
To replace verbal communication between doctor and patient.
questions.explanation: A written consent form serves as legal documentation confirming that the patient was properly informed and agreed to the specified procedure. Part 3: Breaking Bad News (Q35–Q50)
questions.sourceRef: Ethics&consent &breaking bad news — Q34
questions.sourceEvidence: consent slide, PDF page 14: supports the tested concept.
questions.imageAlt: consent - Copy.pptx, Slide 14; related to Consent

questions.question: How is "Bad News" formally defined in a clinical context?
options: Any diagnostic test result that takes longer than 48 hours to process.
A minor surgical complication that resolves spontaneously.
Any hospital administrative policy change affecting visiting hours.
Any information which adversely and seriously affects an individual's view of their future, or creates feelings of no hope or a threat to mental/physical well-being.
questions.explanation: Bad news is defined as any information that severely and adversely alters a person's outlook on their future or threatens their well-being
questions.sourceRef: Ethics&consent &breaking bad news — Q35
questions.sourceEvidence: BREAKING BAD NEWS slide, PDF page 2: supports the tested concept.
questions.imageAlt: BREAKING BAD NEWS 2026.pptx, Slide 2; related to Breaking Bad News

questions.question: What percentage of patients, according to medical literature and studies (such as Jenkins et al.), generally express a desire to know the truth if they have a diagnosis of cancer?
questions.explanation: Evidence indicates that the vast majority of patients (50% to 90% overall, and up to 98% in specific studies like Jenkins) want full honesty and truth regarding serious diagnoses like cancer
questions.sourceRef: Ethics&consent &breaking bad news — Q36
questions.sourceEvidence: BREAKING BAD NEWS slide, PDF page 4: supports the tested concept.
questions.imageAlt: BREAKING BAD NEWS 2026.pptx, Slide 4; related to Breaking Bad News

questions.question: Why do doctors and healthcare workers frequently experience anxiety or reluctance when breaking bad news?
options: Because they lack medical knowledge about the disease.
Fear of causing pain, distress, and suffering, fear of negative evaluation, uncertainty about patient response, and fear of blame.
Because hospital regulations forbid doctors from speaking directly to patients.
Because bad news is legally classified as a criminal offense.
questions.explanation: Clinicians often struggle with breaking bad news due to fears of causing distress, uncertainty, appearing incompetent, being blamed, or destroying hope
questions.sourceRef: Ethics&consent &breaking bad news — Q37
questions.sourceEvidence: BREAKING BAD NEWS slide, PDF page 5: supports the tested concept.
questions.imageAlt: BREAKING BAD NEWS 2026.pptx, Slide 5; related to Breaking Bad News

questions.question: What characterized the traditional and old concepts regarding breaking bad news?
options: Full immediate disclosure of all statistics to every relative.
Mandatory video-recording of all breaking bad news sessions.
Protective and authoritative attitudes where doctors acted as guardians of patient interest, sometimes withholding truth or deferring to relatives' wishes ("we do not want him to know").
Delegating all bad news delivery exclusively to hospital chaplains.
questions.explanation: Older paradigms relied on paternalistic, protective, and authoritative models where doctors shielded patients from distressing diagnoses
questions.sourceRef: Ethics&consent &breaking bad news — Q38
questions.sourceEvidence: BREAKING BAD NEWS slide, PDF page 6: supports the tested concept.
questions.imageAlt: BREAKING BAD NEWS 2026.pptx, Slide 6; related to Breaking Bad News

questions.question: What does the "SPIKES" protocol stand for in the context of breaking bad news?
options: Symptoms, Prognosis, Investigation, Knowledge, Empathy, Support.
Surgery, Patient inquiry, Key information, Evaluation, Solutions.
Screening, Pathology, Intervention, Communication, Execution, Safety.
Setting up the interview, Perception, Invitation, Knowledge, Emotions, Strategy and summary.
questions.explanation: SPIKES is a structured 6-step model: Setting up, Perception, Invitation, Knowledge, Emotions, and Strategy/Summary
questions.sourceRef: Ethics&consent &breaking bad news — Q39
questions.sourceEvidence: BREAKING BAD NEWS slide, PDF page 8: supports the tested concept.
questions.imageAlt: BREAKING BAD NEWS 2026.pptx, Slide 8; related to Breaking Bad News

questions.question: During the "Setting up" (S) step of SPIKES, what environmental factor is most critical?
options: Ensuring privacy, arranging comfortable seating at eye-level, eliminating interruptions (phones, pagers, staff), and allowing support persons if desired.
Conducting the conversation in a busy, active hallway for transparency.
Standing directly over the patient's bed to project clinical authority.
Turning off all room lights to calm the patient.
questions.explanation: Proper setting requires privacy, unhurried time, eye-level positioning, absence of interruptions, and welcoming chosen family or support staff
questions.sourceRef: Ethics&consent &breaking bad news — Q40
questions.sourceEvidence: BREAKING BAD NEWS slide, PDF page 9: supports the tested concept.
questions.imageAlt: BREAKING BAD NEWS 2026.pptx, Slide 9; related to Breaking Bad News

questions.question: What is the purpose of assessing the patient's "Perception" (P) during SPIKES before delivering news?
options: To find out what the patient already knows, understand their expectations, and identify any denial or unrealistic beliefs.
To determine if they can pay for specialized oncology drugs.
To bypass the need for informed consent.
questions.explanation: Assessing perception ("What have other doctors told you?") helps the clinician tailor information to the patient's current understanding and mental state
questions.sourceRef: Ethics&consent &breaking bad news — Q41
questions.sourceEvidence: BREAKING BAD NEWS slide, PDF page 10: supports the tested concept.
questions.imageAlt: BREAKING BAD NEWS 2026.pptx, Slide 10; related to Breaking Bad News

questions.question: What does the "Invitation" (I) step in the SPIKES model involve?
options: Inviting hospital executives to witness the consultation.
Forcing every patient to review complete raw pathology slides.
Asking patients how much information they wish to know (e.g., "Would you like me to give you the full details or would you prefer I speak with a family member?").
Inviting legal counsel prior to discussing diagnosis.
questions.explanation: Invitation respects patient autonomy by asking how much detail they want to receive at that moment or if they prefer someone else to be briefed
questions.sourceRef: Ethics&consent &breaking bad news — Q42
questions.sourceEvidence: BREAKING BAD NEWS slide, PDF page 18: supports the tested concept.
questions.imageAlt: BREAKING BAD NEWS 2026.pptx, Slide 18; related to Breaking Bad News

questions.question: What technique is recommended when sharing "Knowledge" (K) during the SPIKES interview?
options: Deliver all intricate pathological details rapidly in complex medical terminology.
Send the diagnosis via an automated text message to avoid emotional confrontation.
Avoid mentioning any serious diagnosis until surgery is completed.
Use a warning shot, start at the patient's comprehension level, use non-technical words (e.g., "spread" instead of "metastasis"), deliver information in small chunks, and pause frequently.
questions.explanation: Knowledge should be shared gently using warning shots ("I'm afraid it looks serious"), simple non-technical language, and digestible small chunks with pauses
questions.sourceRef: Ethics&consent &breaking bad news — Q43
questions.sourceEvidence: BREAKING BAD NEWS slide, PDF page 19: supports the tested concept.
questions.imageAlt: BREAKING BAD NEWS 2026.pptx, Slide 19; related to Breaking Bad News

questions.question: How should a clinician respond to patient "Emotions" (E) such as shock, crying, or silence according to the SPIKES model?
options: Identify the emotion, connect with empathy (e.g., "I can see how upsetting this is to you"), allow silence, and offer realistic hope.
Immediately change the subject to lighten the mood.
Tell the patient not to cry because everything will definitely be cured.
Leave the room immediately to give them privacy.
questions.explanation: Emotional responses require empathetic acknowledgment, validating statements, tolerance of silence, and compassionate support
questions.sourceRef: Ethics&consent &breaking bad news — Q44
questions.sourceEvidence: BREAKING BAD NEWS slide, PDF page 20: supports the tested concept.
questions.imageAlt: BREAKING BAD NEWS 2026.pptx, Slide 20; related to Breaking Bad News

questions.question: What is the primary goal of the final "Strategy and Summary" (S) step in SPIKES?
options: To summarize the discussion, establish a clear future care plan, schedule follow-up, explore patient ICE (ideas, concerns, expectations), and provide written info or support resources.
To dismiss the patient from outpatient care.
To prevent the patient from asking further questions.
questions.explanation: Strategy and summary ensure the patient leaves with a clear plan, understanding of future steps, available support services, and documentation in the medical record
questions.sourceRef: Ethics&consent &breaking bad news — Q45
questions.sourceEvidence: BREAKING BAD NEWS slide, PDF page 21: supports the tested concept.
questions.imageAlt: BREAKING BAD NEWS 2026.pptx, Slide 21; related to Breaking Bad News

questions.question: Why is documentation of the bad news conversation critical?
options: It is solely used for medical legal defense against lawsuits.
It fulfills mandatory health insurance claim requirements.
It ensures continuity of care by making the information, patient reactions, and future plans known to the rest of the healthcare team and general practitioner.
It allows hospital archives to track mortality rates.
questions.explanation: Accurate documentation records what was communicated and the patient's reactions, facilitating seamless coordination among the medical team, GP, and support services
questions.sourceRef: Ethics&consent &breaking bad news — Q46
questions.sourceEvidence: BREAKING BAD NEWS slide, PDF page 31: supports the tested concept.
questions.imageAlt: BREAKING BAD NEWS 2026.pptx, Slide 31; related to Breaking Bad News

questions.question: How do cultural differences influence patients' preferences when receiving bad news or discussing terminal diagnoses?
options: All cultures globally share identical preferences for direct disclosure.
Cultural background has zero impact on medical communication.
Physicians should ignore cultural nuances to maintain standard hospital protocols.
Cultural and spiritual beliefs vary significantly; for instance, some cultures or immigrant groups may believe discussing death brings it closer, requiring tailored, sensitive communication.
questions.explanation: Studies demonstrate wide cultural variations in preferences for disclosure and end-of-life decision-making, necessitating cultural sensitivity from clinicians
questions.sourceRef: Ethics&consent &breaking bad news — Q47
questions.sourceEvidence: BREAKING BAD NEWS slide, PDF page 13: supports the tested concept.
questions.imageAlt: BREAKING BAD NEWS 2026.pptx, Slide 13; related to Breaking Bad News

questions.question: What common pitfall was reported by patients and families who experienced suboptimal bad news encounters?
options: The physician was too blunt, chose an inappropriate place/time, or gave the impression that there was zero hope.
The physician was too compassionate and spent too much time talking.
The physician used overly simple language.
Too many written information leaflets were provided.
questions.explanation: Patients cited negative experiences when doctors were overly blunt, lacked sensitivity, created an inappropriate setting, or stripped away all hope
questions.sourceRef: Ethics&consent &breaking bad news — Q48
questions.sourceEvidence: BREAKING BAD NEWS slide, PDF page 11: supports the tested concept.
questions.imageAlt: BREAKING BAD NEWS 2026.pptx, Slide 11; related to Breaking Bad News

questions.question: What percentage of information do studies indicate patients typically retain or remember accurately after a consultation involving complex bad news?
options: Very little; many patients experience cognitive/emotional deficits, misunderstand survival statistics, or forget significant portions of details discussed.
Exactly 95% if written down on a napkin.
Only statistical data, forgetting emotional aspects entirely.
questions.explanation: Due to shock and emotional overload, patients often retain very little technical detail, highlighting why information must be delivered in small chunks with written summaries
questions.sourceRef: Ethics&consent &breaking bad news — Q49
questions.sourceEvidence: BREAKING BAD NEWS slide, PDF page 17: supports the tested concept.
questions.imageAlt: BREAKING BAD NEWS 2026.pptx, Slide 17; related to Breaking Bad News

questions.question: Which of the following statements best summarizes the art of breaking bad news?
options: Breaking bad news is an innate personality trait that cannot be taught or learned through medical training.
Doctors should delegate bad news entirely to nurses to protect their own emotional well-being.
Bad news cannot be changed, but clinicians can learn specialized communication skills to deliver it compassionately, minimize distress, and provide realistic hope.
Minimizing the severity of the diagnosis is always the best ethical approach.
questions.explanation: While clinicians cannot alter the bad news itself, mastering structured communication models transforms the encounter, ensuring empathy, clarity, and sustained support

questions.question: Which biochemical process is inhibited by azathioprine in a transplant recipient?
options: Both de novo and salvage purine synthesis
questions.explanation: Azathioprine is converted to 6-mercaptopurine and inhibits both pathways of purine synthesis.

questions.question: A transplant recipient taking azathioprine must also receive allopurinol. According to the review, how should the azathioprine dose be adjusted if this combination is unavoidable?
questions.explanation: Allopurinol blocks azathioprine metabolism and increases pancytopenia risk; the review recommends a 75% dose reduction.
questions.imageAlt: Original transplant operative illustration from Schwartz; it provides topic context and does not show the keyed answer.

questions.explanation: The source lists catecholamines, aldosterone, antidiuretic hormone, cortisol, and growth hormone as injury-response hormones.
questions.sourceRef: General Surgery Board and ABSITE Review, 4th ed., Matthew J. Blecha, PDF p. 93

The kidney converts glucose to glycogen

options: They are mobilized because protein catabolism accelerates
They are conserved because protein breakdown stops
They are converted directly into glycogen stores
They remain unchanged until oral feeding resumes
questions.explanation: After trauma, accelerated protein catabolism mobilizes nitrogen reserves.

The ebb phase continues with low glucose and high insulin
Glucose and insulin both become undetectable

Urinary potassium and sodium excretion only

title: Day 15 — Trauma, Shock, Hemorrhage & Surgical Oncology
description: 80 English MCQs: 20 non-septic shock and hemorrhage, 20 blood products and transfusion, 20 wound healing, and 20 principles of surgical oncology. All factual content is drawn from the user-designated Garden textbook.

questions.question: Which option is presented as hypovolaemic shock in the chapter’s ‘Types of shock’ discussion?
options: Loss of intravascular volume due to blood loss or fluid/electrolyte loss
Failure of the heart to maintain cardiac output because of acute myocardial infarction
Loss of sympathetic tone causing vasodilation
An immediate hypersensitivity reaction after exposure to an allergen
questions.explanation: The book describes hypovolaemic shock as arising from reduced intravascular volume, including blood or fluid/electrolyte loss.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 1, ‘Metabolic response to injury, fluid and electrolyte balance and shock’, PDF p. 31 (printed p. 18).
questions.sourceEvidence: The hypovolaemic shock paragraph identifies reduced intravascular volume from blood loss, gastrointestinal haemorrhage, plasma loss or fluid/electrolyte loss.

questions.question: What physiological change does the book identify as characteristic of neurogenic shock?
options: Increased preload from acute intravascular fluid expansion
Loss of sympathetic tone to vascular smooth muscle, producing vasodilation
Primary elevation of systemic vascular resistance
Reduced circulating volume caused by haemorrhage
questions.explanation: The chapter attributes neurogenic shock to loss of sympathetic tone to vascular smooth muscle, with vasodilation and reduced systemic vascular resistance.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 1, ‘Metabolic response to injury, fluid and electrolyte balance and shock’, PDF p. 32 (printed p. 19).
questions.sourceEvidence: The neurogenic shock text says sympathetic tone to vascular smooth muscle is lost, typically following spinal or cervical cord injury, causing reduced SVR.

questions.question: According to the chapter, the commonest cause of cardiogenic shock is which event?
options: Loss of sympathetic tone after spinal injury
questions.explanation: The cardiogenic shock section identifies acute myocardial infarction as the most common cause.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 1, ‘Metabolic response to injury, fluid and electrolyte balance and shock’, PDF p. 40 (printed p. 26).
questions.sourceEvidence: The cardiogenic shock section opens by stating that its commonest cause is acute (anterior) myocardial infarction.

questions.question: Which set contains only causes of haemorrhagic hypovolaemic shock listed in Table 1.14?
options: Myocardial infarction, tamponade and pulmonary embolus
Trauma, ruptured aneurysm and obstetric haemorrhage
questions.explanation: Table 1.14 lists trauma, ruptured aneurysm, obstetric and gastrointestinal haemorrhage among the causes.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 1, ‘Metabolic response to injury, fluid and electrolyte balance and shock’, PDF p. 31 (printed p. 18).
questions.sourceEvidence: Table 1.14 groups gastrointestinal haemorrhage, trauma, ruptured aneurysm, obstetric haemorrhage and pulmonary haemorrhage as causes.

questions.question: According to Garden, which combination of physiological effects contributes to anaphylactic shock?
options: Vasodilation, intravascular volume redistribution, capillary leak, and reduced cardiac output
Isolated loss of red-cell mass with preserved vascular tone and cardiac output
Increased systemic vascular resistance with expansion of intravascular volume
Primary failure of renal sodium retention without a change in vascular permeability
questions.explanation: Garden describes anaphylactic shock as resulting from vasodilation, intravascular volume redistribution, capillary leak, and a reduction in cardiac output.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 1, ‘Metabolic response to injury, fluid and electrolyte balance and shock’, PDF p. 32 (printed p. 19).
questions.sourceEvidence: The anaphylactic shock passage states that it results from vasodilation, intravascular volume redistribution, capillary leak and a reduction in cardiac output.

questions.question: What estimated blood volume does the chapter give for a 70 kg adult man?
questions.explanation: The book estimates normal adult blood volume at about 7% of body weight, or around 5000 ml for a 70 kg man.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 1, ‘Metabolic response to injury, fluid and electrolyte balance and shock’, PDF p. 36 (printed p. 23).
questions.sourceEvidence: The text states normal adult blood volume is approximately 7% of body weight; a 70 kg man has an estimated volume around 5000 ml.

questions.question: A patient has lost 10% of estimated blood volume. Which class best fits the book’s haemorrhagic shock classification?
questions.explanation: Class I is defined as blood loss below 15% of estimated blood volume, a compensated state.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 1, ‘Metabolic response to injury, fluid and electrolyte balance and shock’, PDF p. 36 (printed p. 23).
questions.sourceEvidence: The text classifies class I as less than 15% estimated blood volume loss and describes it as compensated.

questions.question: Which estimated blood-volume loss threshold defines class IV haemorrhagic shock in the chapter?
questions.explanation: Class IV is defined as loss exceeding 40% of estimated blood volume and is immediately life threatening.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 1, ‘Metabolic response to injury, fluid and electrolyte balance and shock’, PDF p. 36 (printed p. 23).
questions.sourceEvidence: The text describes class IV as greater than 40% estimated blood volume loss and immediately life threatening.

questions.question: Which is one of the book’s stated definitions of massive haemorrhage?
options: Loss of 50% of estimated blood volume in 3 hours
Loss of 10% of estimated blood volume in 24 hours
Loss of one unit of blood over a week
questions.explanation: The text lists loss of 50% of estimated blood volume within 3 hours as one definition of massive haemorrhage.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 1, ‘Metabolic response to injury, fluid and electrolyte balance and shock’, PDF p. 37 (printed p. 24).
questions.sourceEvidence: The listed definitions include loss of estimated blood volume in 24 hours, 50% loss in 3 hours, or blood loss at least 150 ml/min.

questions.question: On clinical examination, which pulse finding is consistent with a low-output state?
options: Regular, bounding pulse with warm peripheries
A pulse finding has no relevance to output
questions.explanation: The clinical assessment table associates a low-volume, thready pulse with a low-output state.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 1, ‘Metabolic response to injury, fluid and electrolyte balance and shock’, PDF p. 36 (printed p. 23).
questions.sourceEvidence: Table 1.16 describes a low-volume, thready pulse as consistent with low output; a high-volume, bounding pulse is associated with high output.

questions.question: Cold peripheries in a shocked patient most strongly suggest which vascular response in the assessment table?
options: Vasodilation with reduced systemic vascular resistance
Vasoconstriction with increased systemic vascular resistance
questions.explanation: The table links cold peripheries to vasoconstriction and increased systemic vascular resistance.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 1, ‘Metabolic response to injury, fluid and electrolyte balance and shock’, PDF p. 36 (printed p. 23).
questions.sourceEvidence: Table 1.16 states cold peripheries suggest vasoconstriction (increased SVR); warm peripheries suggest vasodilation (reduced SVR).

questions.question: Which urine output does the book identify as suggestive of renal hypoperfusion?
questions.explanation: The clinical assessment table identifies urine output below 0.5 ml/kg/h as suggestive of renal hypoperfusion.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 1, ‘Metabolic response to injury, fluid and electrolyte balance and shock’, PDF p. 36 (printed p. 23).
questions.sourceEvidence: Table 1.16 gives urine output <0.5 ml/kg/h as suggestive of renal hypoperfusion.

questions.question: Which central venous finding is consistent with hypovolaemia in the clinical assessment table?
options: Low CVP with collapsing central veins
High CVP with distended central veins
CVP is not informative in volume assessment
questions.explanation: The table identifies low CVP accompanied by collapsing central veins as consistent with hypovolaemia.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 1, ‘Metabolic response to injury, fluid and electrolyte balance and shock’, PDF p. 36 (printed p. 23).
questions.sourceEvidence: Table 1.16 says low CVP with collapsing central veins is consistent with hypovolaemia.

questions.question: How does the book recommend interpreting isolated measurements during shock assessment?
options: A single blood pressure reading is sufficient to establish severity
Single measurements are not helpful in isolation; combine examination findings and trends
Urine output alone determines the shock type
Laboratory measurements should replace clinical examination
questions.explanation: The chapter cautions against interpreting single measurements alone and emphasizes combining findings and following trends and response to intervention.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 1, ‘Metabolic response to injury, fluid and electrolyte balance and shock’, PDF p. 36 (printed p. 23).
questions.sourceEvidence: The note below Table 1.16 says isolated measurements are not helpful; combined examination findings and trends, including response to fluid challenge, are key.

questions.question: Which pair of principles does the chapter state underpins management of shock?
options: Use vasopressors in every patient before assessing volume
Normalize heart rate first, then defer treating the cause
Identify and treat the underlying cause, and maintain adequate tissue oxygen delivery
Restrict oxygen delivery while observing for spontaneous recovery
questions.explanation: The general principles are treatment of the underlying cause and maintenance of adequate tissue oxygen delivery.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 1, ‘Metabolic response to injury, fluid and electrolyte balance and shock’, PDF p. 36 (printed p. 23).
questions.sourceEvidence: The management section lists identification/treatment of the cause and maintenance of adequate tissue oxygen delivery as its two principles.

questions.question: Which immediate assessment framework does the book recommend for a shocked patient?
options: Circulation, then defer airway and breathing assessment
questions.explanation: The text says immediate assessment and management should follow an ABC approach while diagnosis and treatment proceed together.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 1, ‘Metabolic response to injury, fluid and electrolyte balance and shock’, PDF p. 36 (printed p. 23).
questions.sourceEvidence: The general principles paragraph recommends immediate assessment and management using Airway, Breathing, Circulation, with diagnosis and treatment simultaneous.

questions.question: What does the chapter recommend to rapidly correct or prevent hypoxaemia during initial management?
options: Maintain a clear airway and administer high-flow oxygen
Withhold oxygen until blood gas results are available
Give only low-flow oxygen regardless of clinical state
Prioritize fluid administration and leave the airway unattended
questions.explanation: The airway and breathing section recommends a clear airway and high-flow oxygen, with ongoing assessment of adequacy.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 1, ‘Metabolic response to injury, fluid and electrolyte balance and shock’, PDF p. 36 (printed p. 23).
questions.sourceEvidence: The chapter advises maintaining a clear airway and administering high-flow oxygen (for example 10–15 litres/min) to prevent or rapidly correct hypoxaemia.

questions.question: What should occur concurrently in the initial resuscitation of haemorrhagic hypovolaemic shock?
options: Vasopressor administration and delayed haemorrhage control
Arrest of haemorrhage and intravascular fluid resuscitation
Observation alone until blood pressure falls further
questions.explanation: The chapter explicitly recommends arresting haemorrhage and providing intravascular fluid resuscitation concurrently.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 1, ‘Metabolic response to injury, fluid and electrolyte balance and shock’, PDF p. 37 (printed p. 24).
questions.sourceEvidence: The text states that haemorrhage control and intravascular fluid resuscitation should occur concurrently.

questions.question: Which response to serial 250–500 ml fluid challenges is described as evidence of fluid responsiveness?
options: A stable examination despite increasing pulmonary oedema
Worsening tachycardia with falling blood pressure and urine output
Reduced tachycardia, rising blood pressure, and improving peripheral perfusion and urine output
An isolated increase in CVP without clinical improvement
questions.explanation: The book calls improving heart rate, blood pressure, peripheral perfusion and urine output with fluid challenges evidence of fluid responsiveness.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 1, ‘Metabolic response to injury, fluid and electrolyte balance and shock’, PDF p. 36 (printed p. 23).
questions.sourceEvidence: The text describes reduced tachycardia, increasing pressure, and improving peripheral perfusion and urine output after 250–500 ml challenges as fluid responsiveness.

questions.question: During fluid resuscitation, which development suggests that further fluid is unlikely to be beneficial?
options: Urine output improves after a fluid challenge
Tachycardia decreases and blood pressure rises
Physiological parameters stop improving, especially with falling oxygen saturation and pulmonary oedema
questions.explanation: The text says further fluid is unlikely to help when parameters stop improving, particularly if oxygen saturation falls and pulmonary oedema develops.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 1, ‘Metabolic response to injury, fluid and electrolyte balance and shock’, PDF p. 36 (printed p. 23).
questions.sourceEvidence: The resuscitation passage states that once parameters stop improving, further fluid is unlikely to benefit, particularly with falling oxygen saturation and pulmonary oedema.

questions.question: In life-threatening or continuing haemorrhage, when should blood be introduced into resuscitation?
options: Only after a low haemoglobin is confirmed twice
questions.explanation: Garden states that blood will be required early in resuscitation when haemorrhage is life-threatening or ongoing.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th edition (2012), Chapter 1, “Metabolic response to injury, fluid and electrolyte balance and shock”; PDF p. 37, printed p. 24.
questions.sourceEvidence: The text says blood is required early in life-threatening or continued haemorrhage.

questions.question: Until fully cross-matched packed red cells are available in severe bleeding, which blood may be used?
options: Autologous blood collected from the wound
questions.explanation: The text permits type-specific or O Rh-negative blood until fully cross-matched PRBCs are available.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th edition (2012), Chapter 1, “Metabolic response to injury, fluid and electrolyte balance and shock”; PDF p. 37, printed p. 24.
questions.sourceEvidence: Type-specific or O Rh-negative blood may be used until cross-matched blood becomes available.

questions.question: At what temperature should red-cell concentrates be stored according to Garden?
questions.explanation: Red-cell concentrates are stored refrigerated at +4°C ± 2°C.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th edition (2012), Chapter 2, ‘Transfusion of blood components and plasma products’; PDF p. 31, printed p. 28.
questions.sourceEvidence: Garden specifies storage of red-cell concentrates at +4°C ± 2°C.

questions.question: Which fluid should be used to prime the blood administration set for red-cell transfusion?
questions.explanation: The blood-giving set should be primed with saline; no other solution should be transfused simultaneously.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th edition (2012), Chapter 2, ‘Transfusion of blood components and plasma products’; PDF p. 31, printed p. 28.
questions.sourceEvidence: The red-cell administration instructions specify a sterile set primed with saline and no concurrent other solution.

questions.question: What filter does Garden specify in the blood administration set?
questions.explanation: The text specifies a sterile blood administration set with an in-line macroaggregate filter.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th edition (2012), Chapter 2, ‘Transfusion of blood components and plasma products’; PDF p. 31, printed p. 28.
questions.sourceEvidence: The red-cell transfusion paragraph calls for an in-line macroaggregate filter.

questions.question: An adult platelet dose made from whole-blood donations is pooled from how many separate donations?
questions.explanation: Garden states that an adult dose may be manufactured from four separate donations pooled together or from one apheresis collection.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th edition (2012), Chapter 2, ‘Transfusion of blood components and plasma products’; PDF p. 31, printed p. 28.
questions.sourceEvidence: The platelet section gives four pooled donations as one way to make an adult dose.

questions.question: Which clinical situation is specifically listed as an indication for platelet concentrate in a patient receiving massive transfusion?
options: A prolonged clotting time without bleeding
Microvascular bleeding with oozing from wounds or puncture sites
questions.explanation: Platelets are indicated in massive transfusion when microvascular bleeding is present, such as oozing from mucosa, puncture sites or wounds.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th edition (2012), Chapter 2, ‘Transfusion of blood components and plasma products’; PDF p. 31, printed p. 28.
questions.sourceEvidence: The text names microvascular bleeding during massive transfusion as an indication for platelets.

questions.question: Over what interval does Garden advise infusing a platelet concentrate?
options: As a rapid bolus in under 1 minute
questions.explanation: Platelet concentrates are infused through a standard blood-giving set over less than 30 minutes.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th edition (2012), Chapter 2, ‘Transfusion of blood components and plasma products’; PDF p. 31, printed p. 28.
questions.sourceEvidence: The platelet administration passage specifies infusion in under 30 minutes.

questions.question: Which storage condition is specified for platelet concentrates?
questions.explanation: Platelets are stored at +22°C ± 2°C and cannot be refrigerated, which contributes to bacterial contamination concerns.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th edition (2012), Chapter 2, ‘Transfusion of blood components and plasma products’; PDF p. 31, printed p. 28.
questions.sourceEvidence: Garden explains that platelet concentrates must be kept at 22°C ± 2°C rather than refrigerated.

questions.question: For an RhD-negative girl or woman of child-bearing potential who can receive only RhD-positive platelets, what additional measure does Garden specify?
options: Irradiate the platelet pack at the bedside
questions.explanation: Garden advises RhD-negative platelets for these recipients, or prophylactic RhD immunoglobulin if only RhD-positive platelets are available.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th edition (2012), Chapter 2, ‘Transfusion of blood components and plasma products’; PDF p. 31, printed p. 28.
questions.sourceEvidence: The text explicitly gives prophylactic RhD immunoglobulin as the alternative when RhD-positive platelets must be used.

questions.question: How long can fresh frozen plasma be stored at −30°C according to Garden?
questions.explanation: FFP can be stored frozen at −30°C for a year.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th edition (2012), Chapter 2, ‘Transfusion of blood components and plasma products’; PDF p. 32, printed p. 29.
questions.sourceEvidence: The FFP description states storage at −30°C for one year.

questions.question: Within what time after thawing should FFP be transfused?
questions.explanation: Garden specifies transfusion of thawed FFP within four hours.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th edition (2012), Chapter 2, ‘Transfusion of blood components and plasma products’; PDF p. 32, printed p. 29.
questions.sourceEvidence: The FFP section says it should be transfused within four hours of thawing.

questions.question: Which scenario is an appropriate use of FFP described by Garden?
options: Multiple coagulation-factor deficiencies with severe bleeding
Routine volume expansion when saline is suitable
Correction of an isolated prolonged clotting time in a non-bleeding patient
questions.explanation: FFP is used for multiple coagulation-factor deficiencies associated with severe bleeding; it should not be used simply to correct prolonged clotting times in a patient who is not bleeding or about to undergo immediate surgery.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th edition (2012), Chapter 2, ‘Transfusion of blood components and plasma products’; PDF p. 32, printed p. 29.
questions.sourceEvidence: The text lists multiple factor deficiencies with severe bleeding as an FFP use and rejects correction of prolonged clotting times without bleeding or imminent surgery.

questions.question: Which deficiency is the principal indication for cryoprecipitate stated in Garden?
questions.explanation: Cryoprecipitate is enriched in fibrinogen and is used when fibrinogen levels are low, including in DIC.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th edition (2012), Chapter 2, ‘Transfusion of blood components and plasma products’; PDF p. 32, printed p. 29.
questions.sourceEvidence: The chapter lists low fibrinogen, as in DIC, as the indication for cryoprecipitate.

questions.question: What does the pretransfusion antibody screen assess?
options: Patient serum for clinically significant red-cell antibodies
Donor red cells for bacterial growth only
questions.explanation: Antibody screening uses a panel of cells to detect clinically significant antibodies in the patient's serum.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th edition (2012), Chapter 2, ‘Transfusion of blood components and plasma products’; PDF p. 33, printed p. 30.
questions.sourceEvidence: The listed pretransfusion steps define antibody screening as testing patient serum with a panel of cells.

questions.question: When a patient has a clinically significant red-cell antibody, what crossmatch approach does Garden describe?
options: Issue any ABO-identical unit without further testing
Select antigen-positive units and perform electronic issue
Select donor blood lacking the offending antigen and perform an IAT crossmatch
questions.explanation: Antigen-negative donor blood is identified and an indirect antiglobulin test crossmatch is carried out; this may take several hours.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th edition (2012), Chapter 2, ‘Transfusion of blood components and plasma products’; PDF p. 33, printed p. 30.
questions.sourceEvidence: The crossmatching passage prescribes antigen-negative donor blood and IAT crossmatch when an antibody is present.

questions.question: In a patient with no abnormal red-cell antibodies, what does a rapid-spin crossmatch effectively check?
questions.explanation: Garden says rapid-spin crossmatch can release blood more quickly when no abnormal antibodies are present and effectively checks for ABO incompatibility.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th edition (2012), Chapter 2, ‘Transfusion of blood components and plasma products’; PDF p. 33, printed p. 30.
questions.sourceEvidence: The text characterizes rapid-spin crossmatch in antibody-negative patients as an effective ABO incompatibility check.

questions.question: In a clinically stable patient, at which haemoglobin concentration does Garden say red-cell transfusion is usually not required?
questions.explanation: The chapter states that in a clinically stable situation red-cell transfusion is usually not required at haemoglobin concentrations of 100 g/l or higher.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th edition (2012), Chapter 2, ‘Transfusion of blood components and plasma products’; PDF p. 34, printed p. 31.
questions.sourceEvidence: The indications section gives ≥100 g/l as the stable-patient level at which transfusion is usually unnecessary.

questions.question: When should the blood sample tube be fully labelled, according to the administration safety guidance?
options: At the bedside before leaving the patient
questions.explanation: Patient identity should be established and the sample labelled fully by hand at the bedside before leaving; tubes must not be pre-labelled.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th edition (2012), Chapter 2, ‘Transfusion of blood components and plasma products’; PDF p. 34, printed p. 31.
questions.sourceEvidence: The safety checklist requires bedside handwritten labelling before departure and prohibits pre-labelling sample tubes.

questions.question: What is the required response if the bedside blood checks reveal a discrepancy between the patient and the unit?
options: Proceed if the ABO group appears correct
Start slowly and observe for a reaction
Ask a relative to confirm the donation number
Do not transfuse and inform the laboratory immediately
questions.explanation: Any discrepancy means the unit must not be transfused, and the laboratory must be informed immediately.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th edition (2012), Chapter 2, ‘Transfusion of blood components and plasma products’; PDF p. 35, printed p. 32.
questions.sourceEvidence: The two-person pre-transfusion checks state that discrepant details prohibit transfusion and require immediate laboratory notification.

questions.question: What is the defining event of the lag phase of soft-tissue wound healing?
options: A 2–3-day delay before fibroblasts begin manufacturing collagen
A rapid increase in tensile strength from collagen deposition
questions.explanation: Garden describes the lag phase as the 2–3 days before fibroblasts begin collagen manufacture, accompanied by an inflammatory response.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 18, ‘Principles of wound healing’, PDF p. 295 (printed p. 282).
questions.sourceEvidence: The lag phase is a 2–3-day delay before fibroblasts manufacture collagen to support the wound.

questions.question: During the lag phase, which cells are described as removing dead tissue from the wound area?
questions.explanation: The text states that inflammatory cells migrate into the area and macrophages remove dead tissue.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 18, ‘Principles of wound healing’, PDF p. 295 (printed p. 282).
questions.sourceEvidence: Inflammatory cells enter the wound, and dead tissue is removed by macrophages.

questions.question: What vascular change is noted in the lag phase as part of the inflammatory response?
options: Capillary permeability increases and protein-rich exudate accumulates
Capillary permeability falls and the wound dries immediately
questions.explanation: Increased capillary permeability permits protein-rich exudate to accumulate during the lag phase.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 18, ‘Principles of wound healing’, PDF p. 295 (printed p. 282).
questions.sourceEvidence: The inflammatory response includes increased capillary permeability and accumulation of protein-rich exudate.

questions.question: Which cellular activity is chiefly associated with collagen accumulation during the incremental (proliferative) phase?
questions.explanation: Garden identifies progressive collagen synthesis by fibroblasts during the incremental or proliferative phase.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 18, ‘Principles of wound healing’, PDF p. 295 (printed p. 282).
questions.sourceEvidence: In the proliferative phase, fibroblasts progressively synthesize collagen as tensile strength increases.

questions.question: Approximately how long does the textbook say collagen synthesis increases during the incremental phase?
questions.explanation: The text describes increasing collagen synthesis over about three weeks, with accelerating gain in tensile strength.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 18, ‘Principles of wound healing’, PDF p. 296 (printed p. 283).
questions.sourceEvidence: Collagen synthesis increases over about 3 weeks during the incremental phase.

questions.question: What tissue change is represented by capillary ingrowth into a healing wound?
questions.explanation: The phase summary labels capillary ingrowth as granulation tissue.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 18, Table 18.1, PDF p. 295 (printed p. 282).
questions.sourceEvidence: Table 18.1 lists capillary ingrowth (granulation tissue) in the proliferative phase.

questions.question: In which phase does the textbook list wound contraction?
questions.explanation: Wound contraction is one of the listed features of the incremental or proliferative phase.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 18, Table 18.1, PDF p. 295 (printed p. 282).
questions.sourceEvidence: Table 18.1 includes wound contraction under the incremental/proliferative phase.

questions.question: After approximately three weeks, what happens to the rate of tensile-strength gain?
options: It immediately returns to the original strength
It stops because all collagen synthesis ceases permanently
It levels off as collagen breakdown approaches and then temporarily exceeds synthesis
questions.explanation: The plateau begins after three weeks as collagen breakdown approaches and temporarily surpasses synthesis.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 18, ‘Plateau or maturation phase’, PDF p. 296 (printed p. 283).
questions.sourceEvidence: After 3 weeks tensile-strength gain levels off; collagen breakdown approaches and temporarily surpasses synthesis.

questions.question: According to Garden, what proportion of original tensile strength do skin and fascia usually recover?
questions.explanation: The text states that skin and fascia usually recover only 80% of their original tensile strength.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 18, ‘Plateau or maturation phase’, PDF p. 296 (printed p. 283).
questions.sourceEvidence: Skin and fascia usually recover only 80% of original tensile strength.

questions.question: Which description best matches the textbook's usual scar change after the initial maturation period?
options: It always enlarges beyond the wound margins
It progressively becomes narrow, flat and pale
It becomes permanently blue and depressed
questions.explanation: Following a period of raised, red thickening, scars slowly improve to become narrow, flat and pale.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 18, scar maturation, PDF p. 296 (printed p. 283).
questions.sourceEvidence: After a static period, the scar slowly improves to become narrow, flat and pale.

questions.question: Which feature distinguishes a keloid from a hypertrophic scar in Garden's description?
options: A keloid is always flat and pale
A keloid continues enlarging after 6 months and invades adjacent uninvolved skin
A keloid occurs only in the elderly
questions.explanation: Keloids continue to enlarge after six months and extend into neighbouring uninvolved skin, unlike hypertrophic scars.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 18, ‘Keloids’, PDF p. 296 (printed p. 283).
questions.sourceEvidence: Keloids continue to enlarge after 6 months and invade neighbouring uninvolved skin.

questions.question: How does epithelium heal, according to the chapter?
options: By replacement with dermal collagen only
By permanent contraction without cell division
By regeneration rather than scar formation
questions.explanation: Garden explicitly contrasts epithelial regeneration with scar formation in the dermis.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 18, ‘Epidermis’, PDF p. 296 (printed p. 283).
questions.sourceEvidence: Epithelium heals by regeneration and not by scar formation.

questions.question: What provides the new epithelial cells that replace cells migrating across a wound?
options: Division of basal cells near the wound edge
Collagen fibres in the wound bed
questions.explanation: Migrating cells are replaced by new cells formed through division of basal cells near the wound edge.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 18, ‘Epidermis’, PDF p. 296 (printed p. 283).
questions.sourceEvidence: New epithelial cells form by division of basal cells near the wound edge.

questions.question: Which wound is most likely to heal by primary intention?
options: A wide defect with unopposed edges
A clean incised wound with edges accurately apposed
A grossly contaminated wound left open
A wound whose edges are separated by a large tissue loss
questions.explanation: Primary intention follows close apposition of wound edges, for example by accurate suturing, and produces a fine scar.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 18, ‘Primary and secondary intention’, PDF p. 297 (printed p. 284).
questions.sourceEvidence: Closely approximated wound edges heal by primary intention; epithelial cover is quick and the scar fine.

questions.question: What fills a defect when wound edges are not apposed and healing proceeds by secondary intention?
questions.explanation: In secondary intention, the defect fills with granulation tissue while epidermal continuity is restored more slowly.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 18, ‘Primary and secondary intention’, PDF p. 297 (printed p. 284).
questions.sourceEvidence: When edges are not apposed, the defect fills with granulation tissue and epidermal restoration takes longer.

questions.question: Which factor does the text identify as a key determinant of the rate of collagen synthesis?
questions.explanation: Garden identifies arterial oxygen tension (PaO2) as a key determinant of collagen synthesis rate.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 18, ‘Blood supply’, PDF p. 297 (printed p. 284).
questions.sourceEvidence: Arterial oxygen tension (PaO2) is a key determinant of the rate of collagen synthesis.

questions.question: Which handling practice can make well-vascularized tissue ischaemic and contribute to wound breakdown?
questions.explanation: The chapter warns that tissue crushing, tension on wound edges and overly tight sutures can cause ischaemia and breakdown.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 18, ‘Blood supply’, PDF p. 297 (printed p. 284).
questions.sourceEvidence: Crushing with forceps, tensioned edges and overly tight sutures can make tissue ischaemic.

questions.question: Which nutrient is described as essential for proline hydroxylation and collagen synthesis?
questions.explanation: The text states that vitamin C is essential for proline hydroxylation and collagen synthesis.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 18, ‘Nutritional status’, PDF p. 298 (printed p. 285).
questions.sourceEvidence: Vitamin C is essential for proline hydroxylation and collagen synthesis.

questions.question: Why should dead spaces be avoided during wound closure?
options: They cause excess collagen breakdown in every case
Accumulated blood and exudate encourage infection
questions.explanation: Garden notes that blood and exudate accumulating in dead spaces encourage infection.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 18, ‘Surgical technique’, PDF p. 298 (printed p. 285).
questions.sourceEvidence: Dead spaces should be avoided because accumulated blood and exudate encourage infection.
questions.imageAlt: Clinical photograph of a healing wound from Garden Figure 18.5; visual context only and does not display the keyed explanation.
questions.imageSourceLabel: Garden, Chapter 18, Figure 18.5, PDF p. 297 (printed p. 284) — visual only.

questions.question: What is the recommended general principle for choosing suture size?
options: Use the thickest available suture in every layer
Use non-absorbable sutures for all buried layers
Choose sutures solely by the length of the incision
Use the finest sutures that will hold the wound edges together
questions.explanation: The chapter advises using the finest sutures that will hold the wound edges together; absorbable materials are preferred for buried layers.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 18, ‘Choice of suture and suture materials’, PDF p. 298 (printed p. 285).
questions.sourceEvidence: Use the finest sutures that will hold the edges together; absorbable materials are preferred for buried layers.

questions.question: According to Garden, loss of cell-cycle regulation that drives cancer growth may result from which combination?
options: Increased proliferation and/or decreased programmed cell death
questions.explanation: The chapter attributes unregulated cancer growth to increased cell proliferation, decreased apoptosis, or both.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 6, PDF p. 94 (printed p. 80).
questions.sourceEvidence: Summary Box 6.1 lists increased cell proliferation and decreased programmed cell death as factors in loss of cell-cycle regulation.

questions.question: Which genetic change is identified as a route to cancer formation in Garden’s discussion of carcinogenesis?
options: Permanent activation of all DNA repair mechanisms
questions.explanation: Mutations can activate or over-express oncogenes, inactivate tumour-suppressor genes, or do both.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 6, PDF p. 94 (printed p. 80).
questions.sourceEvidence: The text links mutations to activation/over-expression of oncogenes and/or inactivation of tumour-suppressor genes.

questions.question: What essential property distinguishes malignant from benign tumours in Garden’s account?
options: Benign tumours always cause systemic cachexia
Benign tumours invade blood vessels more often
Malignant tumours have the capacity to invade and metastasize
questions.explanation: The chapter identifies invasive capacity and the ability to metastasize as the essential distinction.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 6, PDF p. 94 (printed pp. 80–81).
questions.sourceEvidence: Benign tumour cells do not invade surrounding tissues; malignant cells invade adjacent tissues and can enter blood or lymphatic channels.

questions.question: What is the rationale for removing benign or pre-invasive lesions in the adenoma–carcinoma progression model?
options: It confirms that distant metastases have already occurred
It removes the need for all future surveillance
It can prevent progression to invasive disease
questions.explanation: The chapter describes progression from benign adenoma through dysplasia to invasive carcinoma; removing precursor lesions can prevent invasive disease.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 6, PDF p. 95 (printed p. 81).
questions.sourceEvidence: The text states that removal of benign or pre-invasive lesions provides the rationale for screening and early detection to prevent invasive disease.

questions.question: Which set correctly describes routes by which a cancer can spread, as outlined in Chapter 6?
options: Direct invasion, bloodstream, lymphatics, and transcoelomic spread
Only direct extension through adjacent tissue
questions.explanation: Garden describes direct infiltration and distant spread through blood, lymphatics, or across body cavities.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 6, PDF p. 96 (printed p. 82).
questions.sourceEvidence: Figure 6.3 depicts direct invasion, haematogenous spread, lymphatic spread, and transcoelomic spread.

questions.question: Why does a screening test need high specificity when the prevalence of cancer in the screened population is low?
options: To increase the number of false-positive results
To reduce false-positive results and unnecessary investigation or treatment
To replace the need for an effective treatment
To ensure every detected lesion is malignant
questions.explanation: The chapter notes that low prevalence makes a low false-positive rate important, otherwise people may undergo unnecessary investigation or inappropriate treatment.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 6, PDF p. 97 (printed p. 83).
questions.sourceEvidence: Successful screening requires a specific test with a low false-positive rate because cancer likelihood in a population is generally low.

questions.question: In a family with a confirmed inherited BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutation, which risk-reducing operation does Garden give as an example for carriers?
questions.explanation: The chapter lists prophylactic bilateral mastectomy for BRCA1/BRCA2 carriers as an example of surgery to reduce subsequent cancer development.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 6, PDF p. 98 (printed p. 84).
questions.sourceEvidence: Carriers of BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations may be offered prophylactic bilateral mastectomy; APC carriers may be offered restorative proctocolectomy.

questions.question: What are the two main purposes of investigations in a patient with suspected cancer?
options: Measure postoperative pain and determine anaesthetic risk
Identify inherited mutations and select a screening interval only
Confirm cure and determine the need for palliation
Confirm the diagnosis cytologically or histologically and assess disease extent
questions.explanation: Investigations are used to establish a cytological or histological diagnosis and to assess local disease and metastatic spread (staging).
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 6, PDF p. 99 (printed p. 85).
questions.sourceEvidence: The chapter identifies diagnosis confirmation and assessment of primary disease extent/metastatic spread as the two purposes.
questions.imageAlt: Cropped mammographic image from Garden Figure 6.7, without caption; visual context only.
questions.imageSourceLabel: Garden, Chapter 6, Figure 6.7, PDF p. 97 (printed p. 83) — visual only.

questions.question: When is a histological or cytological diagnosis generally obtained in the diagnostic pathway described by Garden?
options: As the ultimate aim of progressively more complex diagnostic investigations
Only after all treatment has been completed
Only from a resected distant metastasis
Before any blood tests or imaging are considered
questions.explanation: The text describes a logical progression from simple tests to imaging, aiming ultimately to obtain histological or cytological confirmation.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 6, PDF pp. 99–100 (printed pp. 85–86).
questions.sourceEvidence: Diagnostic investigations progress from simple blood tests through imaging, with the ultimate aim of histological or cytological confirmation.

questions.question: In the UICC TNM system described in Chapter 6, what does N represent?
options: Presence and extent of metastases in regional lymph nodes
Histological grade of the primary tumour
questions.explanation: TNM assesses the primary tumour (T), regional lymph nodes (N), and distant metastases (M).
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 6, PDF p. 101 (printed p. 87).
questions.sourceEvidence: The text defines N as the presence and extent of metastases in regional lymph nodes.

questions.question: What does the prefix p in pTNM denote in Garden’s description?
options: A prediction based only on symptoms
questions.explanation: The modified TNM system includes post-surgical pathological staging, denoted pTNM, alongside pretreatment clinical classification.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 6, PDF p. 101 (printed p. 87).
questions.sourceEvidence: The text distinguishes pretreatment clinical TNM from a post-surgical pathological classification called pTNM.

questions.question: Why can clinical assessment of regional lymph nodes be an unreliable indicator of nodal tumour involvement?
options: Radiology detects every microscopic nodal deposit
Nodal involvement cannot be assessed histologically
Impalpable nodes may contain metastases, while palpable nodes may be reactively enlarged
questions.explanation: Garden notes that palpation is a poor indicator: nodes may harbor occult metastases or be enlarged by reactive hyperplasia.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 6, PDF p. 101 (printed p. 87).
questions.sourceEvidence: The chapter states that impalpable nodes can contain metastases and palpable nodes may show reactive hyperplasia rather than tumour.

questions.question: Which statement best describes the purpose of staging as summarized by Garden?
options: Define disease extent, assess likely prognosis, and support treatment planning
Prove that microscopic metastases are absent
Choose an operation without considering tumour biology
questions.explanation: Staging guides an estimate of extent and prognosis and allows the multidisciplinary team to develop an appropriate treatment plan; it remains a best-guess assessment.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 6, PDF pp. 100–101 (printed pp. 86–87).
questions.sourceEvidence: Summary Box 6.4 lists defining extent, assessing likely prognosis, and allowing treatment planning as purposes of staging.

questions.question: Which group of professionals is identified as commonly forming part of the cancer multidisciplinary team?
options: Surgeons, oncologists, radiologists, pathologists, and clinical nurse specialists
questions.explanation: The chapter describes a team that commonly includes surgeons, oncology specialists, radiologists, pathologists, and clinical nurse specialists.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 6, PDF p. 98 (printed p. 84).
questions.sourceEvidence: The cancer team is described as commonly including surgeons, oncologists, radiologists, pathologists, and clinical nurse specialists.

questions.question: What does a radical cancer operation imply in Garden’s definition?
options: Removal of the visible tumour alone, regardless of margins
Removal of all regional lymph nodes for every tumour type
Removal of tumour-bearing tissue with a margin of unaffected surrounding tissue
Debulking followed by observation without histology
questions.explanation: A radical operation aims to remove the tissue bearing the tumour together with a margin of unaffected tissue.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 6, PDF p. 101 (printed p. 87).
questions.sourceEvidence: The text defines radical surgery as complete removal of tumour-bearing tissue together with a margin of unaffected surrounding tissue.

questions.question: For a tumour with predictable sequential local and lymphatic spread, what is the rationale for en bloc resection?
options: Removing nodes is always purely diagnostic
It prevents the need for histopathology
It is used only when distant metastases are widespread
Removing the primary with locoregional nodes can be curative
