questions.explanation: Where spread is sequential, careful local excision with locoregional lymph nodes (en bloc) may be curative; the role of nodes varies by tumour.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 6, PDF p. 101 (printed p. 87).
questions.sourceEvidence: The chapter says en bloc removal can be curative when tumour spread proceeds locally, then to nodes, then distant organs.

questions.question: What is the purpose of taking care to avoid spillage of malignant cells during cancer surgery?
options: To reduce the risk of cancer recurrence
To improve the sensitivity of screening tests
questions.explanation: The chapter emphasizes avoiding malignant-cell spillage because it may cause recurrence.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 6, PDF p. 101 (printed p. 87).
questions.sourceEvidence: During cancer operations, care is taken to avoid spillage of malignant cells that may cause cancer recurrence.

questions.question: What is the principal role of radiotherapy described in the chapter, reflecting its localized action?
options: Reducing the chance of local recurrence
questions.explanation: Garden describes radiotherapy as localized and used to reduce local recurrence rather than distant metastasis.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 6, PDF p. 102 (printed p. 88).
questions.sourceEvidence: The text states that radiotherapy is administered to reduce local recurrence rather than distant metastasis.

questions.question: Why might radiotherapy be given before surgery to a bulky, fixed tumour?
options: To provide final pathological staging before biopsy
To prevent the need for any local treatment
To shrink or down-stage it and make surgery easier
questions.explanation: Preoperative radiotherapy may down-stage or shrink a bulky fixed tumour, such as rectal cancer, to facilitate surgery.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 6, PDF p. 102 (printed p. 88).
questions.sourceEvidence: The chapter gives preoperative radiotherapy for bulky, fixed rectal cancer as a way to shrink the tumour and ease surgery.

questions.question: What is the intended goal of an operation performed for palliation in incurable cancer?
options: Obtain a definitive negative-margin resection in all cases
Prevent additional suffering rather than attempt cure
questions.explanation: Palliative surgery aims to relieve distressing symptoms, such as by resecting symptomatic metastases or bypassing malignant obstruction, not to cure.
questions.sourceRef: Principles and Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 6, PDF p. 102 (printed pp. 88–89).
questions.sourceEvidence: The text states that the object of a palliative operation is to prevent additional suffering and not to attempt cure.

references.label: Principles & Practice of Surgery, 6th ed. (2012), edited by O. James Garden et al. — user-designated diploma reference

title: Day 16 — Infections, Safety & Ethics
description: 80 English MCQs covering sterilisation and disinfection, Surgical Infections I & II, septic shock, medical ethics, consent, and breaking bad news. All factual content is based exclusively on the user-designated Garden textbook.

questions.question: Which description best defines decontamination in the excerpt?
options: A process that removes or destroys infectious or unwanted material
The physical removal of soil and organic matter only
The removal or destruction of microorganisms but not bacterial spores
The complete destruction of microorganisms including spores
questions.explanation: Decontamination is the broad process of removing or destroying infectious or unwanted material; the other choices define cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 4: Infections and antibiotics, PDF p. 61 (printed p. 48).
questions.sourceEvidence: The excerpt defines decontamination as removal or destruction of infectious or unwanted material.

questions.question: Which process is defined as the physical removal of soil and organic matter?
questions.explanation: The excerpt distinguishes cleaning from processes intended to destroy microorganisms: cleaning physically removes soil and organic matter.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 4: Infections and antibiotics, PDF p. 61 (printed p. 48).
questions.sourceEvidence: Cleaning is defined as physical removal of soil and organic matter.

questions.question: What is the key limitation of disinfection, according to the excerpt?
options: It removes only visible soil, leaving organic matter
It destroys all microorganisms including spores
It is suitable only for skin and not for instruments
It does not remove or destroy bacterial spores
questions.explanation: Disinfection removes or destroys some microorganisms but is not defined as sporicidal; complete destruction including spores is sterilization.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 4: Infections and antibiotics, PDF p. 61 (printed p. 48).
questions.sourceEvidence: The excerpt states that disinfection removes or destroys some microorganisms but not bacterial spores.

questions.question: Which outcome corresponds to sterilization as defined in the excerpt?
options: Removal of soil and organic matter without microbial destruction
Destruction of some microorganisms while spores remain
Complete destruction of all microorganisms, including spores
Reduction of resident skin organisms before incision
questions.explanation: Sterilization is the most complete endpoint among the listed processes, extending to spores as well as other microorganisms.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 4: Infections and antibiotics, PDF p. 61 (printed p. 48).
questions.sourceEvidence: Sterilization is described as complete destruction of all microorganisms including spores.

questions.question: What hand preparation does the excerpt specify for the operating team before each operation on the list?
options: Wash with an aqueous antiseptic surgical solution and use a single-use nail brush
Apply alcohol hand gel regardless of whether hands are soiled
Wash with plain water and reuse a nail brush
Use antiseptic skin preparation without washing the hands
questions.explanation: The stated routine is aqueous antiseptic surgical handwashing before each operation, with a single-use brush for the nails.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 4: Infections and antibiotics, PDF p. 61 (printed p. 48).
questions.sourceEvidence: The operating team should wash hands before each operation using aqueous antiseptic surgical solution and a single-use nail brush.

questions.question: When does the excerpt recommend considering two pairs of surgical gloves?
options: For every operation, regardless of the likelihood or consequences of glove perforation
When perforation risk is high and contamination could have serious consequences, such as with a known or suspected blood-borne virus
Only when the patient has a confirmed bacterial wound infection
Only when sterile gowns and eye protection are unavailable
questions.explanation: The chapter advises considering double gloving when perforation risk is high and the consequences of contamination may be serious, for example in patients known or suspected to have a blood-borne virus.
questions.sourceEvidence: The PPE section advises considering two pairs of gloves when there is a high risk of perforation and contamination consequences may be serious, such as known or suspected blood-borne virus infection.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012); Chapter 4, Infections and antibiotics; PDF page 61, printed page 48.

questions.question: What instrument standard is required to prevent cross-infection during surgery?
options: Instruments need only be visibly clean
Instruments need only undergo thermal disinfection
Instruments may be reused without processing if dry
questions.explanation: The excerpt links prevention of cross-infection to using sterile instruments; cleaning or thermal disinfection alone is not presented as sufficient for operative use.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 4: Infections and antibiotics, PDF p. 61 (printed p. 48).
questions.sourceEvidence: The text states that only sterile instruments are used to prevent cross-infection.

questions.question: At what temperature range do the automated washer disinfectors described in the excerpt operate?
questions.explanation: The excerpt gives 85–95°C for washer-disinfector thermal disinfection; the higher values relate to steam sterilizer examples.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 4: Infections and antibiotics, PDF p. 61 (printed p. 48).
questions.sourceEvidence: Used instruments are washed in automated washer disinfectors operating at 85–95°C.

questions.question: Which statement accurately describes the washer-disinfector stage for used surgical instruments?
options: It destroys all microorganisms and spores, making further processing unnecessary
It removes soil but does not kill microorganisms
It removes organic matter and kills most microorganisms except spores
It is performed after steam sterilization to remove spores
questions.explanation: The washer-disinfector provides cleaning and thermal disinfection but leaves spores among the exceptions, so instruments proceed to sterilization.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 4: Infections and antibiotics, PDF p. 61 (printed p. 48).
questions.sourceEvidence: The washer disinfectors remove organic matter and kill most microorganisms except spores, before subsequent sterilization.

questions.question: Why are pressures above atmospheric used in the steam sterilizer or autoclave process described?
options: To keep instruments below boiling temperature
To prevent removal of organic matter
questions.explanation: The excerpt directly explains that elevated pressure is used so that higher temperatures can be achieved during steam sterilization.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 4: Infections and antibiotics, PDF p. 61 (printed p. 48).
questions.sourceEvidence: Pressure above atmospheric is used in the autoclave so higher temperatures can be achieved.

questions.question: Which pair of steam sterilizer time-and-temperature examples is given in the excerpt?
questions.explanation: Both temperature-duration combinations appear as examples for steam sterilization; the alternative pairs change the stated settings.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 4: Infections and antibiotics, PDF p. 61 (printed p. 48).
questions.sourceEvidence: The excerpt gives steam sterilizer examples of 121°C for 20 minutes and 134°C for 5 minutes.

questions.question: What special instrument handling is specified for patients known to have, or at risk of, CJD?
options: Rely on routine decontamination because it destroys prions
Use only thermal disinfection and retain the instruments
Use disposable instruments where possible, then destroy all instruments used by incineration
Sterilize once in a steam autoclave and return the instruments to general use
questions.explanation: The excerpt warns that normal decontamination processes do not destroy prions and specifies disposable instruments where possible, followed by incineration of all instruments used.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 4: Infections and antibiotics, PDF p. 62 (printed p. 49).
questions.sourceEvidence: Routine decontamination does not destroy prions; disposable instruments are preferred where possible and all used instruments must subsequently be incinerated.

questions.question: According to the excerpt, how do commensal organisms help defend against pathogens?
options: They sterilize tissues by producing antibodies against all pathogens
They increase pathogen attachment while limiting immune-cell recruitment
They compete for nutrients, impede pathogen adherence, and release interfering signals
They destroy bacterial spores through routine colonization
questions.explanation: Commensals can restrain pathogens through competition, prevention of adherence, and signalling substances that interfere with pathogen activity.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012); Chapter 4, Infections and antibiotics; PDF page 58; printed page 45
questions.sourceEvidence: Normal commensals can limit pathogen virulence by depriving pathogens of nutrients, preventing adherence, and producing substances that interfere with them.

questions.question: Why may broad-spectrum antibiotics increase the risk of a new infection, as described in the excerpt?
options: They permanently remove all immune cells from the bowel lining
They can replace protective commensals with a pathogen such as Clostridium difficile
They make every bacterial inoculum more virulent
They prevent skin from forming a mechanical barrier
questions.explanation: The excerpt notes that broad-spectrum treatment can disturb normal flora and permit a pathogen to replace commensals.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012); Chapter 4, Infections and antibiotics; PDF page 58; printed page 45
questions.sourceEvidence: Broad-spectrum antibiotics may result in replacement of commensals by a pathogen, with C. difficile in the colon given as an example.

questions.question: Which description best matches the excerpt's account of innate immune defence against bacteria?
options: Macrophages, neutrophils, and complement act through phagocytosis and bacterial lysis
B-lymphocytes and antibodies act only by preventing bacterial entry through skin
CD8 T cells produce sebum to suppress bacteria on body surfaces
Commensal bacteria perform all phagocytosis and complement activation
questions.explanation: The excerpt identifies macrophages, neutrophils, and complement as innate defences that promote phagocytosis and lysis.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012); Chapter 4, Infections and antibiotics; PDF page 59; printed page 46
questions.sourceEvidence: Macrophages, neutrophils, and complement provide innate immunity through phagocytosis and bacterial lysis.

questions.question: Which operative wound classification fits a non-traumatic wound in which a gastrointestinal tract is entered without significant spillage?
questions.explanation: Entry into a respiratory, gastrointestinal, or genitourinary tract without significant spillage is the stated clean-contaminated example.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012); Chapter 4, Infections and antibiotics; PDF page 59; printed page 46
questions.sourceEvidence: A non-traumatic wound with entry into a gastrointestinal tract but insignificant spillage is classified as clean-contaminated.

questions.question: A fresh traumatic wound from a dirty source falls into which wound class in the excerpt?
questions.explanation: The wound-class table explicitly includes a fresh traumatic wound from a dirty source under contaminated wounds.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012); Chapter 4, Infections and antibiotics; PDF page 59; printed page 46
questions.sourceEvidence: The contaminated category includes a fresh traumatic wound from a dirty source.

questions.question: Which listed finding places an operative wound in the contaminated class?
options: Intact respiratory, gastrointestinal, and genitourinary tracts
Insignificant spillage after entry into a hollow tract
A non-traumatic wound without tract entry
Gross spillage from the gastrointestinal tract
questions.explanation: Gross gastrointestinal spillage is specifically listed as a contaminated-wound example, unlike tract entry with insignificant spillage.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012); Chapter 4, Infections and antibiotics; PDF page 59; printed page 46
questions.sourceEvidence: The contaminated category includes gross spillage from the gastrointestinal tract.

questions.question: Which wound class has the highest infection rate with prophylaxis among the classes tabulated in the excerpt?
options: All three have the same rate
questions.explanation: The table reports 10.2% for contaminated wounds, higher than the clean and clean-contaminated rates shown.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012); Chapter 4, Infections and antibiotics; PDF page 59; printed page 46
questions.sourceEvidence: The tabulated infection rates with prophylaxis are 0.8% for clean, 1.3% for clean-contaminated, and 10.2% for contaminated wounds.

questions.question: Which statement about skin as a host defence is supported by the excerpt?
options: It is normally sterile because its surface acidity destroys every organism
It protects only by producing antibodies against resident bacteria
It provides a dry mechanical barrier and sebum fatty acids can suppress or kill pathogens
It acts as a barrier only when covered by antiseptic solution
questions.explanation: Skin's physical barrier and antimicrobial fatty acids in sebum are both described as defences.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012); Chapter 4, Infections and antibiotics; PDF page 59; printed page 46
questions.sourceEvidence: Skin is described as a dry, inhospitable mechanical barrier, and fatty acids in sebum kill or suppress potential pathogens.

questions.question: In the excerpt, which set of practices is collectively referred to as aseptic technique?
options: Antibiotic treatment, wound drainage, patient isolation, and postoperative imaging
Instrument cleaning, patient vaccination, wound closure, and ward screening
Glove use, blood tests, postoperative dressings, and antibiotic courses
Hand washing, surgical scrub, patient skin preparation, maintaining a sterile field, and safe operating practices
questions.explanation: The text defines aseptic technique as specific practices before and during surgery, listing these measures.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012); Chapter 4, Infections and antibiotics; PDF page 60; printed page 47
questions.sourceEvidence: Aseptic technique includes hand washing, surgical scrub, patient skin preparation, maintaining a sterile field, and safe operating practices.

questions.question: For elective surgical patients in England, what preoperative measure has been required since 2008 according to the excerpt?
options: Routine screening for every species of bowel commensal
Mandatory culture of every surgical incision before operation
Universal isolation regardless of screening result
questions.explanation: The excerpt states that hospitals in England have been required to screen all elective surgical patients for MRSA since 2008.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012); Chapter 4, Infections and antibiotics; PDF page 60; printed page 47
questions.sourceEvidence: Since 2008, hospitals in England have been required to screen all elective surgical patients for MRSA.

questions.question: When is alcohol hand gel described as a suitable alternative for hand decontamination on the wards?
options: Whenever hands are visibly soiled with organic matter
Only after a full surgical scrub before every operation
Only when sterile gloves are unavailable
questions.explanation: The excerpt distinguishes ward hand decontamination from the preoperative surgical handwash and permits alcohol gel when hands are not soiled.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012); Chapter 4, Infections and antibiotics; PDF page 61; printed page 48
questions.sourceEvidence: Where hands are not soiled, alcohol hand gel is described as a suitable alternative for decontamination on the wards.

questions.question: What is the stated purpose of applying an antiseptic such as chlorhexidine or povidone-iodine to the surgical site before incision?
options: To sterilize the skin completely before the incision
To replace the need for maintaining a sterile field
To reduce resident organisms and thereby reduce wound-infection risk
To destroy bacterial spores on reusable instruments
questions.explanation: The excerpt says skin cannot be sterilized, but antiseptic preparation reduces resident organisms and wound-infection risk.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012); Chapter 4, Infections and antibiotics; PDF page 61; printed page 48
questions.sourceEvidence: Pre-incision chlorhexidine or povidone-iodine reduces the number of resident organisms on skin and thus the risk of wound infection, although skin cannot be sterilized.

questions.question: When a patient with a surgical infection is stable enough for microbiological sampling, what approach to antibiotic choice does the excerpt recommend?
options: Begin broad-spectrum antibiotics and disregard culture results once treatment starts
Use prophylactic antibiotics as definitive treatment regardless of the organism
Choose treatment solely from the site of infection without microbiological testing
Obtain cultures where possible, then use specific antibiotics guided by sensitivity results
questions.explanation: The text recommends obtaining culture and sensitivity specimens when possible and then tailoring specific therapy to the results; immediate empirical treatment may still be needed when waiting is unsafe.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012); Chapter 4, Infections and antibiotics; PDF page 63, printed page 50.
questions.sourceEvidence: Where possible, specimens should be collected for culture and sensitivity, after which specific antibiotics can be selected; seriously ill patients may need immediate empirical therapy.

questions.question: Which prescribing principle is stated in the excerpt's antibiotic-policy table?
options: Prefer combination therapy and broad-spectrum drugs for routine infections
Use topical forms of antibiotics that are also prescribed systemically
Prefer single agents and narrow-spectrum drugs when possible
Continue antibiotics without review even when culture results become available
questions.explanation: The policy principles favor a single agent and narrow spectrum whenever these are appropriate, while also requiring review as evidence becomes available.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012); Chapter 4, Infections and antibiotics; PDF page 64, printed page 51.
questions.sourceEvidence: The policy table prefers single-agent treatment and narrow-spectrum agents over combinations and broad-spectrum agents whenever possible.

questions.question: According to the excerpt, what is the usual key intervention for an abscess before antibiotics are relied upon?
options: Use systemic antibiotics alone until the collection resolves
Achieve adequate surgical or radiological drainage
Apply systemic antibiotics directly to the abscess cavity
Wait for culture results before considering any drainage
questions.explanation: The excerpt explains that pus is poorly penetrated by antibiotics and that abscess management generally requires drainage; antibiotics may be adjunctive in selected situations.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012); Chapter 4, Infections and antibiotics; PDF page 64, printed page 51; PDF page 65, printed page 52.
questions.sourceEvidence: Antibiotics should generally not be used for an abscess unless adequate surgical or radiological drainage has been achieved; cellulitic infection may be treated medically, but an abscess requires drainage.

questions.question: A postoperative patient has suspected intra-abdominal infection, but examination is inconclusive. Which investigation does the excerpt identify as useful for detecting leaks or pus collections?
questions.explanation: Clinical examination may be unreliable in intra-abdominal infection, and the text recommends CT or MRI, preferably with contrast, to identify leaks and collections.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012); Chapter 4, Infections and antibiotics; PDF page 63, printed page 50.
questions.sourceEvidence: Because examination can mislead, CT or MRI preferably with contrast is recommended to detect peritoneal leaks and collections of pus.

questions.question: Which finding in a catheterized patient with bacteriuria does the excerpt say, by itself, does not warrant antibiotics?
options: Urinary organisms without white cells or signs of systemic illness
Pyelonephritis with rigors and renal-angle tenderness
A urinary infection supported by symptoms and culture
questions.explanation: The text notes that catheterized patients frequently have organisms in urine; in the absence of systemic illness, this finding alone does not require antibiotics.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012); Chapter 4, Infections and antibiotics; PDF page 65, printed page 52.
questions.sourceEvidence: In catheterized patients, urine may contain organisms without white cells, and this does not require antibiotics unless systemic illness is present.

questions.question: What diagnostic combination does the excerpt describe for suspected respiratory tract infection in a surgical patient?
options: A positive sputum culture alone, regardless of symptoms or signs
Clinical history and examination with chest imaging and appropriate cultures
Urine microscopy and culture with abdominal imaging
A wound swab and tissue biopsy without respiratory assessment
questions.explanation: The text describes diagnosis using history, examination, chest X-ray, cultures (blood, sputum and bronchial washings), and sometimes specialist imaging; a positive sputum culture alone is insufficient evidence of infection.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012); Chapter 4, Infections and antibiotics; PDF page 66, printed page 53.
questions.sourceEvidence: Respiratory infection diagnosis combines clinical assessment with chest X-ray and cultures, sometimes supplemented by CT; a positive sputum culture without clinical infection does not automatically merit treatment.

questions.question: Which statement about suspected Clostridium difficile infection (CDI) is supported by the excerpt?
options: A positive sputum culture is the preferred diagnostic test
Faecal toxin testing by enzyme immunoassay or toxin-gene PCR can establish the diagnosis
Diagnosis is made only by identifying organisms in urine
Clinical improvement after antibiotics is the specified diagnostic test
questions.explanation: The excerpt identifies detection of faecal toxins by enzyme immunoassay and PCR detection of toxin genes as diagnostic approaches.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012); Chapter 4, Infections and antibiotics; PDF page 66, printed page 53.
questions.sourceEvidence: CDI diagnosis is based on toxin detection in faeces by enzyme immunoassay or, with greater sensitivity and specificity, PCR detection of toxin genes.

questions.question: For CDI treatment, which pairing matches the excerpt's recommendations by severity?
options: Oral metronidazole for mild-to-moderate disease; oral vancomycin for severe disease
Oral vancomycin for mild-to-moderate disease; oral metronidazole for severe disease
Fluconazole for mild-to-moderate disease; caspofungin for severe disease
Ciprofloxacin for mild-to-moderate disease; gentamicin for severe disease
questions.explanation: The excerpt specifies oral metronidazole for mild or moderate CDI and notes better response to oral vancomycin in severe disease.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012); Chapter 4, Infections and antibiotics; PDF page 66, printed page 53.
questions.sourceEvidence: Mild-to-moderate CDI is treated with oral metronidazole, whereas severe disease responds better to oral vancomycin.

questions.question: For a diabetic foot ulcer, which sample does the excerpt identify as most useful for microbiological diagnosis?
options: A surface swab of the ulcer alone
A urine sample collected from the patient
A sputum specimen collected before antibiotics
questions.explanation: Tissue and bone samples best support microbiological diagnosis in diabetic foot infection; surface swabs mainly identify colonizing organisms.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012); Chapter 4, Infections and antibiotics; PDF page 67, printed page 54.
questions.sourceEvidence: For diabetic foot infection, tissue and bone biopsy cultures are preferred because surface swabs indicate organisms colonizing the wound or ulcer.

questions.question: What clinical pattern does the excerpt describe as characteristic of progressing necrotizing fasciitis?
options: A painless superficial rash with no systemic features throughout
Isolated urinary frequency followed by sterile urine
Severe pain and systemic toxicity, with skin that may initially appear deceptively normal
A chronic cough with a positive sputum culture but no clinical signs
questions.explanation: The infection can begin after minor trauma, with a febrile, toxic patient in severe pain; early skin appearance can underestimate the underlying disease.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012); Chapter 4, Infections and antibiotics; PDF page 67, printed page 54.
questions.sourceEvidence: Necrotizing fasciitis may cause fever, toxicity, and severe pain while the overlying skin initially appears deceptively normal, later developing oedema, discoloration, and crepitus.

questions.question: What is the essential immediate surgical management described for necrotizing fasciitis?
options: Observation until antibiotics alone have controlled the infection
Superficial swabbing followed by delayed treatment only if cultures are positive
Urgent debridement of all necrotic tissue, sometimes requiring repeated operations
Device removal without debridement of affected tissue
questions.explanation: Necrotic tissue must be excised urgently; the excerpt notes that patients may need several trips to theatre, with antimicrobial therapy as an adjunct.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012); Chapter 4, Infections and antibiotics; PDF page 67, printed page 54.
questions.sourceEvidence: Urgent surgical debridement of all necrotic tissue is essential in necrotizing fasciitis, and more than one operation may be required.

questions.question: Which finding supports a diagnosis of osteomyelitis in a patient with diabetic foot infection, according to the excerpt?
options: A surface swab identifying colonizing organisms
A positive urine culture without urinary symptoms
A chest X-ray showing no respiratory infection
An abnormality assessed using plain X-rays or MRI
questions.explanation: The excerpt names plain radiographs and MRI as radiological investigations for osteomyelitis; a wound surface swab does not establish the causative organisms in tissue or bone.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012); Chapter 4, Infections and antibiotics; PDF page 67, printed page 54.
questions.sourceEvidence: Radiological investigation for osteomyelitis in diabetic foot infection includes plain X-rays and MRI.

questions.question: Which description best matches the excerpt’s definition of septic shock?
options: A localized infection with viable bacteria detected in the bloodstream
Systemic inflammatory response syndrome without confirmed or presumed infection
Sepsis accompanied by any single abnormal temperature, pulse, respiratory rate, or white-cell count
Sepsis with hypotension and/or tissue hypoperfusion persisting despite adequate fluid resuscitation
questions.explanation: The defining feature is sepsis-related hypotension and/or tissue hypoperfusion that persists despite adequate fluid resuscitation.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012); Chapter 1, Metabolic response to injury, fluid and electrolyte balance and shock; PDF page 31, printed page 18.
questions.sourceEvidence: The excerpt defines septic shock by sepsis-induced hypotension and/or tissue hypoperfusion that persists despite adequate fluid resuscitation.

questions.question: Which combination of findings is identified as evidence of tissue hypoperfusion in the excerpt’s septic-shock definition?
options: Warm peripheries or a raised pulse pressure
Fever or an increased white-cell count
questions.explanation: The text gives elevated lactate and oliguria as examples of tissue hypoperfusion in septic shock.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012); Chapter 1, Metabolic response to injury, fluid and electrolyte balance and shock; PDF page 31, printed page 18.
questions.sourceEvidence: The definition names elevated lactate and oliguria as examples of tissue hypoperfusion.

questions.question: According to the excerpt, what is the systemic response to infection called when SIRS occurs with confirmed or presumed infection?
questions.explanation: The excerpt defines sepsis as SIRS in the presence of confirmed or presumed infection; organ dysfunction and persistent hypoperfusion are separate qualifiers.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012); Chapter 1, Metabolic response to injury, fluid and electrolyte balance and shock; PDF page 32, printed page 19.
questions.sourceEvidence: Sepsis is described as the systemic response to infection, defined as SIRS with confirmed or presumed infection.

questions.question: Which two infection sites account for the largest stated proportions of infections leading to sepsis?
questions.explanation: The excerpt lists the lungs at 50–70% and the abdomen at 20–25%, ahead of the urinary tract and skin.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012); Chapter 1, Metabolic response to injury, fluid and electrolyte balance and shock; PDF page 31, printed page 18.
questions.sourceEvidence: The listed common infection sites are lungs (50–70%), abdomen (20–25%), urinary tract (7–10%), and skin.

questions.question: Which cellular signaling event is linked in the excerpt to the initial vasodilation of septic shock?
options: Cytokine-induced endothelial nitric oxide synthetase expression and nitric oxide production
Reduced endothelial nitric oxide synthetase expression and nitric oxide depletion
Catecholamine-mediated endothelial constriction and reduced nitric oxide production
Mitochondrial ATP excess and increased vascular smooth-muscle contraction
questions.explanation: Proinflammatory cytokines induce endothelial nitric oxide synthetase; nitric oxide relaxes vascular smooth muscle, lowering vascular resistance.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012); Chapter 1, Metabolic response to injury, fluid and electrolyte balance and shock; PDF page 33, printed page 20.
questions.sourceEvidence: TNF-α and IL-1β promote endothelial nitric oxide synthetase and nitric oxide production, causing smooth-muscle relaxation and vasodilation.

questions.question: What is the typical initial cardiovascular response to septic vasodilation described in the excerpt?
options: Reflex bradycardia and reduced stroke volume, lowering cardiac output
Reflex tachycardia and increased stroke volume, raising cardiac output
Reduced heart rate and increased systemic resistance, preserving cardiac output
Reduced stroke volume and reduced systemic resistance, lowering cardiac output
questions.explanation: The initial reflex response increases heart rate and stroke volume, which raises cardiac output to compensate for vasodilation.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012); Chapter 1, Metabolic response to injury, fluid and electrolyte balance and shock; PDF page 33, printed page 20.
questions.sourceEvidence: The initial cardiovascular response is reflex tachycardia plus increased stroke volume, resulting in increased cardiac output.

questions.question: Which bedside pattern is associated with the initial, higher-output phase of septic shock in the excerpt?
options: Pale, clammy peripheries, collapsed veins, and prolonged capillary refill
Warm, well-perfused peripheries, low diastolic pressure, and raised pulse pressure
Warm, dry peripheries, bradycardia, and profound hypotension
Cool, poorly perfused peripheries, narrow pulse pressure, and raised diastolic pressure
questions.explanation: The early vasodilated presentation is described by warm, well-perfused peripheries, low diastolic pressure, and raised pulse pressure.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012); Chapter 1, Metabolic response to injury, fluid and electrolyte balance and shock; PDF page 33, printed page 20.
questions.sourceEvidence: The excerpt associates the initial septic response with warm, well-perfused peripheries, low diastolic blood pressure, and raised pulse pressure.

questions.question: Why may a fit young patient appear relatively well compensated early in septic shock, according to the excerpt?
options: The patient’s cells remain unaffected until arterial pressure becomes severely low
The patient’s microcirculation necessarily maintains normal oxygen delivery to every cell
The patient’s cardiac output falls early, reducing tissue oxygen requirements
The patient may compensate for haemodynamic changes despite compromised cellular oxygen delivery and utilization
questions.explanation: The text notes that fit young patients may compensate relatively well for the cardiovascular changes even while cellular oxygen delivery and utilization are compromised.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012); Chapter 1, Metabolic response to injury, fluid and electrolyte balance and shock; PDF page 33, printed page 20.
questions.sourceEvidence: Fit young patients may compensate for these changes even though cellular oxygen delivery and utilization are compromised.

questions.question: Which progression helps explain why septic-shock signs can later resemble a low-output state?
options: Endothelial repair increases intravascular volume, while ventricular function raises cardiac output further
Endothelial dysfunction causes fluid extravasation and intravascular volume loss, while ventricular dysfunction limits the cardiac-output response
Reduced vascular permeability increases circulating volume, while stroke volume rises without limit
Loss of sympathetic tone causes bradycardia, while systemic resistance returns to normal
questions.explanation: Progressive endothelial leak reduces intravascular volume, and ventricular dysfunction impairs the compensatory rise in cardiac output; peripheral perfusion then falls.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012); Chapter 1, Metabolic response to injury, fluid and electrolyte balance and shock; PDF page 33, printed page 20.
questions.sourceEvidence: As septic shock progresses, endothelial dysfunction causes fluid extravasation and intravascular volume loss, and ventricular dysfunction impairs the cardiac-output increase.

questions.question: What microvascular flow pattern does the excerpt describe in septic shock?
options: Fewer small vessels with uniformly continuous flow
More small vessels with absent or intermittent flow
More small vessels with uniformly continuous flow
Fewer small vessels with absent or intermittent flow
questions.explanation: The figure description states that septic shock increases the number of small vessels with absent or intermittent flow, illustrating heterogeneous microcirculatory perfusion.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012); Chapter 1, Metabolic response to injury, fluid and electrolyte balance and shock; PDF page 33, printed page 20.
questions.sourceEvidence: The septic-shock microcirculation is described as having increased numbers of small vessels with absent or intermittent flow.

questions.question: How can oxygen delivery increase globally while cellular oxygen supply remains impaired in septic shock?
options: Increased arterial oxygen content prevents oxygen from reaching the microcirculation
Low cardiac output uniformly reduces oxygen delivery to all tissues during the initial phase
Microcirculatory dysfunction disrupts effective oxygen delivery to cells despite a global increase in delivery
Increased oxygen extraction blocks oxygen delivery by raising systemic vascular resistance
questions.explanation: The excerpt distinguishes global oxygen delivery from its effective distribution: microcirculatory dysfunction can impair delivery at the cellular level despite increased overall delivery.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012); Chapter 1, Metabolic response to injury, fluid and electrolyte balance and shock; PDF page 31, printed page 18.
questions.sourceEvidence: Despite a global increase in oxygen delivery, microcirculatory dysfunction impairs oxygen delivery to cells.

questions.question: Which microvascular mechanism in sepsis is specifically linked to pathological arterio-venous shunting?
options: Down-regulated inducible nitric oxide synthetase and increased smooth-muscle adrenergic sensitivity
Up-regulated inducible nitric oxide synthetase and reduced smooth-muscle adrenergic sensitivity
Reduced endothelial activation and increased capillary barrier integrity
Increased red-cell deformability and reduced platelet aggregation
questions.explanation: The excerpt links increased inducible nitric oxide synthetase and loss of adrenergic sensitivity in smooth muscle to pathological shunting.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012); Chapter 1, Metabolic response to injury, fluid and electrolyte balance and shock; PDF page 33, printed page 20.
questions.sourceEvidence: Sepsis up-regulates inducible nitric oxide synthetase, and smooth muscle loses adrenergic sensitivity, producing pathological arterio-venous shunting.

questions.question: How does septic microvascular activation contribute to microthrombus formation, according to the excerpt?
options: Endothelial and inflammatory-cell activation disrupts the barrier and widely activates coagulation, allowing microthrombi to obstruct capillary flow
Endothelial quiescence restores barrier function and suppresses coagulation, preventing capillary flow
Reduced inflammatory-cell activity increases red-cell flexibility and removes capillary obstruction
Increased capillary flow dissolves platelet aggregates before coagulation is activated
questions.explanation: Barrier disruption and widespread coagulation activation promote microthrombi, which can occlude capillary flow; platelet and coagulation-factor consumption follows.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012); Chapter 1, Metabolic response to injury, fluid and electrolyte balance and shock; PDF page 33, printed page 20.
questions.sourceEvidence: Endothelial and inflammatory-cell activation disrupts microvascular barrier function and activates coagulation; microthrombi can occlude capillaries.

questions.question: What cellular mechanism is described as a cause of lactate accumulation in septic shock, beyond impaired oxygen delivery?
options: Increased glycolysis and pyruvate generation combined with pyruvate dehydrogenase dysfunction
Reduced glycolysis and pyruvate generation combined with increased pyruvate dehydrogenase activity
Increased oxidative phosphorylation combined with accelerated pyruvate entry into the Krebs cycle
Reduced sympathetic activity combined with decreased pyruvate production
questions.explanation: The text explains that sympathetic stimulation increases glycolysis and pyruvate generation, while pyruvate dehydrogenase dysfunction contributes to pyruvate and lactate accumulation.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012); Chapter 1, Metabolic response to injury, fluid and electrolyte balance and shock; PDF page 34, printed page 21.
questions.sourceEvidence: In sepsis, increased sympathetic activity raises glycolysis and pyruvate generation; pyruvate dehydrogenase dysfunction contributes to pyruvate and lactate accumulation.

questions.question: What does the term “cytopathic shock” refer to in the excerpt?
options: Sepsis-associated increase in mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation and ATP production
Sepsis-associated isolated reduction in cardiac output without cellular dysfunction
Sepsis-associated mitochondrial dysfunction with marked inhibition of oxidative phosphorylation
Sepsis-associated increase in oxygen extraction with fully preserved cellular metabolism
questions.explanation: The excerpt uses “cytopathic shock” for the cellular energy-utilization problem characterized by mitochondrial dysfunction and inhibited oxidative phosphorylation.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012); Chapter 1, Metabolic response to injury, fluid and electrolyte balance and shock; PDF page 34, printed page 21.
questions.sourceEvidence: The text describes septic mitochondrial dysfunction and marked inhibition of oxidative phosphorylation as ‘cytopathic shock.’

questions.question: Which neurologic complication is noted as potentially complicating the clinical picture of septic shock?
options: Loss of cardiac accelerator fibres and anhidrosis
Progressive peripheral neuropathy with absent reflexes
Isolated cerebral infarction from arterial embolism
questions.explanation: The excerpt specifically notes that septic encephalopathy and delirium can complicate the neurologic presentation of septic shock.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012); Chapter 1, Metabolic response to injury, fluid and electrolyte balance and shock; PDF page 35, printed page 22.
questions.sourceEvidence: In septic shock, the clinical picture may be complicated by septic encephalopathy and/or delirium.

questions.question: Which set of principles does principalism use to assess possible actions in an ethical dilemma?
options: Beneficence, capacity, consent, and professional integrity
questions.explanation: The excerpt identifies these four principles as the framework used by principalism.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 5: Ethics, preoperative considerations, anaesthesia and analgesia, PDF p. 69 (printed p. 56).
questions.sourceEvidence: Principalism assesses ethical actions against autonomy, beneficence, non-malfeasance, and justice.

questions.question: A competent patient refuses a life-saving blood transfusion because of strongly held beliefs. According to the excerpt, what should the surgeon do?
options: Override the refusal whenever the treatment could save life
Delay the decision until the patient accepts the recommended treatment
Provide the transfusion if the surgeon judges it to be in the patient's best interests
Uphold the refusal, even if the treating team considers it unwise
questions.explanation: Respect for autonomy means a competent patient's informed refusal is upheld, even when clinicians disagree.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 5: Ethics, preoperative considerations, anaesthesia and analgesia, PDF p. 70 (printed p. 57).
questions.sourceEvidence: The text says a competent patient's refusal of a life-saving transfusion based on strongly held beliefs should be upheld.

questions.question: How does the excerpt describe reaching a decision about which course of action will do the most good for a patient?
options: Through discussion between patient and surgeon, taking preferences and medical advice into account
By relying solely on the surgeon's historical judgement of the patient's best interest
By following the patient's preference without considering medical advice
By selecting the least expensive option regardless of patient preference
questions.explanation: Beneficence is framed as a shared decision that considers both the patient's preferences and clinical advice.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 5: Ethics, preoperative considerations, anaesthesia and analgesia, PDF p. 70 (printed p. 57).
questions.sourceEvidence: The text contrasts historical surgeon-led judgements with agreement after discussion that considers patient preferences and medical advice.

questions.question: When does a treatment with inherent risks avoid violating non-malfeasance, as described in the excerpt?
options: Whenever the surgeon believes the potential benefit outweighs the risk, regardless of consent
Only when the treatment has no possible complications
When its risk is proportionate to its potential benefit from the competent patient's perspective and consent follows reasonable information
Whenever a patient signs a form, regardless of the information provided
questions.explanation: The excerpt allows treatment risks when proportionate to potential benefit and accepted by a competent patient on a reasonable information basis.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 5: Ethics, preoperative considerations, anaesthesia and analgesia, PDF p. 70 (printed p. 57).
questions.sourceEvidence: Non-malfeasance is not violated when risk is proportionate to potential benefit for the competent patient and consent is based on reasonable information.

questions.question: Which statement best describes the limit of patient autonomy in relation to treatment?
options: Autonomy requires the surgeon to provide any treatment a patient requests.
A surgeon may impose treatment whenever the patient’s choice seems unwise.
Autonomy applies only when the patient agrees with the surgeon’s recommendation.
A competent patient may refuse treatment, but autonomy does not give a right to demand treatment.
questions.explanation: The source explains that autonomy respects an individual's choices and beliefs, while explicitly stating that it does not give the patient a right to treatment on demand.
questions.sourceEvidence: Autonomy respects the individual's right to opinions, make choices and act on personal values and beliefs ... Autonomy does not, however, give the patient the right to treatment on demand.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 5, PDF p. 70 (printed p. 57).

questions.question: When prioritizing individual patients for a limited surgical resource, which basis does the source identify as appropriate?
options: Clinical grounds, such as threat to life or degree of pain.
The patient’s social status and ability to advocate for themselves.
A first-come, first-served rule in every circumstance.
The patient’s age or religious beliefs.
questions.explanation: For individual prioritization, the text gives clinical need—including threat to life or degree of pain—as examples of grounds for allocating resources.
questions.sourceEvidence: The focus for the surgeon is more likely to involve individual patients and how their interests should be prioritized ... Resources may be allocated on clinical grounds such as threat to life or degree of pain.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 5, PDF p. 70 (printed p. 57).

questions.question: In multidisciplinary team working, what information may be shared with a third party to enable treatment?
options: Only information necessary to enable the third party’s treatment.
The patient’s complete record, regardless of relevance.
Any information requested by a colleague, even if unrelated to care.
No information under any circumstances, including protection of others.
questions.explanation: Confidentiality is central, but the source permits and expects limited disclosure where needed for treatment; only necessary information should be divulged. It also notes exceptions for protecting others, such as notifiable diseases.
questions.sourceEvidence: There are exceptions where confidentiality can and should be breached for the protection of others (e.g. notifiable diseases such as tuberculosis). In the context of multidisciplinary team working, only information necessary to enable treatment by a third party should be divulged.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 5, PDF p. 72 (printed p. 59).

questions.question: What should a doctor do if they have good reason to believe that they or a colleague may be putting patients at risk?
options: Wait until a patient has been harmed before raising the concern.
Discuss it informally only if the colleague asks for feedback.
Keep the concern confidential and take no action.
questions.explanation: The listed duties of a doctor include acting without delay when there is good reason to believe that the doctor or a colleague may be putting patients at risk.
questions.sourceEvidence: Be honest and open and act with integrity ... Act without delay if you have good reason to believe that you or a colleague may be putting patients at risk.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 5, PDF p. 70 (printed p. 57).

questions.question: Which statement reflects a doctor's professional accountability?
options: A doctor is personally accountable for professional practice and must be prepared to justify decisions and actions.
Responsibility for decisions rests solely with the employing institution.
Only decisions that cause harm need to be justified.
Professional accountability ends when a decision is delegated.
questions.explanation: The source expressly states that doctors are personally accountable for their professional practice and must always be prepared to justify their decisions and actions.
questions.sourceEvidence: You are personally accountable for your professional practice and must always be prepared to justify your decisions and actions.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 5, PDF p. 70 (printed p. 57).

questions.question: When treating a patient who lacks capacity, what approach to decision-making does the excerpt recommend?
options: Base the decision only on the surgeon's personal values and proceed without consultation
Ask the closest relative to decide without considering the patient's previously expressed wishes
Defer all treatment decisions until the patient regains capacity, regardless of urgency
Consider the patient's known beliefs, preferences and advance directives, involve relevant people, and decide in the patient's best interests while preserving future options
questions.explanation: The text calls for decisions grounded in the patient's known wishes and beliefs, inclusive of relevant parties, and made in the patient's best interests while maximizing future options.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 5: Ethics, preoperative considerations, anaesthesia and analgesia, PDF p. 72 (printed p. 59).
questions.sourceEvidence: Decision-making should take account of the patient's beliefs, preferences, and advance directives and relevant others, with decisions in the patient's best interests that maximize future options.

questions.question: Which combination of abilities defines capacity to consent in the excerpt?
options: Recall every prior treatment, compare costs, and sign a written form
Understand the diagnosis, accept the surgeon's recommendation, and attend follow-up
Understand and retain information, weigh the options' implications, and communicate a decision
Express a preference, have no mental illness, and agree to treatment
questions.explanation: The excerpt specifies understanding and retention, weighing implications including risks and benefits, and communicating the decision.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 5, Ethics, preoperative considerations, anaesthesia and analgesia, PDF p. 71 (printed p. 58).
questions.sourceEvidence: Capacity is present when the patient can understand and retain presented information, weigh the options' implications, and communicate a decision.

questions.question: For which group should capacity generally be presumed unless there is evidence to the contrary?
options: All patients who have undergone surgery before
All adults accompanied by a relative
All patients who agree with the proposed treatment
questions.explanation: The text says capacity should be assumed for conscious adults unless there is contrary evidence.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 5, Ethics, preoperative considerations, anaesthesia and analgesia, PDF p. 71 (printed p. 58).
questions.sourceEvidence: Capacity is to be presumed for conscious adults unless evidence indicates otherwise.

questions.question: According to the excerpt, what is the best practice when a patient lacks sufficient English for the consent process?
options: Ask a family member to interpret as the standard approach
Proceed using written English information alone
Defer all discussion until the patient learns English
questions.explanation: The passage expressly identifies an official translator as best practice rather than relying on an informal interpreter.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 5, Ethics, preoperative considerations, anaesthesia and analgesia, PDF p. 71 (printed p. 58).
questions.sourceEvidence: Where English is insufficient, the excerpt recommends an official translator; written information should be in the appropriate language where possible.

questions.question: When may responsibility for obtaining consent be delegated by the surgeon performing the procedure?
options: When the delegate is suitably trained and qualified, knows the procedure and its risks, and understands the consent process
Whenever the delegate is available, regardless of their knowledge of the procedure
Only when the delegate is a family member chosen by the patient
Only when the patient has already signed a consent form
questions.explanation: The text allows delegation if the person meets all three listed requirements concerning qualifications, procedure knowledge, and understanding of consent.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 5, Ethics, preoperative considerations, anaesthesia and analgesia, PDF p. 71 (printed p. 58).
questions.sourceEvidence: A delegate must be suitably trained and qualified, sufficiently knowledgeable about the procedure including risks, and understand the consent process.

questions.question: Which set of information does the excerpt say should be explained when presenting treatment options?
options: Only the recommended treatment's likely benefits and expected duration
Only common minor complications, excluding serious rare outcomes
The surgeon's preferred option without alternatives
No treatment as an option, with risks, side effects, potential benefits and burdens, and the possibility of failure
questions.explanation: The passage requires detailing all options, including no treatment, and the relevant risks, side effects, benefits, burdens, and chance of unsuccessful treatment.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 5, Ethics, preoperative considerations, anaesthesia and analgesia, PDF p. 71 (printed p. 58).
questions.sourceEvidence: Information should cover every treatment option including no treatment, alongside risks, side effects, potential benefits and burdens, and treatment failure risk.

questions.question: How should serious adverse outcomes be handled in consent discussions, according to the excerpt?
options: Discuss only serious outcomes that are statistically common
Omit rare serious outcomes if minor complications are explained
Mention serious outcomes only after the patient has agreed to treatment
Discuss all potential serious adverse outcomes, however rare, as well as more frequent minor complications
questions.explanation: The excerpt explicitly says all potential serious adverse outcomes should be discussed regardless of rarity, alongside more frequent minor complications.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 5, Ethics, preoperative considerations, anaesthesia and analgesia, PDF p. 71 (printed p. 58).
questions.sourceEvidence: The consent discussion should include every potential serious adverse outcome, however rare, and the more frequent minor complications.

questions.question: Under what condition may information requested to be withheld be withheld under the passage's description of therapeutic privilege?
options: Whenever disclosure could make the patient anxious
When serious psychological harm might result, not merely because the patient may be upset or refuse treatment
Whenever the surgeon believes the patient will reject the recommendation
Whenever a relative asks that the information be kept from the patient
questions.explanation: Therapeutic privilege is described narrowly: serious psychological harm must be a concern; anticipated upset or refusal alone is insufficient.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 5, Ethics, preoperative considerations, anaesthesia and analgesia, PDF p. 71 (printed p. 58).
questions.sourceEvidence: Information may be withheld on this basis only where serious psychological harm might ensue, not simply because the patient may be upset or refuse treatment.

questions.question: Which statement accurately distinguishes implied and explicit consent in the excerpt?
options: Implied consent is required for all procedures, while explicit consent is limited to research
Implied consent may suffice for routine negligible-risk interventions through cooperation; most interventions require explicit consent, oral or written
Written explicit consent is legally required for every procedure
Oral consent is never considered explicit consent
questions.explanation: The passage gives cooperative participation in a routine, negligible-risk intervention as implied consent, while most interventions need explicit consent, which may be oral or written.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 5, Ethics, preoperative considerations, anaesthesia and analgesia, PDF p. 71 (printed p. 58).
questions.sourceEvidence: Cooperation can imply consent for routine interventions with negligible risks; most interventions require explicit consent, either oral or written.

questions.question: According to the excerpt's UK-specific statement, for which treatments is written consent a legal requirement?
questions.explanation: Although written consent is obtained for most procedures, the text identifies organ donation and fertility treatment as the legal requirements in the UK.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 5, Ethics, preoperative considerations, anaesthesia and analgesia, PDF p. 71 (printed p. 58).
questions.sourceEvidence: The excerpt states that written consent is legally required in the UK for organ donation and fertility treatment.

questions.question: What should happen if a translator reads written information to a patient because an appropriate-language version is unavailable?
options: The patient should sign immediately, with questions deferred until after treatment
A family member should replace the translator for questions
The patient should have an opportunity to ask questions through the translator, and the process should be documented in the medical record
The reading need not be recorded if the patient appears to understand
questions.explanation: The passage provides for questions through the translator and says the medical record should clearly document that the process occurred.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 5, Ethics, preoperative considerations, anaesthesia and analgesia, PDF p. 71 (printed p. 58).
questions.sourceEvidence: If written information in the appropriate language is unavailable, the translator should read it aloud; the patient can ask questions through the translator and the record should document the process.

questions.question: What emotional response is common among women presenting with breast lumps?
options: Only women with proven malignancy are distressed
Distress is described as uncommon before treatment
questions.explanation: The passage states that most women presenting with breast lumps are emotionally distressed.
questions.sourceEvidence: Most women who present with breast lumps are emotionally distressed.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 19: The Breast, Psychological aspects, PDF p. 333 (printed p. 320)

questions.question: When beginning a conversation to break bad news, what should the doctor first explore?
options: The patient's perception of what is wrong
questions.explanation: The passage identifies checking the patient's perception of what is wrong as the first step.
questions.sourceEvidence: The first step in breaking bad news is to check the patient's perception of what is wrong.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 19: The Breast, Psychological aspects, PDF p. 333 (printed p. 320)

questions.question: Approximately what proportion of patients with breast cancer already suspect that their lump is malignant?
questions.explanation: The passage says almost two-thirds of patients with breast cancer already suspect malignancy.
questions.sourceEvidence: Almost two-thirds of patients with breast cancer already suspect their lump is malignant.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 19: The Breast, Psychological aspects, PDF p. 333 (printed p. 320)

questions.question: For a patient with proven breast malignancy, what is the doctor's role in communicating the diagnosis?
options: Ask a nurse counsellor to make the diagnosis
Wait until the patient independently identifies the disease
questions.explanation: For patients with proven malignancy, the passage says the doctor's role is to confirm it.
questions.sourceEvidence: For proven malignancy, the doctor confirms the diagnosis.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 19: The Breast, Psychological aspects, PDF p. 333 (printed p. 320)

questions.question: After confirming proven breast cancer, which approach is described in the passage?
options: Pause to allow the patient to take in the news
Continue immediately with a detailed treatment discussion
Change the subject to the patient's surgical options
Ask the patient to leave and return after reading written information
questions.explanation: The passage advises confirming the diagnosis and pausing so the patient can absorb it.
questions.sourceEvidence: After confirming the diagnosis, allow a pause for the patient to absorb the news.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 19: The Breast, Psychological aspects, PDF p. 333 (printed p. 320)

questions.question: When a patient shows distress after a confirmed diagnosis, what should the doctor do according to the passage?
options: Reassure the patient that there is no reason to feel distressed
Acknowledge the distress and establish which concerns contribute to it
Defer discussing concerns until after surgery
Focus only on explaining the treatment plan
questions.explanation: The passage recommends acknowledging distress and identifying the concerns contributing to it.
questions.sourceEvidence: The doctor should acknowledge distress and establish the concerns contributing to it.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 19: The Breast, Psychological aspects, PDF p. 333 (printed p. 320)

questions.question: How should the doctor adjust the pace when a patient is unaware that she has cancer?
questions.explanation: The passage specifically says to break the news more slowly when the patient is unaware that she has cancer.
questions.sourceEvidence: If the patient is unaware that she has cancer, the doctor should communicate the news more slowly.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 19: The Breast, Psychological aspects, PDF p. 333 (printed p. 320)

questions.question: Which set of functions is attributed to specialist nurse counsellors in breast units?
options: Confirm malignancy, select the operation, and prescribe adjuvant therapy
Explain the disease and its treatment, advise on post-surgical prostheses, and help identify and support patients with significant psychiatric problems
Provide radiotherapy, assess tumour response, and arrange reconstructive surgery
Replace the doctor in communicating every diagnosis and determine whether treatment is needed
questions.explanation: Nurse counsellors help patients understand the disease and treatment, advise about prostheses after surgery, and help recognize and support significant psychiatric problems.
questions.sourceEvidence: Nurse counsellors inform patients about the disease and treatment, advise on prostheses after surgery, and help recognize and support significant psychiatric problems.
questions.sourceRef: Principles & Practice of Surgery: With Student Consult Online, 6th ed. (2012), Chapter 19: The Breast, Psychological aspects, PDF p. 333 (printed p. 320)
